modules.title: SQL Commands and Categories
modules.goal: Classify SQL commands and use the right one safely.

topics.title: What Are SQL Commands?
topics.simple: SQL command ek instruction hai jo database ko kuch karne bolta hai — data laana, badalna, structure banana ya permission dena.
topics.pro: An SQL command is a statement the server parses and executes; commands are grouped by intent such as defining structure, manipulating rows, querying, controlling access or managing transactions.
points: A statement ends with a semicolon.
The command category describes its job, not its difficulty.
PostgreSQL also has utility commands such as EXPLAIN and VACUUM.

example.sql: SELECT 1 AS ready;

topics.title: DDL — Data Definition Language
topics.simple: DDL structure define karta hai — table, schema, index, view.
topics.pro: DDL defines and changes database objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, COMMENT and RENAME.
points: DDL changes the schema, not individual row values.
In PostgreSQL, most DDL is transactional.
DDL takes locks that can block concurrent work.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: DML — Data Manipulation Language
topics.simple: DML rows ke data ko badalta hai — insert, update, delete.
topics.pro: DML changes row data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE; it is transactional and can be filtered with WHERE.
points: DML works inside the table structure.
Every DML statement can be rolled back in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Aarav');

topics.title: DQL — Data Query Language
topics.simple: DQL data padhne ke liye hai — mainly SELECT.
topics.pro: DQL reads data without changing it; SELECT is the core DQL statement, including joins, aggregates and window functions.
points: Some curricula fold DQL into DML; both names describe SELECT.
SELECT can call functions and use CTEs.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: DCL — Data Control Language
topics.simple: DCL permissions deta aur hataata hai — GRANT aur REVOKE.
topics.pro: DCL manages privileges and access: GRANT and REVOKE on databases, schemas, tables, sequences and functions.
points: Roles are the subjects of privileges.
GRANT and REVOKE are transactional in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON students TO analyst;

topics.title: TCL — Transaction Control Language
topics.simple: TCL transaction ko control karta hai — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
topics.pro: TCL groups statements into atomic units: BEGIN/START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.
points: A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
An error aborts the transaction until rollback.

topics.title: CREATE
topics.simple: CREATE naya object banata hai — database, schema, table, view, index, role.
topics.pro: CREATE defines a new database object with its columns, constraints, options and owner.
points: CREATE TABLE needs column names and types.
Use IF NOT EXISTS when re-running scripts.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: ALTER
topics.simple: ALTER existing object ki definition badalta hai — column add, type change, constraint add.
topics.pro: ALTER modifies an existing object; ALTER TABLE can add/drop columns, change types, rename objects and manage constraints.
points: Some changes rewrite the table and take time.
Use USING when a type change needs an explicit cast.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;

topics.title: DROP
topics.simple: DROP object ko poora hata deta hai — structure, data aur uske dependents.
topics.pro: DROP removes an object and its data; DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, DROP INDEX, DROP SCHEMA and DROP DATABASE are DDL.
points: DROP is destructive and usually irreversible.
Use IF EXISTS for idempotent scripts.
CASCADE also drops dependent objects; use it deliberately.

example.sql: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS students;

topics.title: TRUNCATE
topics.simple: TRUNCATE table ke saare rows jaldi hata deta hai, table structure rehta hai.
topics.pro: TRUNCATE removes every row from a table in one operation, resets storage, keeps the table and is transactional in PostgreSQL.
points: It does not fire row-level DELETE triggers.

example.sql: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

topics.title: SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT data padhta hai — columns, rows aur expressions.
topics.pro: SELECT projects columns and filters rows; it is DQL and the most common read command.
points: SELECT does not change stored rows.
ORDER BY and LIMIT shape the result.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: INSERT
topics.simple: INSERT table me naye rows add karta hai.
topics.pro: INSERT adds one or more rows; RETURNING returns generated values such as identity ids.
points: INSERT ... SELECT copies rows from a query.
A failed INSERT does not add a partial row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Meera') RETURNING id;

topics.title: UPDATE
topics.simple: UPDATE existing rows ke values badalta hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE changes column values for rows matched by WHERE; without WHERE every row is updated.
points: Always test the WHERE with SELECT first.
An UPDATE can fire row-level triggers.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav Sharma' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name;

topics.title: DELETE
topics.simple: DELETE selected rows ko hataata hai, structure rehta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE removes rows matched by WHERE; without WHERE every row is deleted.
points: DELETE can be filtered and rolled back.
It does not reset identity sequences.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 2 RETURNING id;

topics.title: GRANT
topics.simple: GRANT role ko permission deta hai — read, write, execute.
topics.pro: GRANT gives privileges on objects to roles; privileges include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, USAGE and EXECUTE.
points: Schema USAGE is often required before table access.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON students TO analyst;

topics.title: REVOKE
topics.simple: REVOKE di hui permission wapas leta hai.
topics.pro: REVOKE removes privileges from roles; CASCADE also revokes dependent grants, RESTRICT refuses if dependents exist.
points: REVOKE ALL removes every privilege on the object.

example.sql: REVOKE INSERT ON students FROM analyst;

topics.title: COMMIT
topics.simple: COMMIT transaction ke changes ko permanent karta hai.
topics.pro: COMMIT ends the transaction and makes its changes durable and visible to other sessions.
points: Commit only when the unit is complete.
An aborted transaction cannot be committed.

topics.title: ROLLBACK
topics.simple: ROLLBACK transaction ke uncommitted changes ko undo karta hai.
topics.pro: ROLLBACK aborts the current transaction and discards its changes; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after that savepoint.
points: An error puts the transaction in a failed state.
DROP DATABASE cannot be rolled back because it cannot run in a transaction.

topics.title: Command Differences and Classification
topics.simple: Har command ka category alag hai; same result alag commands se aa sakta hai, par risk aur locking alag hoti hai.
topics.pro: Classify commands by intent: DDL changes structure, DML changes rows, DQL reads, DCL controls access and TCL controls transactions; some commands are utility commands outside the five groups.
points: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP differ in scope and recovery.
TRUNCATE is commonly grouped with DDL but is transactional in PostgreSQL.
SELECT is DQL even though some teams call it DML.

example.output:
DDL | CREATE TABLE
DML | INSERT
DQL | SELECT

topics.title: Practical Command Classification
topics.simple: Practice me command dekho aur bolo — structure, data, read, permission ya transaction.
topics.pro: In practice, read the verb and the target: CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE are DDL, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE are DML, SELECT is DQL, GRANT/REVOKE are DCL and BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT are TCL.
points: EXPLAIN, VACUUM, ANALYZE and COPY are utility commands.
The category guides review, permissions and rollback planning.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;
example.output: Utility command: shows the query plan.

learn.q: Which category does CREATE TABLE belong to?
options: DDL
DML
DQL
DCL
learn.answer: DDL
learn.why: CREATE defines schema objects, which is DDL.

learn.q: Which category does INSERT belong to?
options: DML
DDL
DQL
TCL
learn.answer: DML
learn.why: INSERT changes row data, which is DML.

learn.q: Which category does SELECT belong to?
options: DQL
DML
DDL
DCL
learn.answer: DQL
learn.why: SELECT reads data; many curricula name that DQL.

learn.q: Which category does GRANT belong to?
options: DCL
DDL
DML
TCL
learn.answer: DCL
learn.why: GRANT controls privileges, which is DCL.

learn.q: Which category does COMMIT belong to?
options: TCL
DCL
DDL
DQL
learn.answer: TCL
learn.why: COMMIT ends a transaction, which is TCL.

learn.q: Which command removes all rows but keeps the table?
options: TRUNCATE
DROP
DELETE
ALTER
learn.answer: TRUNCATE
learn.why: TRUNCATE removes rows and keeps the table definition.

learn.q: Which command removes the table structure and its data?
options: DROP TABLE
TRUNCATE TABLE
DELETE FROM
ALTER TABLE
learn.answer: DROP TABLE
learn.why: DROP removes the object itself.

learn.q: Which command adds a column to an existing table?
options: ALTER TABLE
CREATE TABLE
UPDATE
INSERT
learn.answer: ALTER TABLE
learn.why: ALTER changes an existing table definition.

learn.q: Which command can use a WHERE clause?
options: DELETE
TRUNCATE
DROP
CREATE
learn.answer: DELETE
learn.why: DELETE supports WHERE; TRUNCATE does not.

learn.q: Which command fires row-level DELETE triggers?
options: DELETE
TRUNCATE
DROP
ALTER
learn.answer: DELETE
learn.why: DELETE removes rows one by one and fires row triggers; TRUNCATE does not.

learn.q: Which command gives a role read access?
options: GRANT SELECT
REVOKE SELECT
COMMIT
ALTER
learn.answer: GRANT SELECT
learn.why: GRANT adds a privilege to a role.

learn.q: Which command removes a privilege?
options: REVOKE
GRANT
DROP
ROLLBACK
learn.answer: REVOKE
learn.why: REVOKE takes a privilege away.

learn.q: Which command makes transaction changes durable?
options: COMMIT
ROLLBACK
BEGIN
SAVEPOINT
learn.answer: COMMIT
learn.why: COMMIT ends the transaction and persists its changes.

learn.q: Which command undoes uncommitted changes?
options: ROLLBACK
COMMIT
GRANT
TRUNCATE
learn.answer: ROLLBACK
learn.why: ROLLBACK aborts the transaction.

learn.q: Which command starts a transaction in PostgreSQL?
options: BEGIN
START
OPEN
COMMIT
learn.answer: BEGIN
learn.why: BEGIN or START TRANSACTION starts a transaction.

learn.q: Which command is DDL?
options: TRUNCATE
INSERT
SELECT
GRANT
learn.answer: TRUNCATE
learn.why: TRUNCATE is commonly grouped with DDL because it resets table storage.

learn.q: Which command is DML?
options: MERGE
CREATE
REVOKE
COMMIT
learn.answer: MERGE
learn.why: MERGE inserts, updates or deletes rows, so it is DML.

learn.q: Which command is a utility command, not DML?
options: EXPLAIN
UPDATE
DELETE
INSERT
learn.answer: EXPLAIN
learn.why: EXPLAIN reports a plan and does not change rows.

learn.q: Which statement is true about TRUNCATE in PostgreSQL?
options: It can be rolled back
It automatically commits
It accepts WHERE
It fires row DELETE triggers
learn.answer: It can be rolled back
learn.why: PostgreSQL TRUNCATE is transactional, unlike MySQL where it causes an implicit commit.

learn.q: What happens to an UPDATE without WHERE?
options: Every row is updated
No row is updated
Only the first row is updated
The statement fails
learn.answer: Every row is updated
learn.why: Without a WHERE predicate, UPDATE targets the whole table.

interview.q: What are the five common SQL command categories?
interview.answer: DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL. Utility commands such as EXPLAIN and VACUUM sit outside those five.

interview.q: What is DDL?
interview.answer: Data Definition Language defines and changes schema objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, COMMENT and RENAME.

interview.q: What is DML?
interview.answer: Data Manipulation Language changes row data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.

interview.q: Is SELECT DML or DQL?
interview.answer: It is DQL in the five-category model. Some teams call it DML because it operates on data, but it does not modify rows.

interview.q: What is DCL?
interview.answer: Data Control Language manages privileges: GRANT and REVOKE.

interview.q: What is TCL?
interview.answer: Transaction Control Language manages transactions: BEGIN/START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.

interview.q: What is the difference between CREATE and ALTER?
interview.answer: CREATE makes a new object; ALTER changes an existing object definition.

interview.q: What is the difference between DROP and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DROP removes the object and its data; TRUNCATE removes every row but keeps the table definition.

interview.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DELETE can filter with WHERE, fires row triggers and is row-by-row; TRUNCATE removes all rows in one operation, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and resets storage.

interview.q: Is TRUNCATE transactional in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Yes. It can be rolled back in PostgreSQL. In MySQL, TRUNCATE causes an implicit commit.

interview.q: Does DELETE reset an identity sequence?
interview.answer: No. DELETE leaves the sequence alone; TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY resets it.

interview.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE dangerous?
interview.answer: It updates every row in the table. Test the predicate with SELECT and use a transaction.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: It returns rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in the same statement, including generated ids.

interview.q: What is the difference between GRANT and REVOKE?
interview.answer: GRANT gives privileges to a role; REVOKE removes them.

interview.q: Why is schema USAGE needed before table access?
interview.answer: Object names live in a schema. A role needs USAGE on the schema and a privilege on the table to query it.

interview.q: What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?
interview.answer: COMMIT makes transaction changes durable; ROLLBACK discards them.

interview.q: What is a SAVEPOINT?
interview.answer: A named point inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after it.

interview.q: Can CREATE DATABASE run inside a transaction?
interview.answer: No. PostgreSQL rejects CREATE DATABASE and DROP DATABASE inside a transaction block.

interview.q: Which commands are utility commands?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN, VACUUM, ANALYZE and COPY are utility commands; they are not DDL, DML, DQL, DCL or TCL.

interview.q: Is MERGE DML?
interview.answer: Yes. PostgreSQL 15+ supports MERGE, which inserts, updates or deletes rows in one statement.

labs.title: Create a table
labs.task: Create a students table with id and name.
labs.solution: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

labs.title: Alter the table
labs.task: Add an email column.
labs.solution: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;

labs.title: Insert a row
labs.task: Insert id 1, Aarav.
labs.solution: INSERT INTO students (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Aarav');

labs.title: Read the row
labs.task: Select id and name for id 1.
labs.solution: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Update the row
labs.task: Rename id 1 to Aarav Sharma.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav Sharma' WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Delete the row
labs.task: Delete id 1.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Truncate the table
labs.task: Remove every row and keep the table.
labs.solution: TRUNCATE TABLE students;

labs.title: Drop the table
labs.task: Remove the students table if it exists.
labs.solution: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS students;

labs.title: Create a role
labs.task: Create analyst as a login role.
labs.solution: CREATE ROLE analyst LOGIN;

labs.title: Grant read access
labs.task: Give analyst SELECT on students.
labs.solution: GRANT SELECT ON students TO analyst;

labs.title: Revoke write access
labs.task: Remove INSERT on students from analyst.
labs.solution: REVOKE INSERT ON students FROM analyst;

labs.title: Commit a transaction
labs.task: Insert id 2, Meera, and commit.

labs.title: Rollback a transaction
labs.task: Delete every row, then rollback.

labs.title: Use a savepoint
labs.task: Insert one row, save, insert another, roll back to the savepoint.

labs.title: Truncate and restart identity
labs.task: Remove every row and reset the identity sequence.
labs.solution: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY;

labs.title: Create a table from a query
labs.task: Create students_backup from students.
labs.solution: CREATE TABLE students_backup AS SELECT * FROM students;

labs.title: Insert from a query
labs.task: Copy every students row into students_backup.
labs.solution: INSERT INTO students_backup SELECT * FROM students;

labs.title: Update with RETURNING
labs.task: Update id 2 and return the changed row.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET name = 'Meera S' WHERE id = 2 RETURNING id, name;

labs.title: Delete with RETURNING
labs.task: Delete id 2 and return it.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 2 RETURNING id, name;

labs.title: Classify a command
labs.task: Classify EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students.
labs.solution: SELECT 'utility' AS category, 'EXPLAIN' AS command;

logic.q: Why is TRUNCATE faster than DELETE for all rows?
logic.answer: TRUNCATE removes the table storage in one operation instead of scanning and deleting rows one by one.

logic.q: Why is DELETE often safer than TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: DELETE supports WHERE, fires row triggers and can be rolled back row by row; TRUNCATE always removes every row.

logic.q: Why is DROP more dangerous than TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: DROP removes the table definition, data, indexes and constraints; TRUNCATE keeps the table.

logic.q: Why can PostgreSQL roll back TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL implements TRUNCATE transactionally, so it can be undone before COMMIT.

logic.q: Why does MySQL commit after TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: MySQL performs an implicit commit for TRUNCATE, so it cannot be rolled back there.

logic.q: Why does TRUNCATE not fire row-level DELETE triggers?
logic.answer: It does not delete rows one by one; PostgreSQL offers statement-level TRUNCATE triggers instead.

logic.q: Why should GRANT follow least privilege?
logic.answer: A role should get only the privileges its job needs, limiting the damage of a mistake or a compromised account.

logic.q: Why is schema USAGE required?
logic.answer: The role must be able to resolve names in the schema before table privileges can be used.

logic.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE a production incident?
logic.answer: It changes every row in the table, and a mistaken predicate can corrupt the whole dataset.

logic.q: Why test a WHERE with SELECT before DELETE?
logic.answer: The SELECT shows exactly which rows will be removed before the destructive statement runs.

logic.q: Why is SELECT classified as DQL?
logic.answer: It reads rows without modifying them; DQL exists to separate reading from DML.

logic.q: Why is CREATE TABLE AS classified as DDL?
logic.answer: It creates a new table object, even though its source is a query.

logic.q: Why is EXPLAIN not DML?
logic.answer: It reports the planner’s access path and does not change rows.

logic.q: Why is MERGE DML?
logic.answer: MERGE can insert, update or delete rows based on a source relation.

logic.q: Why can DROP DATABASE not be rolled back?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow DROP DATABASE inside a transaction block.

modules.title: CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE
modules.goal: Build a correct, constrained PostgreSQL schema from scratch.

topics.title: CREATE DATABASE
topics.simple: CREATE DATABASE ek naya database banata hai — apne tables, schemas aur users ke saath.
topics.pro: CREATE DATABASE creates a new database catalog from a template; it must run outside a transaction block and requires the CREATEDB privilege or superuser.
points: The creator becomes the owner unless OWNER is given.
You cannot run it inside BEGIN ... COMMIT.

example.sql: CREATE DATABASE school;

topics.title: Database Naming Rules
topics.simple: Database ka naam clear aur consistent rakho; unquoted naam lowercase ban jaate hain.
topics.pro: Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase, are limited to 63 bytes and should avoid reserved words; quoted mixed-case names must be quoted forever.

example.sql: CREATE DATABASE SchoolDB;
example.output: Creates schooldb (unquoted names fold to lowercase).

topics.title: CREATE DATABASE Options
topics.simple: Database banate waqt owner, template aur encoding choose kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: CREATE DATABASE accepts OWNER, TEMPLATE, ENCODING, locale, CONNECTION LIMIT and IS_TEMPLATE options; template0 is the safe base when changing encoding or locale.
points: Set the owner explicitly in shared environments.

example.sql: CREATE DATABASE school OWNER analyst TEMPLATE template0 ENCODING 'UTF8';

topics.title: CREATE TABLE
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE columns, types aur rules ke saath naya table banata hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE defines a relation with ordered columns, types and constraints; it is DDL and takes a lock on the new table name.
points: Constraints enforce rules at write time.
The table is created in the current schema.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Table Structure
topics.simple: Table structure ka matlab columns, unke types aur constraints ka plan.
topics.pro: A table structure is its ordered column list, data types, defaults, nullability and constraints; psql shows it with \d.
points: Column order is part of the definition.

example.sql: \d students
example.output:
Table "public.students"
 id   | integer | not null
 name | text    | not null

topics.title: Defining Columns
topics.simple: Har column ka naam, type aur optional default ya constraint likho.
topics.pro: A column definition is `name type [constraints]`; defaults and constraints are evaluated when rows are written.
points: Put NOT NULL on required fields.
Defaults apply when the column is omitted.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL, credits SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 3);

topics.title: Defining Data Types
topics.simple: Column ke liye sahi type choose karo — number, text, date ya boolean.
topics.pro: Choose types by domain: integers for counts, NUMERIC for exact decimals, TEXT/VARCHAR for strings, BOOLEAN for flags and TIMESTAMPTZ for instants.
points: The type controls valid values and storage.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE marks (student_id INTEGER, score NUMERIC(5,2) CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100));

topics.title: Column Constraints
topics.simple: Constraints rules hain — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, PRIMARY KEY, REFERENCES.
topics.pro: Column constraints enforce nullability, uniqueness, value ranges, defaults and referential integrity; named constraints are easier to migrate later.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE);

topics.title: Creating Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Ek table me jitne columns chahiye, comma se likho.
topics.pro: A table can declare many columns in one CREATE TABLE; order is preserved and each column has its own type and constraints.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE demo (id INTEGER, title TEXT, active BOOLEAN, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());

topics.title: Creating Multiple Tables
topics.simple: Ek schema me alag-alag tables banao — students, courses, enrollments.
topics.pro: Create related tables in dependency order: parent tables first, then tables with foreign keys.
points: Create referenced tables before referencing tables.
One statement per table is easier to review.

example.sql:
CREATE TABLE teachers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE rooms (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Table Schema
topics.simple: Schema table ka blueprint hai — columns, types, keys aur rules.
topics.pro: A table schema is its declared structure and constraints, distinct from the data it currently holds.
points: Inspect both structure and data separately.

example.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'students' ORDER BY ordinal_position;
example.output: One row per column with its type.

topics.title: CREATE SCHEMA and search_path
topics.simple: Schema database ke andar namespace hai; search_path batata hai unqualified naam kahan dhoondhna hai.
topics.pro: CREATE SCHEMA creates a namespace; search_path controls the order in which unqualified object names are resolved.
points: Put trusted schemas first in search_path.

example.sql:
CREATE SCHEMA school;
SET search_path TO school, public;

topics.title: CREATE TABLE AS
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE AS query ka result ek naye table me save karta hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE AS creates a table and fills it from a SELECT; it copies column names and data but not most constraints or indexes.
points: It does not copy primary keys automatically.
The command tag is SELECT N.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE top_students AS SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Creating Tables from Existing Data
topics.simple: Existing table ki structure ya data se naya table bana sakte hain.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE ... (LIKE source INCLUDING ALL) copies the structure; CREATE TABLE AS copies data; INSERT ... SELECT fills an existing table.
points: CTAS copies rows but not constraints.
INSERT ... SELECT keeps the target definition.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students_copy (LIKE students INCLUDING ALL);

topics.title: IF NOT EXISTS
topics.simple: IF NOT EXISTS table already ho to error ke bajaye skip kar deta hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS skips creation when the relation name already exists; it does not compare or migrate the existing definition.
points: It emits a notice when skipping.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
example.output: CREATE TABLE (or NOTICE: relation already exists, skipping)

topics.title: Table Naming Conventions
topics.simple: Table ka naam plural, lowercase aur descriptive rakho — students, course_enrollments.
topics.pro: Use lower_snake_case, plural nouns and descriptive relationship names; avoid reserved words and quoted mixed case.
points: Name join tables after both sides.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, enrolled_on DATE);

topics.title: Inspecting Table Structure
topics.simple: Table banne ke baad \d ya information_schema se structure check karo.
topics.pro: psql \d shows columns, types, indexes and constraints; information_schema.columns is the portable catalog query.

example.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'courses';

topics.title: Common CREATE Errors
topics.simple: CREATE fail ho sakta hai duplicate table, missing type, duplicate column ya missing parent table se.
topics.pro: Common failures are relation already exists, column specified more than once, missing type, invalid default, missing referenced relation and permission denied.
points: Read the first error and the object name.
Use IF NOT EXISTS only when skipping is correct.
Create parent tables before foreign keys.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE bad (id);

topics.title: CREATE TABLE with Foreign Keys
topics.simple: Foreign key child table ko parent table se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A foreign key references a candidate key in a parent table and enforces referential integrity; choose ON DELETE behaviour deliberately.
points: The parent key must be UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, grade TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Practical Student Database Design
topics.simple: Ab students, courses aur enrollments ka real schema banate hain.
topics.pro: A small school schema uses students, courses and a junction table with a composite primary key and foreign keys to both parents.
points: Every table has a primary key.
The junction table enforces one enrollment per pair.

learn.q: Which command creates a new database?
options: CREATE DATABASE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE SCHEMA
INSERT
learn.answer: CREATE DATABASE
learn.why: CREATE DATABASE creates a separate database catalog.

learn.q: Can CREATE DATABASE run inside a transaction block?
options: No
Yes, always
Only in psql
Only with IF NOT EXISTS
learn.answer: No
learn.why: PostgreSQL rejects CREATE DATABASE inside BEGIN ... COMMIT.

learn.q: What happens to unquoted database names?
options: They fold to lowercase
They stay uppercase
They are rejected
They become quoted
learn.answer: They fold to lowercase
learn.why: PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase.

learn.q: What is the maximum identifier length in PostgreSQL?
options: 63 bytes
32 bytes
128 bytes
255 bytes
learn.answer: 63 bytes
learn.why: Identifiers are limited to NAMEDATALEN - 1 bytes, 63 by default.

learn.q: Which command creates a table?
options: CREATE TABLE
CREATE ROW
MAKE TABLE
ADD TABLE
learn.answer: CREATE TABLE
learn.why: CREATE TABLE defines columns and constraints.

learn.q: What does CREATE TABLE AS do?
options: Creates a table from a query result
Copies only constraints
Creates an index
Creates a schema
learn.answer: Creates a table from a query result
learn.why: CTAS creates and fills a table from SELECT.

learn.q: What does CREATE TABLE ... LIKE source INCLUDING ALL copy?
options: Structure, not rows
Rows, not structure
Only indexes
Only data
learn.answer: Structure, not rows
learn.why: LIKE copies the table definition; it does not copy rows.

learn.q: Does CREATE TABLE AS copy primary keys and indexes automatically?
options: No
Yes, all of them
Only primary keys
Only indexes
learn.answer: No
learn.why: CTAS copies columns and data, not most constraints or indexes.

learn.q: What does CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS do when the table exists?
options: Skips creation and emits a notice
Drops and recreates it
Adds missing columns
Fails with an error
learn.answer: Skips creation and emits a notice
learn.why: It does not compare or migrate the existing definition.

learn.q: Which schema is the default in a new PostgreSQL database?
options: public
main
dbo
default
learn.answer: public
learn.why: public is the default schema in a standard PostgreSQL database.

learn.q: What does search_path control?
options: Which schemas resolve unqualified names
The database encoding
The table owner
The backup location
learn.answer: Which schemas resolve unqualified names
learn.why: search_path is the lookup order for unqualified object names.

learn.q: Which constraint uniquely identifies each row?
options: PRIMARY KEY
NOT NULL
CHECK
DEFAULT
learn.answer: PRIMARY KEY
learn.why: A primary key is unique and not null.

learn.q: Which constraint rejects NULL values?
options: NOT NULL
UNIQUE
CHECK
REFERENCES
learn.answer: NOT NULL
learn.why: NOT NULL requires a value.

learn.q: Which constraint enforces a value range?
options: CHECK
UNIQUE
DEFAULT
PRIMARY KEY
learn.answer: CHECK
learn.why: CHECK accepts rows only when its predicate is true.

learn.q: Which constraint links a child table to a parent?
options: FOREIGN KEY
CHECK
UNIQUE
NOT NULL
learn.answer: FOREIGN KEY
learn.why: A foreign key references a candidate key in another table.

learn.q: Which identity syntax is preferred for new PostgreSQL tables?
options: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
SERIAL
AUTO_INCREMENT
IDENTITY()
learn.answer: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
learn.why: IDENTITY is standard SQL; SERIAL is legacy.

learn.q: Which psql command shows a table definition?
options: \d students
\l
\c
\q
learn.answer: \d students
learn.why: \d describes columns, indexes and constraints.

learn.q: Which catalog view lists column types?
options: information_schema.columns
pg_stat_activity
pg_roles
pg_database
learn.answer: information_schema.columns
learn.why: It exposes column metadata in a standard shape.

learn.q: What does a duplicate column name in CREATE TABLE cause?
options: An error
A warning only
A silent rename
A new table
learn.answer: An error
learn.why: A table cannot have two columns with the same name.

learn.q: Which privilege is needed to create a database?
options: CREATEDB
SELECT
USAGE
EXECUTE
learn.answer: CREATEDB
learn.why: The role needs CREATEDB or superuser status.

interview.q: What is the difference between a database and a schema?
interview.answer: A database is a separate catalog with its own connections; a schema is a namespace inside a database that groups objects.

interview.q: Why can CREATE DATABASE not run in a transaction?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow database creation inside a transaction block, so it cannot be rolled back like a table change.

interview.q: What is template1 vs template0?
interview.answer: template1 is the default template and may carry local customizations; template0 is pristine and is the safe base when changing encoding or locale.

interview.q: Who owns a newly created database?
interview.answer: The role that created it, unless OWNER is specified.

interview.q: Why does database encoding matter?
interview.answer: Encoding determines which characters can be stored and how text is represented; UTF8 is the usual choice for multilingual data.

interview.q: What are PostgreSQL identifier rules?
interview.answer: Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase, are limited to 63 bytes and must not be empty; reserved words need quoting.

interview.q: What does CREATE TABLE define?
interview.answer: Ordered columns, their data types, defaults and constraints, plus table-level constraints and storage options.

interview.q: What does a primary key guarantee?
interview.answer: Uniqueness and non-nullness for the key columns, backed by a unique index.

interview.q: Does a foreign key require a unique parent key?
interview.answer: Yes. The referenced columns must be a primary key or have a unique constraint.

interview.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
interview.answer: When the parent row is deleted, matching child rows are deleted automatically.

interview.q: What is the difference between SERIAL and IDENTITY?
interview.answer: SERIAL is a legacy pseudo-type that creates a sequence and default; GENERATED AS IDENTITY is standard SQL and preferred for new tables.

interview.q: What is the difference between CTAS and CREATE TABLE LIKE?
interview.answer: CTAS copies columns and rows from a query but not most constraints; LIKE copies the structure and can include constraints but no rows.

interview.q: Why is IF NOT EXISTS not a migration tool?
interview.answer: It only checks the relation name; it does not add missing columns or reconcile a different definition.

interview.q: What is search_path?
interview.answer: The ordered list of schemas PostgreSQL uses to resolve unqualified object names.

interview.q: How do you inspect a table in psql?
interview.answer: Use \d table for columns, indexes and constraints; \d+ adds storage and description details.

interview.q: What are common CREATE TABLE errors?
interview.answer: Relation already exists, duplicate column, missing type, invalid default, missing referenced table and permission denied.

interview.q: Why qualify table names with a schema?
interview.answer: Qualification removes ambiguity and protects against a hostile or unexpected search_path.

interview.q: What is a composite primary key?
interview.answer: A primary key made of two or more columns; the combination must be unique and none may be null.

interview.q: Does CTAS copy indexes?
interview.answer: No. CTAS creates a new table and data; indexes and most constraints must be added separately.

interview.q: What privilege is needed to create tables?
interview.answer: CREATE on the schema, plus USAGE on that schema; the role also needs a database connection.

logic.q: Why can CREATE DATABASE not be rolled back?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL forbids it inside a transaction block, so there is no transaction to roll back.

logic.q: Why do unquoted names fold to lowercase?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL normalizes unquoted identifiers to lowercase; quoted names preserve case.

logic.q: Why is 63 bytes the identifier limit?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL stores names in a fixed 64-byte field, leaving one byte for the terminator.

logic.q: Why use a schema instead of many databases?
logic.answer: Schemas share one database and connection while still namespacing objects, which simplifies backups and cross-schema queries.

logic.q: Why does a primary key create an index?
logic.answer: The unique index enforces uniqueness and speeds up lookups by key.

logic.q: Why must a foreign key parent exist first?
logic.answer: The referenced table and key must exist when the constraint is created.

logic.q: Why does CTAS not copy constraints?
logic.answer: It creates a new relation from a query result; constraints are not part of the query output.

logic.q: Why does LIKE copy no rows?
logic.answer: LIKE copies the table definition only; data must be inserted separately.

logic.q: Why is IF NOT EXISTS unsafe for migrations?
logic.answer: It silently accepts an existing table even if its columns or constraints differ from what the script expects.

logic.q: Why should search_path start with trusted schemas?
logic.answer: An attacker who can create objects in an earlier schema could shadow functions or tables.

logic.q: Why prefer IDENTITY over SERIAL?
logic.answer: IDENTITY is standard SQL, has explicit sequence ownership and avoids legacy pseudo-type behavior.

logic.q: Why add NOT NULL and DEFAULT together?
logic.answer: The column is always present and gets a value when the insert omits it.

logic.q: Why does a CHECK constraint allow NULL?
logic.answer: A CHECK passes when the predicate is true or NULL; add NOT NULL if NULL must be rejected.

logic.q: Why is ON DELETE CASCADE risky?
logic.answer: One parent delete can remove many child rows; use it only for true ownership relationships.

logic.q: Why inspect a table after DDL?
logic.answer: The actual columns, defaults and constraints are the source of truth; the script may have skipped or altered something.

modules.title: INSERT Statement
modules.goal: Write safe, correct INSERTs and handle conflicts deliberately.

topics.title: What Is INSERT?
topics.simple: INSERT table me naya row add karta hai.
topics.pro: INSERT is DML that adds one or more rows to a table, checks every constraint and returns a command tag such as INSERT 0 1.
points: Every row must satisfy the table constraints.
A failed multi-row INSERT adds no rows from that statement.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Aarav', 82);

topics.title: INSERT INTO Syntax
topics.simple: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values) — yahi basic shape hai.
topics.pro: The general form is INSERT INTO table (column list) VALUES (row), (row), ... with an optional RETURNING clause.
points: The value count must match the column count.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Meera', 91);

topics.title: Inserting a Single Row
topics.simple: Ek row ke liye ek VALUES group likho.
topics.pro: A single-row INSERT supplies one parenthesized value list and inserts exactly one row or fails atomically.
points: One row is one VALUES group.
Constraints are checked before the row is stored.
The command tag reports 1 inserted row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Kabir', 67);

topics.title: Inserting Multiple Rows
topics.simple: Ek hi INSERT me comma se multiple rows daal sakte hain.
topics.pro: A multi-row INSERT uses several VALUES groups in one statement, which is faster than many separate round trips and is atomic for the statement.
points: Each group needs the same column count.
One bad row fails the whole statement.
The tag reports the number of inserted rows.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Isha', 88), ('Zoya', 74), ('Dev', 59);

topics.title: Inserting Specific Columns
topics.simple: Jin columns ki value hai unka naam likho; baaki defaults ya NULL lete hain.
topics.pro: Listing only the columns you supply lets defaults, identity values and nullable columns fill the rest.
points: Omitted columns with defaults use the default.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Anaya');

topics.title: Column Order and VALUES
topics.simple: Bina column list ke VALUES table ke column order par depend karta hai — ye fragile hai.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO table VALUES (...) maps values by the table’s physical column order; adding or reordering a column can silently break the statement.
points: A count mismatch raises an error.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (1, 'Rohan', 'rohan@example.com', 77);

topics.title: DEFAULT VALUES
topics.simple: Agar har column ka default ya identity ho, to DEFAULT VALUES se khali row banao.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO table DEFAULT VALUES inserts a row using every column’s default; it fails if a required column has no default.
points: A NOT NULL column without a default rejects it.

example.sql: INSERT INTO settings DEFAULT VALUES;

topics.title: NULL Values and Defaults
topics.simple: NULL ka matlab unknown value hai; DEFAULT ka matlab column ka predefined value.
topics.pro: NULL is an explicit unknown value, while DEFAULT asks PostgreSQL to use the column default; they are not interchangeable.
points: NULL is not an empty string or zero.
DEFAULT in VALUES uses the column default.
NOT NULL rejects an explicit NULL.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Meera', NULL);

topics.title: RETURNING
topics.simple: RETURNING inserted row ki values wapas deta hai — jaise naya id.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns rows produced by the INSERT, including generated identity values and defaults, in the same statement.
points: It avoids a second SELECT for the new id.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Aarav', 82) RETURNING id, name;

topics.title: INSERT INTO SELECT
topics.simple: Ek query ka result doosri table me insert kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO target (columns) SELECT ... copies rows from a query; the selected columns must match the target list in number and compatible types.
points: ORDER BY and LIMIT can shape the source.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students_backup (name, marks) SELECT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Inserting From a Query with All Columns
topics.simple: Agar dono tables ka structure same hai to SELECT * se copy kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM source works only when column order, count and types line up; explicit columns are safer across schema changes.
points: SELECT * depends on both table shapes.
A column added to one table breaks the copy.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students_backup SELECT * FROM students;

topics.title: Identity Columns and INSERT
topics.simple: Identity column khud value banata hai; explicit value dene par rules hain.
topics.pro: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects explicit values unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is used; GENERATED BY DEFAULT accepts them.
points: Use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE only for migrations.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (id, name) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (10, 'Kabir');

topics.title: Handling Duplicate Rows with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
topics.simple: Duplicate unique value aaye to ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING us row ko skip kar deta hai.
topics.pro: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING suppresses a unique or exclusion violation for the targeted conflict and inserts the remaining rows.
points: The conflict target must match a unique constraint.
Skipped rows are not returned by RETURNING.
Without a target it handles any conflict.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (email, name) VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Aarav') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

topics.title: Upsert with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
topics.simple: Conflict aaye to naya row insert karne ke bajaye existing row update kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ON CONFLICT (target) DO UPDATE SET ... performs an upsert; EXCLUDED holds the proposed row values.
points: The target needs a unique constraint.
EXCLUDED refers to the row you tried to insert.
Do not hit the same row twice in one statement.

example.sql:
INSERT INTO students (email, name, marks) VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Aarav S', 90)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, marks = EXCLUDED.marks;

topics.title: INSERT Errors and Constraints
topics.simple: INSERT fail hota hai jab NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY ya type violate ho.
topics.pro: Constraint violations abort the statement: not-null, unique, check, foreign key, invalid input syntax and value too long are the common failures.
points: Read the constraint name in the error.
One failed statement adds no rows.
Fix the value, not the constraint, unless the rule is wrong.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (NULL);
example.output: ERROR: null value in column "name" violates not-null constraint

topics.title: Safe Insertion and Transactions
topics.simple: Important inserts ko transaction me karo taaki failure par rollback ho sake.
topics.pro: Wrap related inserts in BEGIN ... COMMIT; an error aborts the transaction and ROLLBACK discards every uncommitted change.
points: Commit only when the whole unit is correct.

topics.title: Bulk Insert Performance
topics.simple: Bahut rows ke liye multi-row INSERT ya COPY use karo; ek-ek INSERT slow hota hai.
topics.pro: Multi-row VALUES reduces round trips; COPY is the fastest bulk-load path for large files, at the cost of fewer per-row controls.
points: Batch hundreds of rows per statement.
Indexes and triggers still cost time per row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('A', 60), ('B', 70), ('C', 80);

topics.title: INSERT ... RETURNING Generated IDs
topics.simple: Naya id chahiye to RETURNING id use karo — alag SELECT ki zaroorat nahi.
topics.pro: RETURNING id captures generated identity values for each inserted row, including multi-row inserts.
points: The order of returned rows follows insertion order in practice.
Do not assume ids are contiguous.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Isha'), ('Dev') RETURNING id;

topics.title: INSERT Best Practices
topics.simple: Columns name karo, values validate karo aur bulk operations batch me karo.
topics.pro: Production INSERTs name columns, supply typed values, handle conflicts deliberately, batch where useful and run inside a transaction when rows belong together.
points: Do not hide every conflict with DO NOTHING.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Anaya', 95) RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: Practical Student Enrollment Insert
topics.simple: Students aur enrollments me related rows ek transaction me daalo.
topics.pro: A real enrollment flow inserts the student, captures the generated id with RETURNING, then inserts the enrollment row in the same transaction.
points: The parent row must exist before the child.
Use the returned id, not a guessed one.
Commit only after both inserts succeed.

learn.q: What does INSERT do?
options: Adds rows to a table
Creates a table
Reads rows
Deletes rows
learn.answer: Adds rows to a table
learn.why: INSERT is DML that adds one or more rows.

learn.q: Which clause supplies the values for an INSERT?
options: VALUES
WHERE
SET
FROM
learn.answer: VALUES
learn.why: VALUES supplies one or more row value groups.

learn.q: How many rows does a single VALUES group insert?
options: One
Two
All rows
Zero
learn.answer: One
learn.why: One parenthesized group is one row.

learn.q: How do you insert three rows in one statement?
options: Three comma-separated VALUES groups
Three separate INSERTs only
One group with three values
A CREATE TABLE
learn.answer: Three comma-separated VALUES groups
learn.why: Multi-row INSERT uses multiple value groups.

learn.q: Why list target columns explicitly?
options: It is safer when the table changes
It makes the query slower
It is required by SQL
It removes constraints
learn.answer: It is safer when the table changes
learn.why: Explicit columns do not depend on physical column order.

learn.q: What does INSERT INTO table DEFAULT VALUES do?
options: Inserts a row using defaults
Deletes all rows
Creates a default table
Inserts NULL into every column
learn.answer: Inserts a row using defaults
learn.why: It uses each column default and identity generation.

learn.q: What is the difference between NULL and DEFAULT?
options: NULL is unknown; DEFAULT uses the column default
They are identical
DEFAULT is always NULL
NULL is zero
learn.answer: NULL is unknown; DEFAULT uses the column default
learn.why: They are different values in an INSERT.

learn.q: What does RETURNING do?
options: Returns inserted rows in the same statement
Rolls back the insert
Creates an index
Returns the table definition
learn.answer: Returns inserted rows in the same statement
learn.why: RETURNING exposes generated ids and inserted values.

learn.q: Which statement copies rows from a query?
options: INSERT INTO ... SELECT
CREATE TABLE ... LIKE
ALTER TABLE
TRUNCATE
learn.answer: INSERT INTO ... SELECT
learn.why: It inserts the result of a SELECT into the target table.

learn.q: What does INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM source require?
options: Matching column count and compatible types
Matching table names
A foreign key
No constraints
learn.answer: Matching column count and compatible types
learn.why: The source columns must line up with the target columns.

learn.q: What does GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY do with an explicit value?
options: Rejects it unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is used
Accepts it always
Ignores the column
Converts it to NULL
learn.answer: Rejects it unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is used
learn.why: ALWAYS protects the generated identity.

learn.q: What does ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING do?
options: Skips a row that violates the conflict target
Deletes the conflicting row
Updates the conflicting row
Creates a new table
learn.answer: Skips a row that violates the conflict target
learn.why: It suppresses the conflict instead of raising an error.

learn.q: What does EXCLUDED refer to in an upsert?
options: The proposed inserted row
The existing row
A deleted row
The table
learn.answer: The proposed inserted row
learn.why: EXCLUDED holds the values you tried to insert.

learn.q: What happens when one row in a multi-row INSERT violates a constraint?
options: The whole statement fails and adds no rows
Only that row is skipped
The constraint is disabled
The table is dropped
learn.answer: The whole statement fails and adds no rows
learn.why: The statement is atomic.

learn.q: Which error means a required column was omitted?
options: NOT NULL violation
Unique violation
Foreign key violation
Syntax error
learn.answer: NOT NULL violation
learn.why: The omitted column has no value and is NOT NULL.

learn.q: Which command is best for loading a huge file?
options: COPY
INSERT one row at a time
SELECT
ALTER TABLE
learn.answer: COPY
learn.why: COPY is the bulk-load utility for large datasets.

learn.q: What does INSERT ... RETURNING id help capture?
options: Generated identity values
The table owner
The schema name
The transaction id
learn.answer: Generated identity values
learn.why: RETURNING returns the new ids without a second query.

learn.q: What is the safest way to run related inserts?
options: Inside a transaction
With autocommit off only
One by one without checks
With TRUNCATE first
learn.answer: Inside a transaction
learn.why: A transaction lets you commit all related rows or roll them all back.

learn.q: Does a failed INSERT leave a partial row?
options: No
Yes, always
Only for multi-row inserts
Only with RETURNING
learn.answer: No
learn.why: A failed statement is atomic and adds no rows.

learn.q: Which is PostgreSQL-specific in this module?
options: RETURNING
INSERT INTO
VALUES
DEFAULT VALUES
learn.answer: RETURNING
learn.why: RETURNING is PostgreSQL syntax; some other databases support it too, but not all.

interview.q: What is INSERT?
interview.answer: DML that adds one or more rows to a table and checks every constraint.

interview.q: What is the basic INSERT syntax?
interview.answer: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); with optional RETURNING.

interview.q: How do you insert multiple rows?
interview.answer: Use multiple comma-separated VALUES groups in one INSERT.

interview.q: Why is an explicit column list recommended?
interview.answer: It is independent of physical column order and keeps working when unrelated columns are added.

interview.q: What happens if the column count and value count differ?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL raises a syntax error; the statement inserts nothing.

interview.q: What does DEFAULT VALUES do?
interview.answer: Inserts one row using every column default; it fails if a required column has no default.

interview.q: What is the difference between NULL and DEFAULT in VALUES?
interview.answer: NULL stores an unknown value; DEFAULT asks for the column default.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: Returns inserted rows, including generated ids and defaults, in the same statement.

interview.q: How does INSERT INTO SELECT work?
interview.answer: It inserts the rows produced by a SELECT; the target and source columns must match in number and compatible types.

interview.q: What is an identity column?
interview.answer: A column whose value is generated from an attached sequence; GENERATED ALWAYS is the standard form.

interview.q: How do you insert an explicit value into GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY?
interview.answer: Add OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE to the INSERT; use it only for migrations or imports.

interview.q: What does ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING do?
interview.answer: Skips a row that would violate the targeted unique or exclusion constraint.

interview.q: What does ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE do?
interview.answer: Performs an upsert: updates the existing row with values from the proposed row.

interview.q: What is EXCLUDED?
interview.answer: A pseudo-table holding the values proposed by the INSERT, used in the DO UPDATE SET clause.

interview.q: What is a common INSERT error?
interview.answer: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK or foreign-key violation, invalid input syntax or value too long.

interview.q: Is a multi-row INSERT atomic?
interview.answer: Yes. If any row fails, the whole statement inserts no rows.

interview.q: Why use a transaction for related inserts?
interview.answer: It lets you commit the whole unit or roll it back when a later insert fails.

interview.q: How do you bulk load a large file?
interview.answer: Use COPY, which is much faster than row-by-row INSERTs.

interview.q: What does INSERT ... RETURNING id solve?
interview.answer: It returns generated ids immediately, avoiding a race-prone follow-up SELECT.

interview.q: What is an upsert?
interview.answer: Insert a row, or update the existing row when a unique conflict occurs.

logic.q: Why is an explicit column list safer than relying on column order?
logic.answer: Adding or reordering a column changes the physical order; an explicit list keeps the statement correct.

logic.q: Why is a multi-row INSERT faster than many single-row INSERTs?
logic.answer: It sends one statement and one round trip instead of many network and planning cycles.

logic.q: Why does one bad row fail a multi-row INSERT?
logic.answer: The statement is atomic; a constraint violation aborts the whole statement.

logic.q: Why is NULL different from DEFAULT?
logic.answer: NULL stores an unknown value; DEFAULT asks PostgreSQL to apply the column default.

logic.q: Why does DEFAULT VALUES fail on a NOT NULL column without a default?
logic.answer: There is no value to store, so the not-null constraint rejects the row.

logic.q: Why is RETURNING useful after an INSERT?
logic.answer: It returns generated ids and defaults without a second query or a race.

logic.q: Why does INSERT INTO SELECT need matching columns?
logic.answer: The selected values are mapped positionally to the target column list.

logic.q: Why does GENERATED ALWAYS reject an explicit id?
logic.answer: ALWAYS protects the sequence-generated value; OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is the deliberate escape hatch.

logic.q: Why does ON CONFLICT need a unique constraint?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL must know which conflict the target identifies; without a matching unique or exclusion constraint it cannot arbitrate.

logic.q: Why can ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE affect one row twice?
logic.answer: If the proposed rows contain the same conflict key twice, PostgreSQL cannot update the same existing row twice and raises an error.

logic.q: Why is DO NOTHING dangerous as a default?
logic.answer: It silently hides data-quality problems that should be fixed or reported.

logic.q: Why use a transaction for a student plus enrollment?
logic.answer: The two rows belong together; a failure in the second should not leave a half-written flow.

logic.q: Why is COPY faster than INSERT for bulk data?
logic.answer: COPY streams rows with far less per-row overhead and fewer round trips.

logic.q: Why can INSERT fire triggers?
logic.answer: Row-level INSERT triggers run for each inserted row; they are part of the write cost.

logic.q: Why should you not assume generated ids are contiguous?
logic.answer: Rolled-back inserts and sequences can leave gaps; ids are unique, not gapless.

modules.title: SELECT Statement
modules.goal: Read and shape result sets with correct projection and expressions.

topics.title: Introduction to SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT database se data padhne ka command hai — jo columns chahiye, wo choose karta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT is DQL that projects a result set from one or more relations, evaluates expressions and returns rows without modifying stored data.
points: It can return zero, one or many rows.
The result columns are defined by the select list.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
example.output: One row per student with name and marks.

topics.title: Basic SELECT Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: SELECT columns FROM table.
topics.pro: The core syntax is SELECT select_list FROM relation [WHERE ...] [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...]; the select list defines the output columns.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: SELECT *
topics.simple: SELECT * table ke saare columns deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT * expands to every column in the relation at planning time; it is convenient for exploration but fragile in production.
points: It returns every column, including future ones.
Column order follows the table definition.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students;
example.output: Every column and row from students.

topics.title: Selecting Specific Columns
topics.simple: Sirf zaroori columns choose karo — network aur result chhota rehta hai.
topics.pro: A projection list names the columns to return; omitted columns are not read into the result, which can reduce I/O and payload.
points: The output order is the list order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Selecting Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Comma se multiple columns likho.
topics.pro: Multiple columns are separated by commas and appear in the same order as the select list, regardless of table order.
points: A trailing comma is a syntax error.

example.sql: SELECT id, name, email, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Column Aliases
topics.simple: Alias result column ka temporary naam hota hai.
topics.pro: An alias renames a result column for the query output; it does not rename the underlying table column.
points: Aliases are not visible in WHERE in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: SELECT name AS student_name, marks AS score FROM students;

topics.title: AS Keyword
topics.simple: AS alias ko explicit banata hai — padhne me clear.
topics.pro: AS introduces a column or table alias; it is optional for column aliases but required for some derived-table aliases.
points: AS is optional for column aliases.
Quoted aliases preserve case and spaces.
Aliases last for the query only.

example.sql: SELECT name AS "Student Name" FROM students;

topics.title: Calculated Columns
topics.simple: SELECT me expression se naya column bana sakte hain.
topics.pro: The select list can contain expressions, not just columns; each expression becomes an output column with a computed value per row.
points: Calculations do not change stored data.
Use an alias to name the result.
The expression is evaluated per row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks + 5 AS boosted FROM students;

topics.title: Arithmetic Operations
topics.simple: SELECT me +, -, *, /, % use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Arithmetic operators follow standard precedence; integer division truncates, while a numeric operand keeps the fraction.

example.sql: SELECT 7 / 2 AS int_div, ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) AS num_div;

topics.title: Concatenating Columns
topics.simple: || operator strings ko jodta hai.
topics.pro: The || operator concatenates text; cast non-text values explicitly when the result must be predictable.
points: NULL concatenated with anything is NULL.

example.sql: SELECT name || ' scored ' || marks::text AS label FROM students;

topics.title: Selecting Expressions
topics.simple: SELECT me literals, functions aur arithmetic — sab expressions hain.
topics.pro: A select-list item can be a column, literal, function call or arithmetic expression; PostgreSQL names an unaliased expression ?column?.
points: Use aliases for stable column names.
Functions run per row unless aggregated.

example.sql: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS result;

topics.title: SELECT DISTINCT
topics.simple: DISTINCT duplicate result rows hata deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the final result after projection; it applies to the whole select list, not to one column.
points: DISTINCT is applied after SELECT expressions.
It treats NULLs as equal for duplicate removal.
It can cost a sort or hash.

example.sql: SELECT DISTINCT marks FROM students;

topics.title: Duplicate Values
topics.simple: Table me same value kai rows me ho sakti hai; DISTINCT unhe ek baar dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Duplicates are normal in relational data unless a constraint forbids them; duplicate removal is a query-time decision, not a storage rule.
points: A primary key prevents duplicate rows by key.
DISTINCT changes the result, not the table.

example.sql: SELECT marks FROM students;

topics.title: DISTINCT with Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns ke saath DISTINCT unique combinations deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT DISTINCT a, b removes duplicate pairs; it does not return one row per distinct a.
points: Column order does not change the set.
Use GROUP BY when you need aggregates per key.

example.sql: SELECT DISTINCT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Logical Query Order
topics.simple: SQL likhne ka order aur database ke evaluate karne ka order alag hai.
topics.pro: Logical evaluation is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT, which explains alias visibility and filter timing.
points: Aliases are available in ORDER BY.

example.sql: SELECT name AS n FROM students ORDER BY n;
example.output: Rows sorted by the alias n.

topics.title: Understanding Query Results
topics.simple: Result ek table jaisa hota hai — columns aur rows; zero rows bhi valid result hai.
topics.pro: A SELECT result is a relation with named columns and zero or more rows; an empty result is not an error and does not mean NULL.
points: Zero rows is a valid answer.
Column names come from the select list.
NULL is a value, not an empty result.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 100;

topics.title: SELECT Query Execution
topics.simple: Database query ko parse, plan aur execute karta hai.
topics.pro: The server parses the statement, rewrites it, plans access paths, then executes; EXPLAIN shows the plan without running the query.
points: The planner chooses scans and joins.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Common SELECT Mistakes
topics.simple: Common galtiyan: galat column, missing comma, alias WHERE me use karna, integer division bhoolna.
topics.pro: Typical mistakes are misspelled columns, trailing commas, assuming alias visibility in WHERE, integer division and expecting DISTINCT to apply to one column.

example.sql: SELECT names FROM students;

topics.title: SELECT Without FROM
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me FROM ke bina bhi expression select kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: SELECT without FROM evaluates the select list once and returns one row; it is useful for testing expressions and functions.
points: No table means one synthetic row.

example.sql: SELECT 1 + 1 AS answer;

topics.title: Practical Student Report Query
topics.simple: Ab columns, alias, calculation aur concatenation mila kar report banao.
topics.pro: A report query combines projection, aliases and expressions to produce a readable result without changing the table.

example.sql: SELECT id, name AS student, marks, marks + 5 AS boosted, name || ' (' || marks::text || ')' AS label FROM students;
example.output: A table with id, student, marks, boosted and label columns.

learn.q: Which category does SELECT belong to?
options: DQL
DML
DDL
DCL
learn.answer: DQL
learn.why: SELECT reads data; many curricula call that DQL.

learn.q: What does SELECT * return?
options: Every column of the relation
Only the first column
Only one row
The table definition
learn.answer: Every column of the relation
learn.why: * expands to every column at planning time.

learn.q: How do you return only name and marks?
options: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
SELECT * FROM students;
SELECT name marks;
SELECT ALL;
learn.answer: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
learn.why: List the columns in the select list.

learn.q: Which keyword gives a result column a temporary name?
options: AS
FROM
WHERE
ORDER
learn.answer: AS
learn.why: AS introduces a column alias.

learn.q: Is AS required for a column alias?
options: No, it is optional
Yes, always
Only in PostgreSQL
Only for numbers
learn.answer: No, it is optional
learn.why: SELECT name n is a valid alias form.

learn.q: What does SELECT 7 / 2 return?
options: An error
learn.why: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates.

learn.q: What does ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) return?
options: An error
learn.why: 7.0 is numeric, so the division keeps the fraction, and ROUND fixes the display scale.

learn.q: Which operator concatenates text?
options: CONCAT
learn.why: PostgreSQL uses || for string concatenation.

learn.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT do?
options: Removes duplicate result rows
Removes duplicate table rows
Sorts the rows
Counts the rows
learn.answer: Removes duplicate result rows
learn.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows.

learn.q: Does DISTINCT apply to one column or the whole select list?
options: The whole select list
Only the first column
Only numeric columns
Only the primary key
learn.answer: The whole select list
learn.why: The entire projected tuple is compared.

learn.q: Which clause runs first logically?
options: FROM
SELECT
ORDER BY
LIMIT
learn.answer: FROM
learn.why: The source rows are established before projection.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in WHERE in PostgreSQL?
options: No
Yes, always
Only with AS
Only for numbers
learn.answer: No
learn.why: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in ORDER BY?
options: Yes
No
Only with AS
Only in MySQL
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so aliases are available.

learn.q: Is SELECT 1; valid in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes, it returns one row
No, FROM is required
Only in psql
Only with an alias
learn.answer: Yes, it returns one row
learn.why: SELECT without FROM evaluates the expression once.

learn.q: What is an unaliased expression column named?
options: ?column?
result
expr
NULL
learn.answer: ?column?
learn.why: PostgreSQL uses ?column? when no alias is given.

learn.q: What does SELECT NULL return?
options: One row with NULL
Zero rows
An error
An empty string
learn.answer: One row with NULL
learn.why: NULL is a value, not an empty result.

learn.q: How many columns does SELECT name FROM students return?
options: One
Two
All columns
Zero
learn.answer: One
learn.why: The select list has one item.

learn.q: What does SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 return?
learn.why: Multiplication binds tighter than addition.

learn.q: What does SELECT (2 + 3) * 4 return?
learn.why: Parentheses force the addition first.

learn.q: What does a SELECT returning zero rows mean?
options: A valid empty result
An error
A NULL row
A missing table
learn.answer: A valid empty result
learn.why: No matching rows is a normal result set.

interview.q: What is SELECT?
interview.answer: DQL that projects a result set from relations and expressions without changing stored rows.

interview.q: What is the basic SELECT syntax?
interview.answer: SELECT select_list FROM relation [WHERE ...] [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...];

interview.q: What is the logical order of query evaluation?
interview.answer: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

interview.q: Why is SELECT * risky in production?
interview.answer: It returns every current and future column, can break consumers and transfers more data than needed.

interview.q: What is a column alias?
interview.answer: A temporary name for a result column; it does not rename the table column.

interview.q: Is AS required for an alias?
interview.answer: No, it is optional for column aliases, but it improves clarity.

interview.q: How do you preserve spaces or case in an alias?
interview.answer: Double-quote it, for example AS "Student Name".

interview.q: What is the difference between DISTINCT and GROUP BY?
interview.answer: DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows; GROUP BY forms groups for aggregates and can be paired with HAVING.

interview.q: Does DISTINCT apply to one column or all selected columns?
interview.answer: All selected columns; the whole tuple is compared.

interview.q: How does DISTINCT treat NULL?
interview.answer: It treats NULLs as equal for duplicate removal, so one NULL survives.

interview.q: Why does 7 / 2 return 3?
interview.answer: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates the fraction.

interview.q: How do you get 3.5 from 7 and 2?
interview.answer: Use a numeric operand and round the display, for example ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1). A bare numeric division can display extra scale digits.

interview.q: What does || do with NULL?
interview.answer: Concatenating NULL with anything returns NULL; use COALESCE if a fallback is needed.

interview.q: Why is an unaliased expression column called ?column??
interview.answer: PostgreSQL needs a name; without an alias it uses ?column? for the expression.

interview.q: Can SELECT run without FROM?
interview.answer: Yes. It evaluates the select list once and returns one row.

interview.q: Is SELECT read-only?
interview.answer: It does not change stored rows, though it can call functions; it is DQL.

interview.q: Why are aliases unavailable in WHERE?
interview.answer: Logical evaluation runs WHERE before SELECT, so the alias has not been defined yet.

interview.q: Why are aliases available in ORDER BY?
interview.answer: ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so the projected alias exists.

interview.q: What does an empty result set mean?
interview.answer: The query matched zero rows; it is not an error and not a NULL row.

interview.q: What is the difference between a column and an expression in SELECT?
interview.answer: A column reads a stored value; an expression computes a new value per row.

logic.q: Why can an alias not be used in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias has not been defined yet.

logic.q: Why is an alias available in ORDER BY?
logic.answer: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so the projected alias exists.

logic.q: Why does DISTINCT apply to the whole select list?
logic.answer: It compares complete projected rows; there is no per-column mode.

logic.q: Why can SELECT * break an application?
logic.answer: A new column changes the result shape and can break consumers that expect a fixed set.

logic.q: Why does 7 / 2 return 3?
logic.answer: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates.

logic.q: Why does 7.0 / 2 keep the fraction?
logic.answer: 7.0 is numeric, so the division uses numeric arithmetic.

logic.q: Why does NULL || text return NULL?
logic.answer: Concatenation with an unknown value is unknown; use COALESCE to supply a default.

logic.q: Why does multiplication run before addition?
logic.answer: SQL arithmetic gives * and / higher precedence than + and -.

logic.q: Why do parentheses matter in expressions?
logic.answer: They override precedence and make the intended grouping explicit.

logic.q: Why is an unaliased expression called ?column??
logic.answer: The result needs a name; PostgreSQL supplies a placeholder when none is given.

logic.q: Why is SELECT without FROM useful?
logic.answer: It evaluates expressions and functions once without needing a table.

logic.q: Why can DISTINCT be expensive?
logic.answer: It may sort or hash the whole result to find duplicates.

logic.q: Why does a zero-row result not mean NULL?
logic.answer: Zero rows is an empty relation; NULL is a value inside a row.

logic.q: Why quote an alias with spaces?
logic.answer: Unquoted identifiers cannot contain spaces and fold to lowercase; quotes preserve the exact text.

logic.q: Why are SQL keywords case-insensitive?
logic.answer: The parser normalizes keywords, so SELECT and select mean the same thing.
