modules.title: WHERE Clause and Filtering
modules.goal: Write precise predicates and avoid NULL and precedence traps.

topics.title: Introduction to WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE rows ko filter karta hai — sirf matching rows result me aate hain.
topics.pro: WHERE is a row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; it keeps only rows whose predicate is true.
points: False or unknown rows are removed.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Filtering Rows
topics.simple: Filter lagane se result chhota aur relevant hota hai.
topics.pro: A predicate is a boolean expression; rows with a true result pass, while false and NULL results are discarded.
points: A predicate returns true, false or unknown.
Unknown behaves like false for filtering.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 60;

topics.title: Equality (=)
topics.simple: = exact match check karta hai.
topics.pro: The equality operator compares two values and returns true only when they are equal; NULL never equals anything.
points: Double quotes are identifiers, not strings.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';

topics.title: Inequality (!= and <>)
topics.simple: Not equal ke liye <> ya != use karo.
topics.pro: Both <> and != mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks <> 80;

topics.title: Greater Than and Less Than
topics.simple: > bada aur < chhota compare karta hai.
topics.pro: > and < compare values using the type’s ordering; they work for numbers, dates and text under the database collation.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Greater Than or Equal and Less Than or Equal
topics.simple: >= aur <= boundary value ko bhi include karte hain.
topics.pro: >= keeps values greater than or equal to the boundary; <= keeps values less than or equal to it.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

topics.title: AND
topics.simple: AND tab true hota hai jab dono conditions true hon.
topics.pro: AND combines predicates with logical conjunction; both sides must be true for the row to pass.
points: One false side rejects the row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 AND marks <= 90;

topics.title: OR
topics.simple: OR tab true hota hai jab koi ek condition true ho.
topics.pro: OR combines predicates with logical disjunction; at least one side must be true for the row to pass.
points: Two false sides reject the row.
NULL on both sides yields unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera';

topics.title: NOT
topics.simple: NOT condition ko ulta karta hai.
topics.pro: NOT negates a boolean predicate; NOT true is false, NOT false is true and NOT unknown is unknown.
points: NOT is not the same as !=.
Negating a NULL predicate stays unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE NOT (marks < 60);
example.output: Students with 60 or more, excluding NULL marks.

topics.title: Combining AND, OR and NOT
topics.simple: Mixed conditions me precedence aur parentheses bahut important hain.
topics.pro: Mixed predicates combine with NOT, AND and OR; AND binds tighter than OR, so parentheses should state the intended grouping.
points: NOT applies to the expression that follows.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN
topics.simple: BETWEEN inclusive range check karta hai.
topics.pro: BETWEEN low AND high is inclusive on both ends; NOT BETWEEN keeps values outside the range.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

topics.title: IN and NOT IN
topics.simple: IN list me se koi match check karta hai.
topics.pro: IN tests membership in a value list; NOT IN tests exclusion, with a dangerous NULL behaviour.
points: IN is shorthand for several ORs.
NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows.
The list values must be comparable.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name IN ('Aarav', 'Meera', 'Kabir');

topics.title: LIKE and NOT LIKE
topics.simple: LIKE pattern matching karta hai, NOT LIKE ulta.
topics.pro: LIKE matches text against a pattern with % and _ wildcards; it is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL, while ILIKE is case-insensitive.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

topics.title: Percent Wildcard
topics.simple: % kisi bhi length ke characters ko match karta hai.
topics.pro: The % wildcard matches zero or more characters in a LIKE pattern.
points: A% matches names starting with A.
A leading % usually prevents a plain index scan.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '%a%';

topics.title: Underscore Wildcard
topics.simple: _ exactly ek character match karta hai.
topics.pro: The _ wildcard matches exactly one character, so it is useful for fixed-position patterns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '_a%';
example.output: Names whose second character is a.

topics.title: IS NULL
topics.simple: NULL check karne ke liye IS NULL use karo, = NULL nahi.
topics.pro: IS NULL is the only reliable null test; equality with NULL returns unknown and filters every row out.
points: IS NULL is the correct predicate.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;

topics.title: IS NOT NULL
topics.simple: IS NOT NULL aise rows deta hai jahan value present ho.
topics.pro: IS NOT NULL keeps rows where the column has a real value rather than NULL.
points: It is the negation of IS NULL.
It does not treat empty string as NULL.
Use it before comparing optional columns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: Boolean Filtering
topics.simple: Boolean column ko seedha WHERE me use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A boolean column is itself a predicate; WHERE active keeps true, WHERE NOT active keeps false, and NULL is excluded from both.
points: Use IS NOT TRUE to include NULL.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM users WHERE active;

topics.title: Operator Precedence
topics.simple: Comparison pehle, phir NOT, phir AND, phir OR.
topics.pro: Comparison operators bind tighter than NOT, NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR; rely on parentheses when mixing.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 OR name = 'Aarav' AND marks > 60;

topics.title: Parentheses
topics.simple: Parentheses se condition ka group clear karo.
topics.pro: Parentheses override precedence and make the intended logic readable; they are the cheapest way to prevent a filter bug.
points: Group OR before AND when needed.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: Case Sensitivity and ILIKE
topics.simple: PostgreSQL text comparison case-sensitive hai; ILIKE case-insensitive match deta hai.
topics.pro: LIKE and = compare text case-sensitively under the collation; ILIKE lowercases both sides for matching, and LOWER(name) is the portable alternative.
points: LOWER() can match but may not use a plain index.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name ILIKE 'aarav';

topics.title: Escaping Wildcards
topics.simple: Literal % ya _ match karna ho to ESCAPE use karo.
topics.pro: A backslash escapes % and _ in a LIKE pattern when ESCAPE is declared; without escaping, the wildcard keeps its special meaning.

example.sql: SELECT code FROM items WHERE code LIKE 'A\_%' ESCAPE '\';
example.output: Codes starting with the literal A_.

topics.title: Complex WHERE Conditions
topics.simple: Real filters me multiple AND, OR, IN, LIKE aur NULL checks combine hote hain.
topics.pro: A complex predicate should be built in layers: isolate each rule, parenthesize OR groups, and test the row count before trusting the result.
points: Write one rule at a time.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE 'M%') AND marks BETWEEN 60 AND 95 AND email IS NOT NULL;
example.output: Matching names with marks in range and a known email.

topics.title: Practical Student Filtering
topics.simple: Ab multiple filters ko mila kar ek useful student report banao.
topics.pro: A production filter combines range, membership, pattern and null checks while keeping each predicate readable and index-friendly.
points: Avoid leading wildcards on large tables.
Verify the row count before shipping.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND name LIKE 'A%' AND email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY marks DESC;
example.output: Students in range whose name starts with A and have an email.

learn.q: What does WHERE do?
options: Filters rows before grouping
Sorts rows
Groups rows
Creates a table
learn.answer: Filters rows before grouping
learn.why: WHERE keeps rows whose predicate is true.

learn.q: Which operator tests equality?
options: eq
learn.why: SQL uses a single = for equality.

learn.q: Which two operators mean not equal?
options: <> and !=
== and =
= and <=
! and ?
learn.answer: <> and !=
learn.why: Both are accepted; <> is standard SQL.

learn.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
options: Yes, both ends
No, both ends excluded
Only the low end
Only the high end
learn.answer: Yes, both ends
learn.why: BETWEEN low AND high includes both boundaries.

learn.q: What is IN shorthand for?
options: Several OR equality checks
Several AND checks
A range check
A null check
learn.answer: Several OR equality checks
learn.why: name IN (a, b) matches either value.

learn.q: Is LIKE case-sensitive in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes
No
Only for numbers
Only with %
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is case-insensitive.

learn.q: Which operator is case-insensitive?
options: ILIKE
LIKE
learn.answer: ILIKE
learn.why: ILIKE lowercases both sides for matching.

learn.q: What does % match in a LIKE pattern?
options: Any sequence of characters
Exactly one character
Only digits
Only spaces
learn.answer: Any sequence of characters
learn.why: % matches zero or more characters.

learn.q: What does _ match in a LIKE pattern?
options: Exactly one character
Any sequence
A literal underscore
Nothing
learn.answer: Exactly one character
learn.why: _ is a single-character wildcard.

learn.q: How do you test for NULL?
options: IS NULL
= NULL
== NULL
NULL()
learn.answer: IS NULL
learn.why: Equality with NULL is unknown and never matches.

learn.q: What does name = NULL return?
options: No rows
All rows
Rows with empty names
An error
learn.answer: No rows
learn.why: The comparison is unknown for every row.

learn.q: What does NOT IN (1, NULL) return?
options: No rows for non-null values
Every row
Only NULL rows
A syntax error
learn.answer: No rows for non-null values
learn.why: Each comparison with NULL becomes unknown, so the NOT IN predicate never passes.

learn.q: Which binds tighter: AND or OR?
options: AND
OR
They are equal
NOT
learn.answer: AND
learn.why: AND has higher precedence than OR.

learn.q: Why use parentheses in mixed conditions?
options: To state the intended grouping
To make queries slower
To remove NULLs
To create an index
learn.answer: To state the intended grouping
learn.why: Parentheses override precedence and prevent logic bugs.

learn.q: What does WHERE active keep?
options: Only true rows
Only false rows
True and NULL rows
All rows
learn.answer: Only true rows
learn.why: A boolean predicate passes only when it is true.

learn.q: What does WHERE active IS NOT TRUE keep?
options: False and NULL rows
Only true rows
Only NULL rows
All rows
learn.answer: False and NULL rows
learn.why: IS NOT TRUE is true for false and unknown.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in WHERE?
options: No
Yes, always
Only with AS
Only for numbers
learn.answer: No
learn.why: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT defines the alias.

learn.q: Can WHERE use aggregate functions?
options: No
Yes, always
Only COUNT
Only with GROUP BY
learn.answer: No
learn.why: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE; use HAVING after grouping.

learn.q: Which pattern matches names starting with A?
options: LIKE 'A%'
LIKE '%A'
LIKE '_A'
LIKE 'A_'
learn.answer: LIKE 'A%'
learn.why: A% means A followed by any sequence.

learn.q: Which pattern matches a second character of a?
options: LIKE '_a%'
LIKE 'a_%'
LIKE '%a'
LIKE 'a%'
learn.answer: LIKE '_a%'
learn.why: _ matches the first character and a is the second.

interview.q: What is WHERE?
interview.answer: A row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; only rows whose predicate is true pass.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

interview.q: What comparison operators does SQL provide?
interview.answer: =, <>, !=, >, <, >= and <=, plus BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and IS NULL predicates.

interview.q: What is the difference between <> and !=?
interview.answer: Both mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.

interview.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
interview.answer: Yes, both the low and high boundaries are included.

interview.q: What is IN equivalent to?
interview.answer: A chain of OR equality comparisons, such as x = a OR x = b.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN with NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: Every comparison with NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate can return no rows unexpectedly.

interview.q: What is the difference between LIKE and ILIKE?
interview.answer: LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is case-insensitive in PostgreSQL.

interview.q: What do % and _ mean in LIKE?
interview.answer: % matches any sequence of characters; _ matches exactly one character.

interview.q: How do you match a literal % or _?
interview.answer: Escape it with a backslash and declare ESCAPE, for example LIKE A\_% ESCAPE '\'.

interview.q: How do you test for NULL?
interview.answer: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches.

interview.q: What is three-valued logic?
interview.answer: SQL predicates can be true, false or unknown; unknown arises from NULL comparisons and is filtered like false.

interview.q: How does WHERE treat a boolean column?
interview.answer: The column is itself the predicate: WHERE active keeps true rows.

interview.q: How do you include false and NULL boolean rows?
interview.answer: Use WHERE active IS NOT TRUE; WHERE NOT active keeps only false.

interview.q: What is the precedence of NOT, AND and OR?
interview.answer: NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR.

interview.q: Why use parentheses?
interview.answer: They override precedence and document the intended grouping.

interview.q: Can a SELECT alias be used in WHERE?
interview.answer: No, because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT.

interview.q: Can WHERE use functions?
interview.answer: Yes, but a function on a column can prevent a plain index scan.

interview.q: Why can a leading % hurt performance?
interview.answer: It prevents a normal B-tree index scan because the pattern has no fixed prefix.

interview.q: How do you filter a date range?
interview.answer: Use >= start AND < next_day for a half-open range, or BETWEEN for inclusive dates.

logic.q: Why does name = NULL return no rows?
logic.answer: Equality with an unknown value is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true rows.

logic.q: Why does NOT IN (1, NULL) return no rows?
logic.answer: Each comparison against NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate never becomes true.

logic.q: Why does AND bind tighter than OR?
logic.answer: SQL gives AND higher precedence, so a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c).

logic.q: Why use parentheses even when precedence is known?
logic.answer: They document intent and prevent a later edit from changing the logic.

logic.q: Why is BETWEEN inclusive?
logic.answer: It expands to low <= x AND x <= high, including both boundaries.

logic.q: Why is LIKE case-sensitive?
logic.answer: It compares text under the collation without case folding; ILIKE performs the case-insensitive match.

logic.q: Why can ILIKE be slower?
logic.answer: It cannot use a plain B-tree index on the original text; it may need a scan or a special index.

logic.q: Why can LOWER(name) prevent an index scan?
logic.answer: A plain index on name does not index LOWER(name); use an expression index if needed.

logic.q: Why does WHERE active exclude NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL boolean is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true.

logic.q: Why does IS NOT TRUE include NULL?
logic.answer: It is true for both false and unknown values.

logic.q: Why does a leading % hurt performance?
logic.answer: The pattern has no fixed prefix, so a normal B-tree cannot seek to a starting point.

logic.q: Why does _ match exactly one character?
logic.answer: It is the single-character wildcard in LIKE patterns.

logic.q: Why use ESCAPE?
logic.answer: It tells LIKE which character makes the next wildcard literal.

logic.q: Why can a SELECT alias not be used in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the surviving rows are grouped and aggregated.

modules.title: ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET
modules.goal: Produce deterministic sorted pages and top-N reports.

topics.title: Introduction to ORDER BY
topics.simple: ORDER BY result rows ko sort karta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY sorts the final result set using one or more sort expressions; it runs after SELECT and DISTINCT and before LIMIT.
points: No ORDER BY means no guaranteed order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Rows
topics.simple: Sorting se rows ek predictable sequence me aate hain.
topics.pro: A sort key defines the comparison used to order rows; equal keys keep an unspecified relative order unless a tie-breaker is added.
points: One key is enough for simple reports.
The result is only guaranteed when the order is total.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks;

topics.title: ASC
topics.simple: ASC ascending order me sort karta hai — chhota se bada.
topics.pro: ASC is the default sort direction and orders values from smallest to largest, or A to Z for text.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC;

topics.title: DESC
topics.simple: DESC descending order me sort karta hai — bada se chhota.
topics.pro: DESC orders values from largest to smallest, or Z to A for text.
points: It is not a stable sort by itself.
Add a tie-breaker for deterministic pages.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Numeric Data
topics.simple: Numbers natural numeric order me sort hote hain, text order me nahi.
topics.pro: Numeric columns sort by value, so 9 comes before 10; storing numbers as text would sort 10 before 9.
points: Use numeric types for numeric sorting.
Casting text to numeric changes the order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Text Data
topics.simple: Text sort collation par depend karta hai; case aur language order badal sakta hai.
topics.pro: Text ordering follows the column collation, which controls case and locale rules; use LOWER() or a case-insensitive collation when needed.
points: A and a may sort differently by collation.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY LOWER(name);

topics.title: Sorting Date Values
topics.simple: Dates chronological order me sort hoti hain.
topics.pro: Date and timestamp values sort chronologically; DESC gives newest first.
points: Earlier dates come first in ASC.
Timestamps include time within the day.

example.sql: SELECT student_id, enrolled_on FROM enrollments ORDER BY enrolled_on DESC;

topics.title: Multiple Sort Keys
topics.simple: Pehla key main order deta hai, doosra key ties todta hai.
topics.pro: Multiple ORDER BY expressions are applied left to right: the first is primary, later keys break ties.
points: Each key has its own direction.
The last key should make the order deterministic.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, name ASC;
example.output: Highest known marks first, ties alphabetical.

topics.title: Sorting by Aliases and Expressions
topics.simple: ORDER BY alias ya expression use kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY can reference a select-list alias or repeat an expression, because it is evaluated after SELECT.
points: Aliases do not work in WHERE.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks * 2 AS doubled FROM students ORDER BY doubled DESC;
example.output: Rows ordered by the doubled value.

topics.title: NULL Sorting
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me ASC default NULLs last, DESC default NULLs first.
topics.pro: By default PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than any non-null value: ASC places NULLs last and DESC places them first; NULLS FIRST/LAST overrides it.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC NULLS LAST;
example.output: Known marks ascending, NULL marks last.

topics.title: LIMIT
topics.simple: LIMIT result ki maximum row count set karta hai.
topics.pro: LIMIT caps the number of rows returned after sorting; LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary subset.
points: Use ORDER BY for meaningful top-N.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3;

topics.title: OFFSET
topics.simple: OFFSET starting rows skip karta hai.
topics.pro: OFFSET skips a number of rows after sorting and before the limit is applied.
points: Large offsets still scan skipped rows.
Use with ORDER BY for stable pages.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;

topics.title: Pagination
topics.simple: Pagination me page size aur page number se LIMIT/OFFSET nikalte hain.
topics.pro: A page uses LIMIT page_size OFFSET (page - 1) * page_size, with a deterministic ORDER BY so rows do not shift between pages.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

topics.title: Top N Records
topics.simple: Top N ke liye ORDER BY DESC aur LIMIT N use karo.
topics.pro: Top-N queries sort by the ranking key descending and cap the result; ties need an explicit tie-breaker or a window function for exact semantics.
points: Ties can make the cut arbitrary.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5;

topics.title: Bottom N Records
topics.simple: Bottom N ke liye ascending order aur LIMIT use karo.
topics.pro: Bottom-N queries sort ascending and cap the result; NULL placement can affect what counts as the bottom.
points: NULLS LAST keeps unknown values out of the bottom.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5;

topics.title: Deterministic Ordering
topics.simple: Deterministic order ke liye unique tie-breaker add karo.
topics.pro: A total ordering uses a unique key as the final sort expression, so equal values cannot swap between pages or runs.
points: Add id as the last key.
Without it, LIMIT can change between runs.
Stable pages need a total order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC;
example.output: Marks descending, NULLs last, id breaking every tie.

topics.title: Positional ORDER BY
topics.simple: ORDER BY 2 select list ke doosre column ko refer karta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY can use a select-list position, but positional references are fragile when the projection changes and should be avoided in application SQL.
points: Position 1 is the first output column.
It breaks when columns are reordered.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY 2 DESC;
example.output: Rows ordered by marks, the second column.

topics.title: ORDER BY with WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE pehle filter karta hai, phir ORDER BY sort karta hai.
topics.pro: Logical evaluation filters rows in WHERE, projects them in SELECT, then sorts the surviving rows in ORDER BY.
points: Sorting only the filtered rows is cheaper.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Performance
topics.simple: Bade result ko sort karna costly hota hai; index madad kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: A sort may use memory or disk; a matching B-tree index can return rows already ordered and avoid a sort for prefix-ordered queries.
points: Indexes help matching ORDER BY prefixes.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10;
example.output: An Index Scan or a Sort depending on available indexes.

topics.title: Practical Ranking Report
topics.simple: Ab filter, sort, tie-breaker aur limit mila kar ranking report banao.
topics.pro: A reliable ranking report combines a filter, a deterministic ORDER BY, an explicit NULL policy and a LIMIT, and is reviewed with EXPLAIN when it grows.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks IS NOT NULL ORDER BY marks DESC, id ASC LIMIT 10;
example.output: Top ten known marks with stable ties.

learn.q: What does ORDER BY do?
options: Sorts the result rows
Filters rows
Groups rows
Creates a table
learn.answer: Sorts the result rows
learn.why: ORDER BY defines the final row order.

learn.q: Which direction is the default?
options: ASC
DESC
Random
None
learn.answer: ASC
learn.why: ASC is assumed when no direction is written.

learn.q: What does DESC do?
options: Sorts largest to smallest
Sorts smallest to largest
Removes duplicates
Limits rows
learn.answer: Sorts largest to smallest
learn.why: DESC reverses the comparison order.

learn.q: How do you sort by marks highest first?
options: ORDER BY marks DESC
ORDER BY marks ASC
ORDER BY marks
ORDER BY DESC marks
learn.answer: ORDER BY marks DESC
learn.why: DESC puts the largest values first.

learn.q: How do you break ties after marks?
options: Add name ASC as a second key
Use LIMIT
Use OFFSET
Use DISTINCT
learn.answer: Add name ASC as a second key
learn.why: Later sort keys break ties from earlier keys.

learn.q: Can ORDER BY use a select-list alias?
options: Yes
No
Only with AS
Only for numbers
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so aliases exist.

learn.q: Does PostgreSQL put NULLs first or last for ASC?
options: Last by default
First by default
Always first
Always last
learn.answer: Last by default
learn.why: NULL sorts as larger than non-null values, so ASC puts it last.

learn.q: Does PostgreSQL put NULLs first or last for DESC?
options: First by default
Last by default
Always last
Never
learn.answer: First by default
learn.why: DESC reverses the default, so NULLs come first.

learn.q: Which clause overrides NULL placement?
options: NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST
LIMIT
OFFSET
DISTINCT
learn.answer: NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST
learn.why: Both are ORDER BY modifiers.

learn.q: What does LIMIT 5 return?
options: At most five rows
Exactly five rows
Five columns
Five pages
learn.answer: At most five rows
learn.why: The result can have fewer rows.

learn.q: What does OFFSET 10 do?
options: Skips the first ten rows
Returns ten rows
Sorts ten rows
Deletes ten rows
learn.answer: Skips the first ten rows
learn.why: OFFSET drops rows before the limit is applied.

learn.q: What is page 3 with page size 10?
options: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 10
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 3
learn.answer: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
learn.why: Offset is (page - 1) × size.

learn.q: What is the top-N pattern?
options: ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT N
ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N
LIMIT N without ORDER BY
OFFSET N
learn.answer: ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT N
learn.why: Sort the ranking key descending, then cap.

learn.q: What is the bottom-N pattern?
options: ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N
ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT N
LIMIT N only
OFFSET N only
learn.answer: ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N
learn.why: Ascending puts the smallest first.

learn.q: Why add a unique tie-breaker?
options: To make the order deterministic
To remove duplicates
To speed up filtering
To add an index
learn.answer: To make the order deterministic
learn.why: A total order prevents equal keys from swapping.

learn.q: What does ORDER BY 2 refer to?
options: The second output column
The second table
Two rows
The second schema
learn.answer: The second output column
learn.why: Positional ORDER BY references the select list.

learn.q: Should application SQL use positional ORDER BY?
options: No, it is fragile
Yes, always
Only with LIMIT
Only in PostgreSQL
learn.answer: No, it is fragile
learn.why: Changing the projection can silently change the sort.

learn.q: Does WHERE run before ORDER BY?
options: Yes
No
They run together
ORDER BY runs first
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: Rows are filtered before they are sorted.

learn.q: What does LIMIT without ORDER BY return?
options: An arbitrary subset
The first rows by primary key
The last rows
An error
learn.answer: An arbitrary subset
learn.why: Without ORDER BY there is no guaranteed row order.

learn.q: Which clause applies last?
options: LIMIT
WHERE
SELECT
ORDER BY
learn.answer: LIMIT
learn.why: Logical order ends with LIMIT/OFFSET.

interview.q: What is ORDER BY?
interview.answer: The clause that sorts the final result set using one or more expressions.

interview.q: What is the default sort direction?
interview.answer: ASC, from smallest to largest or A to Z.

interview.q: How do you sort descending?
interview.answer: Add DESC after the sort expression.

interview.q: How do multiple ORDER BY keys work?
interview.answer: They are applied left to right; later keys break ties from earlier keys.

interview.q: Can ORDER BY use an alias?
interview.answer: Yes, because ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT.

interview.q: Can WHERE use a SELECT alias?
interview.answer: No, because WHERE runs before SELECT.

interview.q: How does PostgreSQL sort NULLs by default?
interview.answer: As larger than non-null values: NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC.

interview.q: How do you force NULLs last?
interview.answer: Add NULLS LAST to the ORDER BY expression.

interview.q: What does LIMIT do?
interview.answer: Caps the number of rows returned after sorting.

interview.q: What does OFFSET do?
interview.answer: Skips a number of rows before the limit is applied.

interview.q: How do you calculate a pagination offset?
interview.answer: Offset = (page - 1) × page_size, with page 1 at offset 0.

interview.q: Why is LIMIT without ORDER BY unsafe?
interview.answer: The database may return any subset because no row order is guaranteed.

interview.q: Why is a tie-breaker important for pagination?
interview.answer: Equal sort keys can swap between pages; a unique final key makes the order total.

interview.q: What is top-N SQL?
interview.answer: ORDER BY ranking_key DESC LIMIT n, with a tie-breaker for stable results.

interview.q: What is the difference between LIMIT and FETCH FIRST?
interview.answer: LIMIT is PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite syntax; FETCH FIRST is standard SQL and also supported by PostgreSQL.

interview.q: Why can a large OFFSET be slow?
interview.answer: The database still has to scan and discard the skipped rows.

interview.q: What is keyset pagination?
interview.answer: Paginating by a stable key, such as WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n, instead of skipping a large offset.

interview.q: How can an index help ORDER BY?
interview.answer: A B-tree index matching the sort prefix can return rows already ordered and avoid a sort.

interview.q: Why does text sort vary?
interview.answer: Text ordering follows the collation, which controls case and locale rules.

interview.q: Can ORDER BY use an expression?
interview.answer: Yes, including functions and arithmetic, but the expression must be evaluated for each row.

logic.q: Why is ORDER BY without LIMIT potentially expensive?
logic.answer: The database may sort the entire result before returning any rows.

logic.q: Why is LIMIT without ORDER BY arbitrary?
logic.answer: There is no guaranteed row order, so any subset may be chosen.

logic.q: Why add a unique tie-breaker?
logic.answer: Equal sort keys can swap between runs and pages; a unique final key makes the order total.

logic.q: Why does ASC put NULLs last in PostgreSQL?
logic.answer: NULL sorts as larger than any non-null value in the default ordering.

logic.q: Why does DESC put NULLs first?
logic.answer: DESC reverses the default ordering, so the largest value (NULL) comes first.

logic.q: Why can text sorting surprise you?
logic.answer: Collation controls case and locale rules, so A and a may not sort as expected.

logic.q: Why does a large OFFSET get slower?
logic.answer: The server still scans and discards every skipped row.

logic.q: Why is keyset pagination often faster?
logic.answer: It seeks directly after the last key instead of counting and discarding rows.

logic.q: Why does an alias work in ORDER BY but not WHERE?
logic.answer: ORDER BY runs after SELECT defines the alias; WHERE runs before it.

logic.q: Why is positional ORDER BY fragile?
logic.answer: Changing the select list reorders or removes the referenced position.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before ORDER BY?
logic.answer: Filtering first reduces the rows that must be sorted.

logic.q: Why does SELECT DISTINCT restrict ORDER BY expressions?
logic.answer: For DISTINCT, ORDER BY expressions must appear in the select list so the sort is defined on the projected rows.

logic.q: Why can an index satisfy ORDER BY?
logic.answer: A B-tree index matching the sort prefix returns rows in the requested order without a separate sort.

logic.q: Why does LIMIT apply after ORDER BY?
logic.answer: The rows must be ordered before the first N can be chosen.

logic.q: Why is ORDER BY random() expensive?
logic.answer: It computes a random value for every row and sorts the whole set with no useful index.

modules.title: UPDATE, DELETE and Data Modification
modules.goal: Modify and remove rows safely, with verification and rollback.

topics.title: What Is UPDATE?
topics.simple: UPDATE existing rows ke values badalta hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE is DML that changes column values for rows matched by an optional WHERE clause and returns a count of affected rows.
points: Without WHERE it targets every row.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: UPDATE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is UPDATE table SET column = expression [, ...] [FROM ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].
points: SET lists assignments separated by commas.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S' WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating One Column
topics.simple: Ek column ki value badalne ke liye ek assignment likho.
topics.pro: A single-column UPDATE assigns one expression to one column for every matched row.
points: Use the primary key in WHERE for a single row.
The new value must satisfy the column type.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns ko comma se update karo.
topics.pro: Multiple assignments run in one statement; all expressions see the row values from before the statement, not the just-assigned values.
points: Assignments are evaluated from the old row.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S', marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se sirf intended rows update karo.
topics.pro: A WHERE predicate targets specific rows; a unique key gives the smallest and safest target.
points: Match on a key when possible.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 88 WHERE id = 2;

topics.title: UPDATE with WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE ke bina UPDATE poore table ko chhu sakta hai.
topics.pro: WHERE filters the target rows before assignment; omitting it updates every row in the table.
points: Use IS NULL for null checks.
Test the predicate with SELECT first.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 0 WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with Expressions
topics.simple: New value purani value par calculation ho sakti hai.
topics.pro: The SET expression can reference existing columns, arithmetic, functions and CASE, and is evaluated for each matched row.
points: The result must fit the column type.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with CASE and COALESCE
topics.simple: CASE conditional value deta hai; COALESCE fallback deta hai.
topics.pro: CASE chooses a value per row, while COALESCE replaces NULL with a fallback; both are common in data-repair updates.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET email = COALESCE(email, 'unknown@example.com');

topics.title: UPDATE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se naya value compute kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery in SET must return at most one row and one column; a multi-row result raises an error.
points: A NULL subquery result assigns NULL.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with FROM
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me UPDATE FROM doosri table se values laata hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE ... FROM joins the target to a source relation; each target row should match at most one source row to keep the result deterministic.
points: Duplicate source matches make the update unpredictable.

example.sql: UPDATE students s SET marks = a.marks FROM applicants a WHERE s.email = a.email;

topics.title: RETURNING with UPDATE
topics.simple: RETURNING updated rows wapas deta hai.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the new row values for every updated row, including generated values and expressions.
points: It can return old values only via a CTE or trigger.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: What Is DELETE?
topics.simple: DELETE rows ko table se hataata hai.
topics.pro: DELETE is DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the number deleted.
points: Without WHERE it removes every row.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 3;

topics.title: DELETE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is DELETE FROM table [USING ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

topics.title: DELETE Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se specific row delete karo.
topics.pro: A precise predicate deletes only the intended rows; a primary key is the safest target.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4;

topics.title: DELETE with Conditions
topics.simple: Range, list aur NULL conditions delete me bhi kaam karte hain.
topics.pro: DELETE accepts the same boolean predicates as SELECT, including comparisons, IN, LIKE and IS NULL.
points: Use IS NULL for null checks.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: DELETE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se decide kar sakte hain kaunse rows delete honge.
topics.pro: DELETE with IN or EXISTS uses a subquery to choose rows; beware NOT IN with NULLs, which can match nothing.
points: IN works for a list of keys.
NOT EXISTS is safer with NULLs.
The subquery must be correct before deleting.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

topics.title: DELETE with USING
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me DELETE USING doosri table se join karke rows delete karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE ... USING adds source relations to the WHERE join, removing target rows that match the source.
points: Join the target and source in WHERE.
A row is deleted at most once.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students s USING enrollments e WHERE s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_id = 10;

topics.title: RETURNING with DELETE
topics.simple: RETURNING deleted rows ko wapas deta hai — archive ke liye useful.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the deleted row values, which can be inserted into an archive table in the same statement.
points: Return the rows before they disappear.
Combine with a CTE to archive.
RETURNING does not prevent the delete.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
topics.simple: DELETE filtered aur trigger-friendly hai; TRUNCATE poora table jaldi khali karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE removes selected rows, fires row triggers and is transactional; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and is transactional in PostgreSQL.
points: TRUNCATE resets storage; RESTART IDENTITY resets sequences.

example.sql: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

topics.title: Safe Modification Practices and Common Errors
topics.simple: Bade UPDATE/DELETE se pehle SELECT, transaction aur row count check karo.
topics.pro: Safe modification means previewing the target rows, wrapping the change in a transaction, checking the affected count and using RETURNING or a backup before committing.
points: Commit only after the count matches.
Use RETURNING for an audit trail.

learn.q: What does UPDATE do?
options: Changes existing rows
Adds rows
Removes rows
Creates a table
learn.answer: Changes existing rows
learn.why: UPDATE is DML that changes column values.

learn.q: What does DELETE do?
options: Removes rows
Changes rows
Adds rows
Creates a table
learn.answer: Removes rows
learn.why: DELETE is DML that removes rows.

learn.q: What happens to UPDATE without WHERE?
options: Every row is updated
No row is updated
Only the first row is updated
The statement fails
learn.answer: Every row is updated
learn.why: Without a predicate, UPDATE targets the whole table.

learn.q: What happens to DELETE without WHERE?
options: Every row is deleted
No row is deleted
Only the first row is deleted
The table is dropped
learn.answer: Every row is deleted
learn.why: Without a predicate, DELETE removes all rows.

learn.q: Which clause limits UPDATE or DELETE?
options: WHERE
LIMIT
ORDER BY
GROUP BY
learn.answer: WHERE
learn.why: WHERE selects the target rows.

learn.q: How do you update two columns at once?
options: Comma-separated SET assignments
Two SET keywords
Two UPDATE statements only
A CREATE TABLE
learn.answer: Comma-separated SET assignments
learn.why: SET name = ..., marks = ... updates both.

learn.q: What does RETURNING do?
options: Returns affected rows
Rolls back the change
Creates an index
Sorts the rows
learn.answer: Returns affected rows
learn.why: RETURNING exposes changed or deleted rows.

learn.q: Which value does SET marks = marks + 5 use?
options: The old marks value
The new marks value
Zero
NULL
learn.answer: The old marks value
learn.why: Assignments read the row as it was before the statement.

learn.q: Which function supplies a fallback for NULL?
options: COALESCE
COUNT
LOWER
ROUND
learn.answer: COALESCE
learn.why: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument.

learn.q: What must a scalar subquery in SET return?
options: At most one row and one column
Any number of rows
Exactly two columns
A table
learn.answer: At most one row and one column
learn.why: A scalar subquery must produce a single value.

learn.q: Which PostgreSQL clause joins a source table to UPDATE?
options: FROM
USING
JOIN
INTO
learn.answer: FROM
learn.why: UPDATE ... FROM adds source relations.

learn.q: Which PostgreSQL clause joins a source table to DELETE?
options: USING
FROM
JOIN
INTO
learn.answer: USING
learn.why: DELETE ... USING adds source relations.

learn.q: Does DELETE keep the table structure?
options: Yes
No
Only with CASCADE
Only without WHERE
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: DELETE removes rows; the table remains.

learn.q: Does TRUNCATE support WHERE?
options: No
Yes
Only with CASCADE
Only on small tables
learn.answer: No
learn.why: TRUNCATE always targets the whole table.

learn.q: Does DELETE fire row-level DELETE triggers?
options: Yes
No
Only with RETURNING
Only with CASCADE
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: DELETE removes rows individually and fires row triggers.

learn.q: Does TRUNCATE fire row-level DELETE triggers?
options: No
Yes
Only with RESTART IDENTITY
Only with CASCADE
learn.answer: No
learn.why: TRUNCATE does not delete rows one by one.

learn.q: Does DELETE reset an identity sequence?
options: No
Yes
Only with CASCADE
Only without WHERE
learn.answer: No
learn.why: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY resets it.

learn.q: Can DELETE be rolled back in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes
No
Only with TRUNCATE
Only outside a transaction
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: DELETE is transactional.

learn.q: What does UPDATE ... RETURNING show?
options: The new row values
The old row values by default
The table definition
The query plan
learn.answer: The new row values
learn.why: RETURNING returns the updated row as stored.

learn.q: What is the safest target for UPDATE?
options: A primary key
A text column with duplicates
A NULL column
Every row
learn.answer: A primary key
learn.why: A unique key targets exactly the intended row.

interview.q: What is UPDATE?
interview.answer: DML that changes column values for rows matched by WHERE and returns the affected count.

interview.q: What is DELETE?
interview.answer: DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the deleted count.

interview.q: What happens without WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE?
interview.answer: The statement targets every row in the table.

interview.q: How do multiple SET assignments evaluate?
interview.answer: All expressions read the row values from before the statement, not values assigned earlier in the same SET list.

interview.q: How do you update from another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use UPDATE ... FROM source WHERE join_condition; each target row should match at most one source row.

interview.q: How do you delete using another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use DELETE FROM target USING source WHERE join_condition; each target row is deleted at most once.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: Returns the changed or deleted rows in the same statement.

interview.q: What is a scalar subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery that returns at most one row and one column, usable where a single value is expected.

interview.q: What happens if a SET subquery returns multiple rows?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL raises an error because the subquery is not scalar.

interview.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DELETE supports WHERE, fires row triggers and removes selected rows; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and resets storage.

interview.q: Is TRUNCATE transactional in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Yes, it can be rolled back there; MySQL performs an implicit commit.

interview.q: Does DELETE reset identity?
interview.answer: No; use TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY or reset the sequence explicitly.

interview.q: How do you archive deleted rows?
interview.answer: Use DELETE ... RETURNING inside a CTE and insert the returned rows into an archive table.

interview.q: Why is DELETE with NOT IN and NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: The NULL comparison makes the predicate unknown, so no rows may be deleted; NOT EXISTS is safer.

interview.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
interview.answer: Child rows still reference the parent and the constraint has no cascade action.

interview.q: What happens if UPDATE changes a primary key?
interview.answer: It can break foreign keys or fail on duplicates; use ON UPDATE CASCADE only when the relationship requires it.

interview.q: Why use a transaction around a large modification?
interview.answer: It lets you verify the affected count and roll back cleanly if the change is wrong.

interview.q: Why can a large UPDATE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates new row versions, writes WAL, updates indexes and can bloat the table until vacuum runs.

interview.q: Why can a large DELETE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates dead tuples, writes WAL and must maintain indexes; batching reduces lock time.

interview.q: What is the safest modification workflow?
interview.answer: Preview with SELECT, open a transaction, run the change with RETURNING, verify the count, then commit or roll back.

labs.title: Update one column
labs.task: Set marks to 95 for id 1.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Update two columns
labs.task: Set name and marks for id 1.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S', marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Update a specific row
labs.task: Set marks to 88 for id 2.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 88 WHERE id = 2;

labs.title: Update with an expression
labs.task: Add five marks to every known mark.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

labs.title: Update with CASE
labs.task: Raise every mark below 60 to 60.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = CASE WHEN marks < 60 THEN 60 ELSE marks END;

labs.title: Fill missing emails
labs.task: Replace NULL emails with unknown@example.com.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET email = COALESCE(email, 'unknown@example.com');

labs.title: Update from a subquery
labs.task: Set NULL marks to the average marks.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) WHERE marks IS NULL;

labs.title: Update from another table
labs.task: Copy marks from applicants by matching email.
labs.solution: UPDATE students s SET marks = a.marks FROM applicants a WHERE s.email = a.email;

labs.title: Update with RETURNING
labs.task: Update id 1 and return the new row.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name, marks;

labs.title: Update with a transaction
labs.task: Update id 1 inside a transaction and commit.

labs.title: Delete one row
labs.task: Delete id 4.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4;

labs.title: Delete with a condition
labs.task: Delete students below 60.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

labs.title: Delete by subquery
labs.task: Delete students enrolled in course 10.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

labs.title: Delete with USING
labs.task: Delete students enrolled in course 10 using a join.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students s USING enrollments e WHERE s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_id = 10;

labs.title: Delete with RETURNING
labs.task: Delete id 3 and return the row.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 3 RETURNING *;

labs.title: Archive deleted rows
labs.task: Delete marks below 60 and insert them into students_archive.
labs.solution: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) INSERT INTO students_archive SELECT * FROM deleted;

labs.title: Truncate the table
labs.task: Remove every row and reset identity.
labs.solution: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

labs.title: Safe update
labs.task: Preview, update, verify and commit in one transaction.

labs.title: Safe delete
labs.task: Delete id 5 inside a transaction and roll back.
labs.expected: The row is returned but the delete is undone.

labs.title: No-op delete
labs.task: Delete id 999 and observe the count.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 999;

logic.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE dangerous?
logic.answer: It changes every row in the table, often with one mistaken statement.

logic.q: Why is DELETE without WHERE dangerous?
logic.answer: It removes every row and leaves an empty table.

logic.q: Why preview with SELECT first?
logic.answer: The SELECT shows exactly which rows the predicate matches before you modify them.

logic.q: Why wrap a modification in a transaction?
logic.answer: You can verify the affected count and roll back if the change is wrong.

logic.q: Why use RETURNING?
logic.answer: It shows the changed rows and supports an audit or archive without a second query.

logic.q: Why does DELETE support WHERE but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE removes selected rows one by one; TRUNCATE is a whole-table storage operation.

logic.q: Why does DELETE fire row triggers but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE processes rows individually; TRUNCATE does not visit them as row deletes.

logic.q: Why is changing a primary key risky?
logic.answer: Foreign keys reference the old value; without ON UPDATE CASCADE the change can fail or orphan relationships.

logic.q: Why must a SET subquery be scalar?
logic.answer: A column assignment needs one value per row; multiple rows cannot fit.

logic.q: Why can UPDATE FROM be unpredictable with duplicate sources?
logic.answer: A target row matched by several source rows may be updated more than once with no defined winner.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN with a NULL subquery unsafe for DELETE?
logic.answer: The NULL comparison makes the predicate unknown, so it can delete nothing.

logic.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
logic.answer: Referencing child rows still exist and the constraint has no cascade action.

logic.q: Why batch a very large DELETE?
logic.answer: Small batches reduce lock time, WAL spikes and blocking for other sessions.

logic.q: Why vacuum after many updates or deletes?
logic.answer: The old row versions become dead tuples; vacuum reclaims that space.

logic.q: Why does DELETE not reset identity?
logic.answer: The sequence is a separate object; only an explicit restart changes it.

revision.q: What does UPDATE do?
revision.answer: Changes existing rows matched by WHERE.

revision.q: What does DELETE do?
What happens without WHERE?
How do you update two columns?
How do you return changed rows?
How do you update from another table?
How do you delete using another table?
DELETE vs TRUNCATE?

modules.title: Joins
modules.goal: Combine related tables correctly and choose the join type by which rows must survive.

topics.title: Introduction to Joins
topics.simple: Join do tables ko ek related result me combine karta hai.
topics.pro: A join combines rows from two relations using a predicate, typically matching a foreign key to a primary key.
points: Joins combine columns from multiple tables.
The join key defines the relationship.
A missing join condition creates a cross product.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Each student with their enrolled course ids.

topics.title: INNER JOIN
topics.simple: INNER JOIN sirf matching rows deta hai.
topics.pro: INNER JOIN returns only pairs where the ON condition is true; unmatched rows from either side disappear.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s INNER JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Students who have at least one enrollment.

topics.title: LEFT JOIN
topics.simple: LEFT JOIN left table ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left relation and fills unmatched right columns with NULL.
points: Filtering the right table in WHERE can remove the preserved rows.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Every student, with NULL course_id when unenrolled.

topics.title: RIGHT JOIN
topics.simple: RIGHT JOIN right table ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: RIGHT JOIN preserves every row from the right relation and fills unmatched left columns with NULL; it is a mirrored LEFT JOIN.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM enrollments e RIGHT JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id;

topics.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
topics.simple: FULL JOIN dono tables ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from both sides, with NULLs on the missing side.
points: Use COALESCE to pick a non-null key.
It is the union of LEFT and RIGHT joins.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s FULL OUTER JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id;
example.output: Every student and every enrollment, matched where possible.

topics.title: CROSS JOIN
topics.simple: CROSS JOIN har left row ko har right row se pair karta hai.
topics.pro: CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product: every row from the first relation paired with every row from the second.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;

topics.title: SELF JOIN
topics.simple: Self join ek hi table ko do aliases se join karta hai.
topics.pro: A self join uses two aliases for the same table so rows can be compared with other rows in that table.
points: The ON condition defines the relationship.
It is common for hierarchies and comparisons.

example.sql: SELECT a.name AS lower, b.name AS higher FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.marks < b.marks;
example.output: Pairs where the first student scored lower.

topics.title: Join Conditions
topics.simple: ON join ka matching rule likhta hai.
topics.pro: ON defines the boolean condition that decides which row pairs are joined; it is required for INNER and OUTER joins unless USING is used.
points: A wrong key silently produces wrong rows.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: One row per matching student-enrollment pair.

topics.title: Joining on Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Composite key ko ON me AND se match karo.
topics.pro: When the relationship uses a composite key, every key column must appear in the join condition.

example.sql: SELECT e.student_id, cs.room FROM enrollments e JOIN course_sections cs ON cs.course_id = e.course_id AND cs.semester = e.semester;
example.output: Enrollments matched to their section room.

topics.title: Joining Multiple Tables
topics.simple: Ek query me teen ya zyada tables chain ki tarah join hoti hain.
topics.pro: Multi-table joins chain relationships: each new JOIN adds a relation and an ON condition connecting it to the existing result.
points: Check row counts after each added table.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;

topics.title: Table Aliases
topics.simple: Aliases lambi table names ko short aur readable banate hain.
topics.pro: Aliases give each relation a short name used to qualify columns and are mandatory when the same table appears twice.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students AS s JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id;

topics.title: Ambiguous Columns
topics.simple: Same column name do tables me ho to qualify karo.
topics.pro: If a column name exists in more than one joined relation, an unqualified reference is ambiguous and PostgreSQL raises an error.
points: Do not rely on column order.

example.sql: SELECT s.id, s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;
example.output: Student id and name plus course title.

topics.title: JOIN vs Subquery
topics.simple: JOIN columns combine karta hai; subquery value ya membership deta hai.
topics.pro: A join returns columns from both relations, while a subquery is often used for a scalar value, IN membership or EXISTS existence checks.
points: JOIN is natural for output columns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);
example.output: Students enrolled in course 10, once each.

topics.title: JOIN with Aggregation
topics.simple: Join ke baad GROUP BY se counts nikal sakte hain.
topics.pro: Joining and grouping lets you aggregate related rows; LEFT JOIN plus COUNT(right_key) reports zero for rows with no match.
points: COUNT(*) counts the preserved row too.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;
example.output: Every course with its enrollment count, including zero.

topics.title: JOIN with Filtering
topics.simple: Filter join ke baad WHERE se hota hai.
topics.pro: WHERE filters the joined result; for INNER JOIN it is equivalent to putting the predicate in ON, but for OUTER JOIN the placement changes which rows survive.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.credits = 3;

topics.title: ON vs WHERE in Outer Joins
topics.simple: LEFT JOIN me right-table filter ON me rakho, WHERE me nahi.
topics.pro: A predicate on the right table in ON filters only the match, preserving left rows; the same predicate in WHERE removes non-matching left rows and turns the join into an inner join.
points: This is a common reporting bug.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.course_id = 10;
example.output: Every student, with course 10 only where enrolled.

topics.title: Anti-Joins and Missing Rows
topics.simple: Anti-join un rows ko dhoondhta hai jinka match nahi hai.
topics.pro: A LEFT JOIN with WHERE right_key IS NULL, or a NOT EXISTS subquery, returns rows with no matching row on the other side.
points: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is an anti-join.
Avoid NOT IN when NULLs are possible.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL;

topics.title: Common Join Errors
topics.simple: Missing ON, wrong key aur duplicate matches sabse common join bugs hain.
topics.pro: Most join bugs come from a missing or wrong join condition, an ambiguous column, a filter in the wrong clause or a one-to-many relationship that multiplies rows.
points: Check the row count before aggregating.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: One row per enrollment, not one per student.

topics.title: Join Performance
topics.simple: Join keys par index aur selective filters performance decide karte hain.
topics.pro: The planner chooses nested loop, hash or merge join based on statistics, indexes and selectivity; indexes on foreign keys and selective WHERE predicates usually help most.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.id = 10;
example.output: A plan showing the chosen join strategy.

topics.title: Practical Join Examples
topics.simple: Ab joins ko real reports me combine karo.
topics.pro: Practical join work combines the right join type, a correct condition, a filter and an aggregate, and verifies the grain of the result before trusting it.
points: Choose the join type by which rows must survive.
Review the plan for large joins.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title ASC;

learn.q: What does a join do?
options: Combines related rows from two tables
Deletes rows
Creates an index
Sorts one table
learn.answer: Combines related rows from two tables
learn.why: A join pairs rows using a condition.

learn.q: Which join returns only matching rows?
options: INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
FULL JOIN
learn.answer: INNER JOIN
learn.why: INNER JOIN drops non-matching rows.

learn.q: Which join keeps every left row?
options: LEFT JOIN
INNER JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
CROSS JOIN
learn.answer: LEFT JOIN
learn.why: LEFT JOIN preserves the left relation.

learn.q: Which join keeps every right row?
options: RIGHT JOIN
LEFT JOIN
INNER JOIN
CROSS JOIN
learn.answer: RIGHT JOIN
learn.why: RIGHT JOIN preserves the right relation.

learn.q: Which join keeps unmatched rows from both sides?
options: FULL OUTER JOIN
INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
CROSS JOIN
learn.answer: FULL OUTER JOIN
learn.why: FULL JOIN preserves both sides.

learn.q: What does CROSS JOIN produce?
options: Every pair of rows
Only matches
Only unmatched rows
One row
learn.answer: Every pair of rows
learn.why: It is the Cartesian product.

learn.q: What is a self join?
options: A table joined to itself with aliases
A join with no condition
A join across databases
A join on one column
learn.answer: A table joined to itself with aliases
learn.why: Two aliases let rows of one table be compared.

learn.q: Which clause defines the join condition?
options: ON
WHERE
GROUP BY
ORDER BY
learn.answer: ON
learn.why: ON belongs to the JOIN and defines matches.

learn.q: Which clause can also filter joined rows?
options: WHERE
LIMIT
OFFSET
RETURNING
learn.answer: WHERE
learn.why: WHERE filters the final joined rows.

learn.q: What does USING do?
options: Joins on same-named columns
Deletes rows
Creates an alias
Sorts rows
learn.answer: Joins on same-named columns
learn.why: USING (col) is shorthand for equality on that column.

learn.q: Why alias joined tables?
options: To qualify columns and shorten names
To create indexes
To sort rows
To remove duplicates
learn.answer: To qualify columns and shorten names
learn.why: Aliases disambiguate shared column names.

learn.q: What causes an ambiguous column error?
options: The same column name exists in both tables
The table has no primary key
The join uses ON
The query has ORDER BY
learn.answer: The same column name exists in both tables
learn.why: Qualify the column with a table alias.

learn.q: How do you join three tables?
options: Chain two JOIN clauses
Use three FROM clauses only
Use CROSS JOIN only
Use one ON for all
learn.answer: Chain two JOIN clauses
learn.why: Each JOIN adds one relation and its condition.

learn.q: What fills unmatched columns in a LEFT JOIN?
options: NULL
Zero
An empty string
The previous row
learn.answer: NULL
learn.why: The missing side has no value.

learn.q: Which count reports zero for a course with no enrollments?
options: COUNT(e.student_id)
COUNT(*)
SUM(*)
COUNT(1)
learn.answer: COUNT(e.student_id)
learn.why: COUNT(column) ignores NULL; COUNT(*) counts the preserved row.

learn.q: Where should a right-table filter go in a LEFT JOIN?
options: In ON to preserve left rows
In WHERE to preserve left rows
In ORDER BY
In LIMIT
learn.answer: In ON to preserve left rows
learn.why: A WHERE predicate on the right side removes non-matching left rows.

learn.q: What is an anti-join?
options: Rows with no match on the other side
A join with no ON
A cross join
A join on all columns
learn.answer: Rows with no match on the other side
learn.why: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds missing matches.

learn.q: What happens when a join key has duplicate matches?
options: Rows multiply
Rows are deleted
The query fails
Duplicates are removed automatically
learn.answer: Rows multiply
learn.why: Each matching pair becomes an output row.

learn.q: Which index usually helps a join?
options: An index on the join key
An index on every text column
No index
An index on ORDER BY only
learn.answer: An index on the join key
learn.why: The planner can find matches faster.

learn.q: Does NULL = NULL match in a join?
options: No
Yes
Only with LEFT JOIN
Only with CROSS JOIN
learn.answer: No
learn.why: NULL equality is unknown; use a null-safe comparison if needed.

interview.q: What is a join?
interview.answer: An operation that combines rows from two relations using a matching condition.

interview.q: What is a join key?
interview.answer: The column or columns used to match rows, usually a foreign key to a primary key.

interview.q: What is the difference between INNER and LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps every left row and NULL-fills unmatched right columns.

interview.q: What is the difference between LEFT and RIGHT JOIN?
interview.answer: They preserve opposite sides; a RIGHT JOIN is a mirrored LEFT JOIN.

interview.q: What is a FULL OUTER JOIN?
interview.answer: A join that preserves unmatched rows from both sides, NULL-filling the missing side.

interview.q: What is a CROSS JOIN?
interview.answer: The Cartesian product: every row from one relation paired with every row from the other.

interview.q: When do you use a self join?
interview.answer: When rows in one table must be compared with other rows in the same table, such as hierarchies or pairs.

interview.q: What is the difference between ON and WHERE in an outer join?
interview.answer: ON filters the match while preserving the outer side; WHERE filters the final rows and can remove preserved rows.

interview.q: What does USING do?
interview.answer: It joins on same-named columns and outputs one copy of the join column.

interview.q: Why is NATURAL JOIN risky?
interview.answer: It joins on every same-named column, so a schema change can silently change the condition.

interview.q: How do you find rows with no match?
interview.answer: Use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_key IS NULL or NOT EXISTS.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN risky for an anti-join?
interview.answer: A NULL in the subquery makes the predicate unknown and can return no rows.

interview.q: What is the grain of a joined result?
interview.answer: What one output row represents, such as one student-course pair; a one-to-many join changes the grain.

interview.q: Why can COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(right_key) after a LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: COUNT(*) counts the preserved row even when the right side is NULL; COUNT(right_key) counts only real matches.

interview.q: How do you join multiple tables?
interview.answer: Chain JOIN clauses, adding one relation and its ON condition for each relationship.

interview.q: What are the main join algorithms?
interview.answer: Nested loop, hash join and merge join; the planner chooses based on statistics, indexes and selectivity.

interview.q: Why qualify columns in a join?
interview.answer: Shared column names are ambiguous, and qualification documents which table a value comes from.

interview.q: Can a join use a non-unique key?
interview.answer: Yes, but each matching pair becomes a row, so the result can multiply.

interview.q: How do you join on a composite key?
interview.answer: Put every key column in the ON condition, combined with AND.

interview.q: Does join order in SQL determine execution order?
interview.answer: No; the planner may reorder joins while preserving the result.

labs.title: Inner join
labs.task: Return student names with enrolled course ids.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s INNER JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;

labs.title: Three-table join
labs.task: Return student names with course titles.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;

labs.title: Left join
labs.task: Return every student with their course ids.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;

labs.title: Left join count
labs.task: Count enrollments per student, including zero.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS courses FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name;
labs.expected: Every student with a count, including 0.

labs.title: Right join
labs.task: Return every student using a RIGHT JOIN from enrollments.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM enrollments e RIGHT JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id;

labs.title: Full join
labs.task: Return matched and unmatched students and enrollments.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s FULL OUTER JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id;

labs.title: Cross join
labs.task: Return every student-course pair.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;

labs.title: Self join
labs.task: Return pairs where the first student scored lower.
labs.solution: SELECT a.name AS lower, b.name AS higher FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.marks < b.marks;

labs.title: Composite join
labs.task: Match enrollments to sections on course and semester.
labs.solution: SELECT e.student_id, cs.room FROM enrollments e JOIN course_sections cs ON cs.course_id = e.course_id AND cs.semester = e.semester;

labs.title: Aliases
labs.task: Rewrite a three-table join with short aliases.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students AS s JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id;

labs.title: Ambiguous column
labs.task: Return student id and name without ambiguity.
labs.solution: SELECT s.id, s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;

labs.title: Join vs subquery
labs.task: Return students enrolled in course 10 once each.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

labs.title: Aggregate join
labs.task: Count enrollments per course, including zero.
labs.solution: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

labs.title: Filter after join
labs.task: Return students in three-credit courses.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.credits = 3;

labs.title: ON vs WHERE
labs.task: Keep every student while showing only course 10.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.course_id = 10;
labs.expected: All students; course id only for course 10.

labs.title: Anti-join
labs.task: Return students with no enrollments.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL;

labs.title: NOT EXISTS anti-join
labs.task: Return unenrolled students with NOT EXISTS.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: Explain a join
labs.task: Explain the course filter plan.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.id = 10;
labs.expected: A plan with the chosen join strategy.

labs.title: Course report
labs.task: Return course enrollment counts, largest first.
labs.solution: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title ASC;

labs.title: Grain check
labs.task: Count rows and distinct students for the enrollment join.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(DISTINCT e.student_id) AS students FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;

logic.q: When should you use INNER JOIN instead of LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: When only rows with matches are meaningful and unmatched rows should be excluded.

logic.q: When should you use LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: When every row from the left side must appear, even without a match.

logic.q: Why is RIGHT JOIN often rewritten as LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: Swapping the table order makes the preserved side the left side, which is easier to read.

logic.q: Why use FULL OUTER JOIN?
logic.answer: When unmatched rows from both sides matter, such as reconciling two systems.

logic.q: Why is a CROSS JOIN dangerous by accident?
logic.answer: It multiplies every row by every row, producing a huge result and misleading aggregates.

logic.q: Why does a self join need aliases?
logic.answer: The same table appears twice, so aliases distinguish the two row roles.

logic.q: Why does a right-table filter in WHERE break a LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: The WHERE predicate rejects NULL right-side rows, removing the preserved left rows.

logic.q: Why can NULL join keys fail to match?
logic.answer: Equality with NULL is unknown, so NULL = NULL is not true.

logic.q: Why can a one-to-many join inflate a SUM?
logic.answer: A parent row repeated for each child is summed once per child, not once per parent.

logic.q: Why is COUNT(*) different after a LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: It counts the preserved row even when the right side has no match.

logic.q: Why prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN for anti-joins?
logic.answer: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably; NOT IN with a NULL can return no rows.

logic.q: Why use a join instead of a subquery?
logic.answer: A join returns columns from both tables; a subquery is often better for a scalar or an existence check.

logic.q: Why index foreign keys?
logic.answer: The planner can find matching rows without scanning the child table repeatedly.

logic.q: Does the written join order control execution?
logic.answer: No; the planner can reorder joins while preserving the result.

logic.q: Why is NATURAL JOIN fragile?
logic.answer: It silently joins on every same-named column, so schema changes alter the condition.
