modules.title: Subqueries and CTEs
modules.goal: Break complex questions into correct, readable subqueries and CTEs.

topics.title: Introduction to Subqueries
topics.simple: Subquery ek query ke andar doosri query hoti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement; it can supply a value, a row set or an existence test.
points: They run in the context of the outer query.
They can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE and HAVING.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

topics.title: Types of Subqueries
topics.simple: Subquery scalar, multi-row ya correlated ho sakti hai.
topics.pro: Subqueries are classified by shape (scalar or multi-row) and by dependency (uncorrelated or correlated).

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments);
example.output: Students with at least one enrollment.

topics.title: Scalar Subquery
topics.simple: Scalar subquery ek row aur ek column deti hai.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, so it can be used anywhere a single value is accepted.

example.sql: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) AS class_average FROM students;
example.output: Every student with the same class average.

topics.title: Multi-row Subquery
topics.simple: Multi-row subquery multiple values deti hai; IN ya ANY/ALL ke saath use karo.
topics.pro: A multi-row subquery returns one column with many rows and is compared with IN, ANY or ALL rather than a plain equality.
points: A plain = with many rows fails.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

topics.title: Correlated Subquery
topics.simple: Correlated subquery outer query ke row par depend karti hai.
topics.pro: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so conceptually it is evaluated for each outer row.
points: It can be expensive without an index.
It is often rewritten as a join.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;
example.output: Each student with their enrollment count.

topics.title: Subquery in WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE me subquery se filter value ya set deti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in WHERE can compare a column to a scalar or test membership and existence.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

topics.title: Subquery with IN
topics.simple: IN subquery ke result set me membership check karta hai.
topics.pro: IN tests whether a value equals any row returned by the subquery, and handles a multi-row result naturally.
points: NULLs in the list can make NOT IN unsafe.
Duplicates in the subquery do not duplicate output.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);
example.output: Students enrolled in course 10, once each.

topics.title: Subquery with EXISTS
topics.simple: EXISTS subquery ke row hone par true hota hai.
topics.pro: EXISTS returns true as soon as the subquery produces at least one row; the selected columns are irrelevant and the planner can stop early.
points: It can short-circuit on the first match.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
example.output: Students with at least one enrollment.

topics.title: Subquery with NOT EXISTS
topics.simple: NOT EXISTS tab true hota hai jab subquery koi row na de.
topics.pro: NOT EXISTS returns true when the correlated subquery produces no rows, making it a safe anti-join even with NULLs.
points: It usually beats NOT IN with nullable columns.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

topics.title: Subquery in SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT list me scalar subquery ek computed column deti hai.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery in the select list computes one value per output row and must return at most one row and one column.
points: It runs per outer row when correlated.
It can be expensive on large results.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;

topics.title: Subquery in FROM
topics.simple: FROM me subquery derived table ki tarah use hoti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in FROM acts as a derived table and must have an alias in PostgreSQL; its columns are then queried like a normal table.
points: It can aggregate before the outer query.
It is often called a derived table.

example.sql: SELECT t.course_id, t.total FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS t WHERE t.total > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one enrollment.

topics.title: Subquery in HAVING
topics.simple: HAVING me subquery aggregate result se compare kar sakti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in HAVING supplies a scalar threshold or value after grouping, which is useful for comparing groups to a global aggregate.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);
example.output: Courses above the average enrollment count.

topics.title: Introduction to CTEs
topics.simple: CTE WITH clause se named temporary result set banata hai.
topics.pro: A common table expression is a named subquery defined with WITH and visible to the statement that follows it.
points: It is scoped to one statement.

example.sql: WITH high AS (SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80) SELECT * FROM high ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: CTE Syntax
topics.simple: WITH name AS (query) SELECT ... .
topics.pro: The syntax is WITH name [(columns)] AS (subquery) [, ...] SELECT ...; the CTE can be referenced like a table in the main query.

example.sql: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

topics.title: Multiple CTEs
topics.simple: Ek WITH me comma se multiple CTEs define karo.
topics.pro: Multiple CTEs are separated by commas and later CTEs can reference earlier ones, which lets a complex query read top to bottom.

example.sql: WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80), count_high AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM high) SELECT * FROM count_high;

topics.title: Recursive CTE
topics.simple: Recursive CTE anchor aur recursive term se hierarchy ya sequence banata hai.
topics.pro: WITH RECURSIVE runs an anchor term, then repeatedly runs a recursive term that references the CTE until it returns no rows.
points: The recursive term needs a termination condition.

example.sql: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

topics.title: CTE vs Subquery
topics.simple: CTE named aur reusable hai; subquery inline hoti hai.
topics.pro: A CTE names a result for readability and reuse within one statement, while a subquery is inline; PostgreSQL may inline a non-recursive CTE unless MATERIALIZED is specified.
points: CTEs can be referenced multiple times.
Subqueries are local to their expression.

example.sql: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

topics.title: CTE with DML
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me CTE ke andar INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE chal sakta hai.
topics.pro: A data-modifying CTE uses RETURNING to expose changed rows to the main query; the statement executes once and is atomic.
points: DML CTEs need RETURNING to expose rows.

example.sql: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM deleted;

topics.title: Common Subquery Errors
topics.simple: Multi-row scalar, missing alias aur NULL NOT IN sabse common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are a scalar subquery returning multiple rows, a derived table without an alias, a missing correlation condition and NOT IN with NULLs.
points: Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN.

example.sql: SELECT name, (SELECT marks FROM students LIMIT 1) AS sample FROM students;
example.output: A single sample mark per row.

topics.title: Performance Considerations
topics.simple: Subqueries hamesha slow nahi hoti; shape aur indexes matter karte hain.
topics.pro: EXISTS can short-circuit, correlated subqueries can run per row, and CTE materialization can help or hurt; read EXPLAIN instead of guessing.
points: EXISTS often stops at the first match.
CTEs may be inlined or materialized.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
example.output: A plan showing a semi-join or nested loop.

learn.q: What is a subquery?
options: A query nested inside another statement
A copied table
An index
A transaction
learn.answer: A query nested inside another statement
learn.why: It supplies a value or row set to the outer query.

learn.q: What does a scalar subquery return?
options: One row and one column
Many rows
Many columns
A table
learn.answer: One row and one column
learn.why: A scalar is a single value.

learn.q: What does a multi-row subquery return?
options: One column with many rows
One row with many columns
Exactly two rows
A schema
learn.answer: One column with many rows
learn.why: It is used with IN, ANY or ALL.

learn.q: What makes a subquery correlated?
options: It references the outer query
It has ORDER BY
It returns one row
It uses DISTINCT
learn.answer: It references the outer query
learn.why: It depends on the current outer row.

learn.q: Which operator tests membership in a subquery result?
options: IN
LIKE
BETWEEN
IS NULL
learn.answer: IN
learn.why: IN compares against a set of values.

learn.q: What does EXISTS test?
options: Whether the subquery returns any row
Whether a column is NULL
Whether two values are equal
Whether a table exists
learn.answer: Whether the subquery returns any row
learn.why: EXISTS is a boolean existence test.

learn.q: What does NOT EXISTS test?
options: Whether the subquery returns no rows
Whether a column is NOT NULL
Whether a value is unique
Whether a table is empty
learn.answer: Whether the subquery returns no rows
learn.why: It is the safe anti-join.

learn.q: Where can a scalar subquery appear?
options: In SELECT, WHERE or HAVING
Only in FROM
Only in ORDER BY
Only in GROUP BY
learn.answer: In SELECT, WHERE or HAVING
learn.why: Anywhere a single value is accepted.

learn.q: What must a subquery in FROM have?
options: An alias
A primary key
An index
DISTINCT
learn.answer: An alias
learn.why: PostgreSQL requires a derived-table alias.

learn.q: Which clause filters groups using an aggregate?
options: HAVING
WHERE
ORDER BY
LIMIT
learn.answer: HAVING
learn.why: HAVING runs after grouping.

learn.q: What does WITH define?
options: A common table expression
A new table
An index
A trigger
learn.answer: A common table expression
learn.why: WITH names a subquery for the statement.

learn.q: How are multiple CTEs separated?
options: Commas
Semicolons
AND
UNION
learn.answer: Commas
learn.why: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) ... .

learn.q: Which keyword enables a recursive CTE?
options: RECURSIVE
REPEAT
LOOP
ITERATE
learn.answer: RECURSIVE
learn.why: WITH RECURSIVE allows self-reference.

learn.q: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
options: Anchor and recursive term
SELECT and WHERE
INNER and OUTER
BEGIN and COMMIT
learn.answer: Anchor and recursive term
learn.why: The anchor seeds the result; the recursive term expands it.

learn.q: What terminates a recursive CTE?
options: A condition that eventually returns no rows
LIMIT only
ORDER BY
A primary key
learn.answer: A condition that eventually returns no rows
learn.why: Without termination it runs until cancelled.

learn.q: How does a CTE differ from a subquery?
options: It is named and reusable in the statement
It is always faster
It creates a permanent table
It cannot be joined
learn.answer: It is named and reusable in the statement
learn.why: A CTE can be referenced more than once.

learn.q: Which clause exposes changed rows from a DML CTE?
options: RETURNING
OUTPUT
SELECT INTO
VALUES
learn.answer: RETURNING
learn.why: RETURNING makes the changed rows available to the main query.

learn.q: What error does a multi-row scalar subquery raise?
options: More than one row returned
Division by zero
Ambiguous column
Syntax error
learn.answer: More than one row returned
learn.why: A scalar slot cannot hold multiple rows.

learn.q: Why is NOT IN unsafe with NULLs?
options: NULL comparisons make the predicate unknown
It always returns all rows
It removes duplicates
It requires an alias
learn.answer: NULL comparisons make the predicate unknown
learn.why: A NULL in the list can make NOT IN return no rows.

learn.q: Which is usually the safer anti-join?
options: NOT EXISTS
NOT IN
CROSS JOIN
NATURAL JOIN
learn.answer: NOT EXISTS
learn.why: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably.

interview.q: What is a subquery?
interview.answer: A SELECT nested inside another statement, used for a scalar value, a row set or an existence test.

interview.q: What is a scalar subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery returning at most one row and one column, usable as a single value.

interview.q: What is a multi-row subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery returning one column with many rows, used with IN, ANY or ALL.

interview.q: What is a correlated subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery that references a column from the outer query and depends on the current outer row.

interview.q: What is an uncorrelated subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery that can be evaluated independently of the outer query.

interview.q: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
interview.answer: IN compares a value to a set; EXISTS tests whether any row exists and can short-circuit.

interview.q: Why is NOT EXISTS safer than NOT IN?
interview.answer: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably; NOT IN with a NULL can return no rows.

interview.q: What is a derived table?
interview.answer: A subquery in FROM with an alias, queried like a table by the outer query.

interview.q: Why does a FROM subquery need an alias?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL requires a name for the derived relation so its columns can be referenced.

interview.q: What is a CTE?
interview.answer: A named subquery defined with WITH and visible to the statement that follows.

interview.q: What are the advantages of a CTE?
interview.answer: Readability, reuse within one statement and a clean way to structure multi-step queries.

interview.q: What is a recursive CTE?
interview.answer: A CTE with an anchor term and a recursive term that references itself until no more rows are produced.

interview.q: What is the anchor term?
interview.answer: The non-recursive seed query that starts the recursive result.

interview.q: What happens if a recursive CTE has no termination condition?
interview.answer: It keeps producing rows until the statement is cancelled or a resource limit is hit.

interview.q: What is a data-modifying CTE?
interview.answer: A CTE containing INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE with RETURNING, whose rows the main query can read.

interview.q: How many times does a data-modifying CTE execute?
interview.answer: Exactly once, even if the main query references it multiple times.

interview.q: Does a CTE create a temporary table?
interview.answer: No; it is a named query scoped to one statement.

interview.q: Are CTEs always materialized in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: No; since PostgreSQL 12 non-recursive CTEs can be inlined, and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED can control it.

interview.q: What is a semi-join?
interview.answer: A join that returns rows from one side when a match exists, without duplicating them for every match; EXISTS is a common form.

interview.q: How do you performance-tune a correlated subquery?
interview.answer: Index the correlated columns, compare with an EXISTS or join rewrite, and inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

labs.title: Scalar average
labs.task: Return students above the class average.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

labs.title: IN subquery
labs.task: Return students enrolled in course 10.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

labs.title: ANY subquery
labs.task: Return students whose marks equal any applicant mark.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks = ANY (SELECT marks FROM applicants);

labs.title: EXISTS
labs.task: Return students with at least one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: NOT EXISTS
labs.task: Return students with no enrollments.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: Correlated count
labs.task: Return each student with their enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;

labs.title: Subquery in SELECT
labs.task: Return the class average on every row.
labs.solution: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) AS class_average FROM students;
labs.expected: Every student with the same average.

labs.title: Derived table
labs.task: Return courses with more than one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT t.course_id, t.total FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS t WHERE t.total > 1;

labs.title: Subquery in HAVING
labs.task: Return courses above the average enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);

labs.title: Basic CTE
labs.task: Return high scorers using a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH high AS (SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80) SELECT * FROM high ORDER BY marks DESC;

labs.title: Multiple CTEs
labs.task: Count the high scorers using two CTEs.
labs.solution: WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80), count_high AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM high) SELECT * FROM count_high;

labs.title: Recursive numbers
labs.task: Generate 1 through 5 with a recursive CTE.
labs.solution: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

labs.title: Recursive hierarchy
labs.task: Return employees and their manager names.
labs.solution: WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id) SELECT * FROM chain;
labs.expected: The hierarchy from the root down.

labs.title: DML CTE delete
labs.task: Delete low marks and return the deleted rows.
labs.solution: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM deleted;

labs.title: DML CTE update
labs.task: Raise low marks and return the updated rows.
labs.solution: WITH updated AS (UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM updated;

labs.title: CTE vs subquery
labs.task: Rewrite the average filter as a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

labs.title: Materialized CTE
labs.task: Force the average CTE to materialize.
labs.solution: WITH avg_marks AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

labs.title: Explain EXISTS
labs.task: Explain the enrolled-students query.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: Top course count
labs.task: Return courses with the maximum enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) = (SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);

labs.title: Report with CTEs
labs.task: Build a course enrollment report with a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH counts AS (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) SELECT c.title, counts.total FROM courses c JOIN counts ON counts.course_id = c.id ORDER BY counts.total DESC;

logic.q: When is a subquery uncorrelated?
logic.answer: When it can run independently of the outer query and returns the same result for every outer row.

logic.q: Why can a correlated subquery be slower?
logic.answer: It may run once per outer row, so missing indexes multiply the work.

logic.q: Why can EXISTS stop early?
logic.answer: It only needs one matching row to return true.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN dangerous with NULLs?
logic.answer: A NULL comparison is unknown, so the predicate can fail for every row.

logic.q: Why does a scalar subquery fail with multiple rows?
logic.answer: A single-value slot cannot represent more than one row.

logic.q: Why must a FROM subquery have an alias?
logic.answer: The outer query needs a relation name to qualify its columns.

logic.q: Why use a CTE instead of a nested subquery?
logic.answer: A CTE names each step and can be referenced multiple times, improving readability and reuse.

logic.q: Why can a CTE hurt performance?
logic.answer: Materializing a large intermediate result can cost more than letting the planner inline and optimize the query.

logic.q: Why can MATERIALIZED change a plan?
logic.answer: It forces the CTE result to be computed once instead of being inlined into the outer query.

logic.q: Why does a recursive CTE need an anchor?
logic.answer: The anchor produces the starting rows; the recursive term expands from them.

logic.q: Why does a recursive CTE need a termination condition?
logic.answer: Without one it keeps producing rows until cancelled or limited.

logic.q: Why is a CTE scoped to one statement?
logic.answer: It is a named query, not a persistent table, and disappears when the statement ends.

logic.q: Why does a data-modifying CTE execute once?
logic.answer: The statement runs the CTE once even if the main query references its output repeatedly.

logic.q: Why can a subquery in SELECT be expensive?
logic.answer: A correlated scalar subquery may execute for every output row.

logic.q: Why prefer EXISTS over IN for existence checks?
logic.answer: EXISTS expresses the intent directly and can short-circuit on the first match.

modules.title: Aggregate Functions and GROUP BY
modules.goal: Summarize rows at the right grain without inflating counts or averages.

topics.title: Introduction to Aggregates
topics.simple: Aggregate functions many rows ko ek summary value me reduce karte hain.
topics.pro: Aggregates consume a set of rows and return one value per group, turning detail rows into counts, totals, averages, minima and maxima.
points: They can run over the whole table or per group.
They ignore NULL unless told otherwise.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(marks) FROM students;
example.output: One row with the row count and average.

topics.title: COUNT
topics.simple: COUNT rows ya non-null values ginata hai.
topics.pro: COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM students;

topics.title: SUM
topics.simple: SUM numeric values ka total deta hai.
topics.pro: SUM adds non-null numeric values and returns NULL when the input set has no non-null values.
points: Use COALESCE for a zero default.

example.sql: SELECT SUM(marks) AS total_marks FROM students;

topics.title: AVG
topics.simple: AVG non-null values ka average deta hai.
topics.pro: AVG divides the sum by the count of non-null values, so missing values reduce the denominator rather than counting as zero.
points: NULLs are excluded from both parts.
AVG over no rows is NULL.

example.sql: SELECT AVG(marks) AS average_marks FROM students;

topics.title: MIN and MAX
topics.simple: MIN smallest aur MAX largest value deta hai.
topics.pro: MIN and MAX return the smallest and largest non-null values, using the column type’s ordering.

example.sql: SELECT MIN(marks) AS lowest, MAX(marks) AS highest FROM students;

topics.title: GROUP BY
topics.simple: GROUP BY same values wale rows ko groups me baantta hai.
topics.pro: GROUP BY partitions rows by the grouping expressions; each group produces one output row and aggregates run inside each group.
points: Every non-aggregated output column must be grouped.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
example.output: One row per course with its enrollment count.

topics.title: GROUP BY Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns se composite groups bante hain.
topics.pro: Grouping by several columns produces one row for each distinct combination, in the order the expressions are listed.
points: Order of grouping columns does not change the groups.
More columns usually means smaller groups.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id, grade;

topics.title: HAVING
topics.simple: HAVING groups ko filter karta hai.
topics.pro: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can reference aggregate results that WHERE cannot see.
points: It filters groups, not individual rows.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one enrollment.

topics.title: HAVING vs WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE rows filter karta hai; HAVING groups filter karta hai.
topics.pro: WHERE removes rows before grouping and can use only row-level predicates; HAVING removes groups after aggregation and can use aggregate predicates.
points: Filtering early in WHERE is usually cheaper.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments WHERE grade IS NOT NULL GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one graded enrollment.

topics.title: Aggregates and NULL
topics.simple: Aggregates NULL ko ignore karte hain, COUNT(*) ko chhod kar.
topics.pro: COUNT(column), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULL inputs; COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULL values.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(marks) AS known FROM students;
example.output: All rows versus rows with a known mark.

topics.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
topics.simple: COUNT(*) rows ginata hai; COUNT(column) sirf non-null values.
topics.pro: The difference matters after outer joins and with nullable columns: COUNT(*) counts the preserved row, COUNT(column) counts only real matches.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(marks) AS known_marks FROM students;
example.output: Two different counts over the same table.

topics.title: COUNT(DISTINCT ...)
topics.simple: COUNT(DISTINCT column) unique non-null values ginata hai.
topics.pro: DISTINCT inside an aggregate removes duplicate non-null values before the aggregate runs, which is useful for counting unique students, courses or days.
points: It can be more expensive than COUNT(*).

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS unique_students FROM enrollments;
example.output: The number of distinct enrolled students.

topics.title: Grouping by Expressions
topics.simple: GROUP BY column ke bajaye expression par bhi kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Grouping by an expression lets you aggregate by month, category or computed bucket instead of raw column values.
points: Aliases can be used in PostgreSQL GROUP BY.
The same expression should be used consistently.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

topics.title: Aggregates with JOIN
topics.simple: Join ke baad aggregates related rows ko summarize karte hain.
topics.pro: Joining before grouping aggregates related rows, but a one-to-many join changes the grain and can inflate COUNT and SUM unless you count distinct keys or pre-aggregate.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;
example.output: Every course with its enrollment count, including zero.

topics.title: Aggregates without GROUP BY
topics.simple: GROUP BY ke bina aggregate poore result ko ek row me summarize karta hai.
topics.pro: Without GROUP BY, the entire input is one group, so the query returns exactly one row even when the table is empty.
points: No GROUP BY means one group.
Empty input still returns one row.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, AVG(marks) AS average FROM students;
example.output: One summary row for the whole table.

topics.title: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE
topics.simple: Ye multiple grouping levels ek hi query me dete hain.
topics.pro: GROUPING SETS lists exact grouping combinations; ROLLUP adds subtotal levels from left to right; CUBE produces every combination.
points: GROUPING() distinguishes a real NULL from a subtotal placeholder.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY ROLLUP (course_id, grade);
example.output: Course-grade rows plus course subtotals and a grand total.

topics.title: FILTER and Conditional Aggregates
topics.simple: FILTER se aggregate sirf matching rows par chalta hai.
topics.pro: FILTER (WHERE condition) restricts the rows an aggregate sees, enabling conditional counts and sums in one pass without CASE expressions.
points: It avoids separate queries for each condition.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;
example.output: Passed count and total count in one row.

topics.title: Common Aggregate Errors
topics.simple: Non-grouped columns aur WHERE me aggregates sabse common errors hain.
topics.pro: The common failures are selecting a non-grouped column, putting an aggregate in WHERE, missing GROUP BY and expecting COUNT(*) to count only matches after an outer join.
points: Group or aggregate every output column.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Grouped rows with an aggregate filter.

topics.title: Performance of Aggregation
topics.simple: Aggregation memory aur indexes par depend karta hai.
topics.pro: The planner uses hash or group aggregation; filtering before grouping, indexing group keys and pre-aggregating before joins usually reduce the work.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
example.output: A plan with HashAggregate or GroupAggregate.

topics.title: Practical Aggregation Examples
topics.simple: Ab counts, averages aur subtotals ko real reports me combine karo.
topics.pro: A reliable aggregate report states the grain, filters rows before grouping, chooses the right count, and uses HAVING or grouping sets for subtotals.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled, ROUND(AVG(s.marks), 2) AS average_marks FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id LEFT JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title ASC;
example.output: Course report with enrollment count and average marks.

learn.q: What does an aggregate function do?
options: Reduces many rows to one value
Adds a column
Creates an index
Sorts rows
learn.answer: Reduces many rows to one value
learn.why: Aggregates summarize a set of rows.

learn.q: What does COUNT(*) count?
options: All rows
Non-null values only
Distinct rows only
Columns
learn.answer: All rows
learn.why: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs.

learn.q: What does COUNT(column) count?
options: Non-null values
All rows
Distinct values
NULL values
learn.answer: Non-null values
learn.why: NULLs are skipped.

learn.q: What does SUM ignore?
options: NULL values
Zero values
Negative values
Duplicate values
learn.answer: NULL values
learn.why: NULL is not a number to add.

learn.q: What does AVG use as its denominator?
options: The count of non-null values
The total row count
The number of columns
The maximum value
learn.answer: The count of non-null values
learn.why: AVG ignores NULLs in both sum and count.

learn.q: What does MIN return?
options: The smallest non-null value
The first row
Zero
The count
learn.answer: The smallest non-null value
learn.why: MIN uses the column ordering and ignores NULL.

learn.q: What does GROUP BY do?
options: Partitions rows into groups
Sorts the final output
Filters rows
Limits rows
learn.answer: Partitions rows into groups
learn.why: Each group produces one output row.

learn.q: What must every non-aggregated SELECT column do?
options: Appear in GROUP BY
Be a primary key
Be an integer
Have an alias
learn.answer: Appear in GROUP BY
learn.why: Otherwise the value is ambiguous within a group.

learn.q: Which clause filters groups?
options: HAVING
WHERE
ORDER BY
LIMIT
learn.answer: HAVING
learn.why: HAVING runs after aggregation.

learn.q: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
options: WHERE
HAVING
ORDER BY
LIMIT
learn.answer: WHERE
learn.why: WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

learn.q: Can WHERE contain an aggregate?
options: No
Yes
Only COUNT
Only with GROUP BY
learn.answer: No
learn.why: Aggregates are evaluated after WHERE; use HAVING.

learn.q: What does SUM return over no non-null rows?
options: NULL
An error
learn.answer: NULL
learn.why: There is no value to add; use COALESCE for zero.

learn.q: What does COUNT(DISTINCT column) count?
options: Unique non-null values
All rows
NULLs
Duplicate values
learn.answer: Unique non-null values
learn.why: DISTINCT removes duplicates before counting.

learn.q: What does GROUP BY ROLLUP produce?
options: Hierarchical subtotals
Only one group
A random sample
A sorted table
learn.answer: Hierarchical subtotals
learn.why: ROLLUP adds subtotal levels from left to right.

learn.q: What does CUBE produce?
options: Every grouping combination
Only grand totals
Only one column
A cross join
learn.answer: Every grouping combination
learn.why: CUBE generates all combinations of the listed columns.

learn.q: What does GROUPING() help identify?
options: A subtotal NULL versus a real NULL
The number of rows
The average
The sort order
learn.answer: A subtotal NULL versus a real NULL
learn.why: It flags which columns were grouped.

learn.q: What does FILTER do in an aggregate?
options: Restricts rows the aggregate sees
Sorts the groups
Removes duplicates
Creates a group
learn.answer: Restricts rows the aggregate sees
learn.why: FILTER (WHERE ...) applies a condition to the aggregate input.

learn.q: What happens if you select name with COUNT(*) and no GROUP BY?
options: An error
One row per name
All rows
NULL
learn.answer: An error
learn.why: name is not grouped or aggregated.

learn.q: Which count is zero for an empty outer-join group?
options: COUNT(right_key)
COUNT(*)
COUNT(1)
COUNT(*) FILTER
learn.answer: COUNT(right_key)
learn.why: The right key is NULL when there is no match.

learn.q: What is the main risk of aggregating after a one-to-many join?
options: Inflated counts and sums
Lost columns
A syntax error
Automatic DISTINCT
learn.answer: Inflated counts and sums
learn.why: The joined grain repeats parent rows.

interview.q: What is an aggregate function?
interview.answer: A function that summarizes a set of rows into one value, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX.

interview.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
interview.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column.

interview.q: How does SUM treat NULL?
interview.answer: It ignores NULL; if there are no non-null values it returns NULL.

interview.q: How does AVG treat NULL?
interview.answer: It ignores NULL in both the sum and the denominator, averaging only known values.

interview.q: What does GROUP BY do?
interview.answer: It partitions rows into groups by the grouping expressions and produces one output row per group.

interview.q: Why must non-aggregated columns appear in GROUP BY?
interview.answer: A group can contain many rows, so the query cannot choose one value without a grouping rule.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

interview.q: Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?
interview.answer: Yes; the whole result is treated as one group.

interview.q: What does COUNT(DISTINCT column) do?
interview.answer: Counts unique non-null values after removing duplicates.

interview.q: What is a grouping set?
interview.answer: A specified combination of grouping columns; GROUPING SETS runs several combinations in one query.

interview.q: What does ROLLUP do?
interview.answer: Produces hierarchical subtotals by grouping the listed columns from left to right, ending with a grand total.

interview.q: What does CUBE do?
interview.answer: Produces every possible grouping combination of the listed columns.

interview.q: Why does GROUPING() exist?
interview.answer: It distinguishes a NULL produced by a subtotal from a real NULL in the data.

interview.q: What does FILTER do?
interview.answer: Restricts the rows an aggregate sees, enabling conditional counts and sums in one pass.

interview.q: Why can a join inflate an aggregate?
interview.answer: A one-to-many join repeats the parent row for each child, so COUNT and SUM see more rows than the parent grain.

interview.q: How do you count matches after a LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: Use COUNT(right_table.key), which is zero when there is no match.

interview.q: How do you return zero instead of NULL for an empty SUM?
interview.answer: Use COALESCE(SUM(column), 0).

interview.q: What is the grain of an aggregate result?
interview.answer: One row per distinct combination of grouped columns, or one row total without GROUP BY.

interview.q: How does the planner compute aggregates?
interview.answer: With HashAggregate or GroupAggregate, depending on sorting, indexes, memory and statistics.

interview.q: How can you speed up aggregation?
interview.answer: Filter early, index grouping columns, pre-aggregate before joins and avoid unnecessary COUNT(DISTINCT).

labs.solution: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id, grade;

labs.title: HAVING filter
labs.task: Return courses with more than one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

logic.q: Why does COUNT(column) differ from COUNT(*)?
logic.answer: COUNT(column) skips NULL; COUNT(*) counts every row.

logic.q: Why can SUM return NULL?
logic.answer: There are no non-null values to add, so the result is unknown rather than zero.

logic.q: Why can AVG be misleading with NULLs?
logic.answer: It averages only known values, so the denominator is smaller than the row count.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Filtering rows first reduces the data that must be grouped and aggregated.

logic.q: Why does HAVING run after GROUP BY?
logic.answer: It needs the aggregate result for each group before it can filter groups.

logic.q: Why must every non-aggregated column be grouped?
logic.answer: A group can contain many values; without grouping the output value is undefined.

logic.q: Why can a primary key in GROUP BY allow other columns?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL recognizes functional dependency, so columns determined by the grouped key are allowed.

logic.q: Why can a one-to-many join inflate SUM?
logic.answer: The parent value repeats for each child row, so it is added once per child.

logic.q: Why is COUNT(DISTINCT) relatively expensive?
logic.answer: It must track unique values, often with sorting or hashing, instead of a simple counter.

logic.q: Why do grouping sets produce NULLs?
logic.answer: A column that is not part of a grouping set has no single value for the subtotal row.

logic.q: Why use GROUPING() with ROLLUP?
logic.answer: It distinguishes a subtotal placeholder from a real NULL in the grouped column.

logic.q: Why is HAVING without GROUP BY legal?
logic.answer: The whole result is treated as one group, so aggregate filters can apply.

logic.q: Why is an aggregate illegal in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before grouping, when the aggregate value does not exist yet.

logic.q: Why can an index help GROUP BY?
logic.answer: An ordered index can supply grouped rows without a separate sort, enabling GroupAggregate.

logic.q: Why pre-aggregate before joining?
logic.answer: It reduces the row count and prevents a one-to-many join from multiplying the values being summed.

modules.title: CASE, Conditional Logic and NULL Handling
modules.goal: Express conditional logic correctly and treat NULL as unknown, not empty.

topics.title: Introduction to CASE
topics.simple: CASE SQL me if/else ki tarah conditional value deta hai.
topics.pro: CASE evaluates conditions in order and returns the value from the first matching branch, making it the standard SQL conditional expression.

example.sql: SELECT name, CASE WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'Pass' ELSE 'Fail' END AS result FROM students;

topics.title: Simple CASE
topics.simple: Simple CASE ek expression ko fixed values se compare karta hai.
topics.pro: The simple form CASE expression WHEN value THEN result compares one expression for equality against each WHEN value.
points: Use searched CASE for NULL or ranges.

example.sql: SELECT grade, CASE grade WHEN 'A' THEN 'Excellent' WHEN 'B' THEN 'Good' ELSE 'Needs work' END AS comment FROM enrollments;

topics.title: Searched CASE
topics.simple: Searched CASE har WHEN me arbitrary boolean condition leta hai.
topics.pro: The searched form CASE WHEN condition THEN result evaluates independent boolean conditions, so it can express ranges, NULL checks and compound logic.

example.sql: SELECT name, CASE WHEN marks >= 90 THEN 'A' WHEN marks >= 75 THEN 'B' WHEN marks IS NULL THEN 'Missing' ELSE 'C' END AS band FROM students;

topics.title: CASE Evaluation Order
topics.simple: CASE pehla true branch leta hai; baad wale branches chhoot jaate hain.
topics.pro: CASE stops at the first true condition, so a broad condition placed before a narrow one makes the narrow branch unreachable.
points: Order branches from specific to broad.

example.sql: SELECT marks, CASE WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'Pass' WHEN marks >= 90 THEN 'Distinction' ELSE 'Fail' END AS result FROM students;
example.output: Distinction is unreachable because 90 also passes.

topics.title: CASE in SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT list me CASE computed column banata hai.
topics.pro: CASE in the select list derives a label, bucket or flag without changing stored data.
points: It does not modify the table.
All branches should return compatible types.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, CASE WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'Pass' ELSE 'Fail' END AS result FROM students;
example.output: Each row gets a derived result column.

topics.title: CASE in WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE me CASE conditional predicate bana sakta hai.
topics.pro: CASE can produce a boolean inside WHERE, but a plain OR/AND expression is usually clearer and more index-friendly.
points: CASE must return a boolean here.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE CASE WHEN marks IS NULL THEN FALSE ELSE marks >= 60 END;
example.output: Students with a known passing mark.

topics.title: CASE in ORDER BY
topics.simple: CASE se custom sort order define kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: CASE in ORDER BY maps values to sort ranks, enabling a business-defined order instead of alphabetical or numeric order.
points: The CASE is evaluated per row.

example.sql: SELECT title FROM courses ORDER BY CASE title WHEN 'SQL' THEN 1 WHEN 'Python' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END;
example.output: SQL first, Python second, everything else after.

topics.title: CASE in GROUP BY
topics.simple: CASE se rows ko custom buckets me group kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Grouping by a CASE expression creates buckets such as pass/fail or grade bands, and each bucket can then be aggregated.

example.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'Pass' ELSE 'Fail' END AS result, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students GROUP BY result;

topics.title: CASE with Aggregates
topics.simple: CASE aggregate ke andar conditional value deta hai.
topics.pro: CASE inside SUM or COUNT lets one query compute several conditional totals without scanning the table repeatedly.
points: SUM(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts conditions.
COUNT(CASE ... THEN 1 END) counts non-null matches.

example.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;

topics.title: Conditional Aggregation
topics.simple: Conditional aggregation ek hi pass me multiple metrics deta hai.
topics.pro: Conditional aggregation combines CASE or FILTER with aggregates to produce pass counts, fail counts and totals in one grouped query.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks < 60) AS failed FROM students;

topics.title: COALESCE
topics.simple: COALESCE pehla non-null value deta hai.
topics.pro: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument, making it the standard way to supply a fallback for nullable columns.
points: Arguments are evaluated left to right.

example.sql: SELECT name, COALESCE(email, 'none') AS email FROM students;

topics.title: NULLIF
topics.simple: NULLIF equal values ko NULL bana deta hai.
topics.pro: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b and otherwise returns a; it is commonly used to turn zero denominators or blank strings into NULL.
points: The result type follows the first argument.

example.sql: SELECT marks / NULLIF(marks, 0) AS ratio FROM students;
example.output: NULL instead of division by zero.

topics.title: GREATEST and LEAST
topics.simple: GREATEST maximum aur LEAST minimum choose karte hain.
topics.pro: GREATEST returns the largest argument and LEAST the smallest; in PostgreSQL they ignore NULL arguments and return NULL only when every argument is NULL.

example.sql: SELECT GREATEST(marks, 0) AS floored, LEAST(marks, 100) AS capped FROM students;

topics.title: NULL and Three-Valued Logic
topics.simple: NULL unknown hai, false nahi.
topics.pro: SQL logic has three values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN; comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows.
points: NULL is not zero or empty.
UNKNOWN is filtered out by WHERE.

example.sql: SELECT NULL = NULL AS equal, NULL IS NULL AS is_null;

topics.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
topics.simple: NULL check ke liye IS NULL use karo, = NULL nahi.
topics.pro: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the only direct NULL tests; equality with NULL is always UNKNOWN.
points: IS NOT NULL matches known values.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;

topics.title: NULL in Joins and IN
topics.simple: NULL join keys match nahi karte; NOT IN NULL se empty ho sakta hai.
topics.pro: Equality joins skip NULL keys, and a NULL in a NOT IN list makes the predicate UNKNOWN for every row.
points: Use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM for null-safe matching.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE student_id IS NOT NULL);
example.output: Students whose id is not in the known list.

topics.title: NULL in Aggregates and GROUP BY
topics.simple: Aggregates NULL ignore karte hain; GROUP BY NULL ko ek group banata hai.
topics.pro: COUNT(column), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULL, while GROUP BY treats all NULLs as one group; COUNT(*) still counts every row.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(marks) AS known FROM students;

topics.title: NULL in Constraints and Uniqueness
topics.simple: CHECK NULL par pass hota hai; UNIQUE multiple NULLs allow karta hai.
topics.pro: A CHECK constraint passes when its expression is UNKNOWN, so a nullable column needs NOT NULL to enforce presence; a regular UNIQUE constraint allows multiple NULLs.
points: UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: Common CASE and NULL Errors
topics.simple: Missing END, WHEN NULL aur = NULL sabse common mistakes hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are a missing END, a simple CASE trying to match NULL, an unreachable branch, equality with NULL and NOT IN with a NULL subquery.

example.sql: SELECT name, CASE WHEN marks IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE marks END AS safe_marks FROM students;

topics.title: Practical Conditional Reporting
topics.simple: CASE aur NULL handling ko reports me combine karo.
topics.pro: A reliable conditional report handles missing values explicitly, orders buckets intentionally and verifies that every row falls into exactly one branch.
points: Check the totals against the row count.

example.sql: SELECT COALESCE(CASE WHEN marks >= 90 THEN 'A' WHEN marks >= 75 THEN 'B' WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'C' WHEN marks IS NOT NULL THEN 'F' END, 'Missing') AS band, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students GROUP BY band ORDER BY band;
example.output: Grade-band counts with a missing bucket.

learn.q: What does CASE return?
options: A value from the first matching branch
A table
A boolean only
An index
learn.answer: A value from the first matching branch
learn.why: CASE is a conditional expression.

learn.q: Which CASE form supports ranges?
options: Searched CASE
Simple CASE
Both equally
Neither
learn.answer: Searched CASE
learn.why: Searched CASE accepts arbitrary boolean conditions.

learn.q: Which CASE form compares one expression for equality?
options: Simple CASE
Searched CASE
Both
Neither
learn.answer: Simple CASE
learn.why: Simple CASE is equality-only.

learn.q: Does simple CASE WHEN NULL match a NULL value?
options: No
Yes
Only in PostgreSQL
Only with ELSE
learn.answer: No
learn.why: Equality with NULL is UNKNOWN; use searched CASE with IS NULL.

learn.q: What happens if no branch matches and there is no ELSE?
options: NULL is returned
An error is raised
The first row is returned
Zero is returned
learn.answer: NULL is returned
learn.why: ELSE is optional and defaults to NULL.

learn.q: Which branch wins when several conditions are true?
options: The first one
The last one
The most specific one
All of them
learn.answer: The first one
learn.why: CASE stops at the first true condition.

learn.q: Where can CASE be used?
options: In SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY
Only in SELECT
Only in WHERE
Only in ORDER BY
learn.answer: In SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY
learn.why: CASE is an expression usable wherever a value is accepted.

learn.q: What does COALESCE return?
options: The first non-null argument
The last non-null argument
Always NULL
The smallest value
learn.answer: The first non-null argument
learn.why: It supplies a fallback for NULL.

learn.q: What does NULLIF(a, b) return when a = b?
options: NULL
a
b
Zero
learn.answer: NULL
learn.why: NULLIF turns equal values into NULL.

learn.q: What is NULLIF commonly used to prevent?
options: Division by zero
Duplicate rows
Ambiguous columns
Syntax errors
learn.answer: Division by zero
learn.why: NULLIF(denominator, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL.

learn.q: Does PostgreSQL GREATEST ignore NULL arguments?
options: Yes
No
Only for numbers
Only for text
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: It ignores NULL and returns NULL only if all arguments are NULL.

learn.q: What does NULL = NULL evaluate to?
options: UNKNOWN
TRUE
FALSE
learn.answer: UNKNOWN
learn.why: NULL is not equal to anything, including itself.

learn.q: Which predicate matches NULL?
options: IS NULL
= NULL
<> NULL
LIKE NULL
learn.answer: IS NULL
learn.why: Only IS NULL directly tests for NULL.

learn.q: What does WHERE do with UNKNOWN?
options: Filters it out
Keeps it
Converts it to FALSE
Raises an error
learn.answer: Filters it out
learn.why: WHERE keeps only TRUE rows.

learn.q: Do NULL join keys match each other?
options: No
Yes
Only with LEFT JOIN
Only with CROSS JOIN
learn.answer: No
learn.why: Equality with NULL is UNKNOWN.

learn.q: What does a NULL in a NOT IN list do?
options: Can make the result empty
Is ignored
Matches everything
Raises an error
learn.answer: Can make the result empty
learn.why: The comparison becomes UNKNOWN for every row.

learn.q: Does COUNT(*) count NULL rows?
options: Yes
No
Only NULL marks
Only with GROUP BY
learn.answer: Yes
learn.why: COUNT(*) counts rows, not values.

learn.q: Does COUNT(column) count NULL values?
options: No
Yes
Only in PostgreSQL
Only with DISTINCT
learn.answer: No
learn.why: COUNT(column) skips NULL.

learn.q: How does GROUP BY treat NULLs?
options: As one group
As separate rows
It removes them
It raises an error
learn.answer: As one group
learn.why: NULLs compare equal for grouping.

learn.q: What does a CHECK constraint do with NULL?
options: Passes it as UNKNOWN
Always rejects it
Converts it to zero
Raises an error
learn.answer: Passes it as UNKNOWN
learn.why: A CHECK only rejects FALSE; use NOT NULL for presence.

interview.q: What is CASE?
interview.answer: A standard SQL conditional expression that returns the value of the first matching branch.

interview.q: What is the difference between simple and searched CASE?
interview.answer: Simple CASE compares one expression for equality; searched CASE evaluates independent boolean conditions.

interview.q: Why does simple CASE fail to match NULL?
interview.answer: It uses equality, and NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN; use searched CASE with IS NULL.

interview.q: What happens when no CASE branch matches?
interview.answer: Without ELSE the result is NULL.

interview.q: What does COALESCE do?
interview.answer: Returns the first non-null argument, or NULL if all are null.

interview.q: What does NULLIF do?
interview.answer: Returns NULL when the two arguments are equal, otherwise the first argument.

interview.q: Why use NULLIF(denominator, 0)?
interview.answer: It turns a zero denominator into NULL, avoiding division by zero.

interview.q: How do GREATEST and LEAST treat NULL in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: They ignore NULL arguments and return NULL only when every argument is NULL.

interview.q: What are the three SQL truth values?
interview.answer: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN.

interview.q: What is NULL?
interview.answer: A marker for an unknown or missing value, not zero or an empty string.

interview.q: Why does = NULL never match?
interview.answer: Equality with NULL is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE.

interview.q: When should you use IS NULL?
interview.answer: Whenever you need to test whether a value is missing.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN risky with NULLs?
interview.answer: A NULL in the list makes the predicate UNKNOWN for every row, potentially returning no rows.

interview.q: How do you do a null-safe equality join?
interview.answer: Use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM when NULL should match NULL.

interview.q: How do aggregates treat NULL?
interview.answer: COUNT(column), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULL; COUNT(*) counts rows.

interview.q: How does GROUP BY treat NULL?
interview.answer: It groups all NULLs together as one group.

interview.q: How does a CHECK constraint treat NULL?
interview.answer: The check passes because NULL yields UNKNOWN, not FALSE; NOT NULL is needed to require a value.

interview.q: How does UNIQUE treat NULL?
interview.answer: A regular UNIQUE constraint allows multiple NULLs; PostgreSQL 15+ can use NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

interview.q: How do you count passed and failed rows in one query?
interview.answer: Use conditional aggregation with CASE or FILTER.

interview.q: Why order CASE branches carefully?
interview.answer: The first true branch wins, so a broad branch can make later specific branches unreachable.

logic.q: Why does branch order matter in CASE?
logic.answer: The first true branch wins, so a broad condition can shadow a later specific condition.

logic.q: Why does simple CASE not match NULL?
logic.answer: It uses equality, and NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

logic.q: Why is CASE in WHERE often a bad idea?
logic.answer: It can hide index-friendly predicates and make the filter harder for the planner to optimize.

logic.q: Why use COALESCE instead of CASE for a fallback?
logic.answer: COALESCE expresses the first-non-null intent directly and is shorter.

logic.q: Why use NULLIF before division?
logic.answer: It converts a zero denominator into NULL, so the division returns NULL instead of erroring.

logic.q: Why do GREATEST and LEAST behave differently across databases?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL ignores NULL arguments, while some databases return NULL if any argument is NULL.

logic.q: Why is NULL not equal to zero?
logic.answer: NULL means unknown or missing; zero is a known numeric value.

logic.q: Why does WHERE drop UNKNOWN?
logic.answer: WHERE keeps only rows whose predicate is TRUE; UNKNOWN is not TRUE.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN unsafe with NULLs?
logic.answer: A NULL in the list makes the comparison UNKNOWN for every row, so nothing is returned.

logic.q: Why use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM in a join?
logic.answer: It treats NULL as equal to NULL when the business rule requires matching missing keys.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(*) include NULL rows?
logic.answer: It counts rows, not values, so NULL columns do not matter.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(column) skip NULL?
logic.answer: It counts only known values in that column.

logic.q: Why do NULLs form one GROUP BY group?
logic.answer: Grouping treats NULLs as equal to each other for partitioning.

logic.q: Why does a CHECK constraint allow NULL?
logic.answer: A CHECK rejects only FALSE; NULL produces UNKNOWN, which passes.

logic.q: Why does UNIQUE allow multiple NULLs?
logic.answer: NULLs are not considered equal for a regular unique index; use NULLS NOT DISTINCT if that is wrong.

modules.title: String, Date and Numeric Functions
modules.goal: Transform text, dates and numbers correctly at query time.

topics.title: Introduction to SQL Functions
topics.simple: SQL functions values ko transform karte hain.
topics.pro: Functions take input values and return a computed value; string, date and numeric functions let you clean, format and calculate without changing stored data.
points: Functions do not modify the table.
They can be used in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.
NULL input often produces NULL output.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(name) AS shout FROM students;

topics.title: String Concatenation
topics.simple: || aur CONCAT strings ko jodte hain.
topics.pro: The || operator concatenates strings and propagates NULL, while CONCAT ignores NULL arguments and CONCAT_WS joins only non-null values with a separator.

example.sql: SELECT name || ' (' || COALESCE(email, 'none') || ')' AS label FROM students;
example.output: A label with a visible fallback.

topics.title: LENGTH and CHAR_LENGTH
topics.simple: LENGTH string ke characters ginata hai.
topics.pro: LENGTH and CHAR_LENGTH return the number of characters in a string; OCTET_LENGTH counts bytes and BIT_LENGTH counts bits.

example.sql: SELECT name, LENGTH(name) AS chars FROM students;
example.output: Each name with its character count.

topics.title: UPPER and LOWER
topics.simple: UPPER uppercase aur LOWER lowercase karta hai.
topics.pro: UPPER and LOWER change letter case using the database collation, which is useful for display and case-insensitive comparisons.
points: They do not change stored data.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(name) AS uppercase, LOWER(name) AS lowercase FROM students;

topics.title: TRIM, LTRIM and RTRIM
topics.simple: TRIM whitespace ya chosen characters hataata hai.
topics.pro: TRIM removes leading and trailing characters, LTRIM only leading and RTRIM only trailing; BTRIM is the explicit both-sides function.
points: You can specify the character set.
It does not remove inner spaces.

example.sql: SELECT TRIM('  Aarav  ') AS cleaned;

topics.title: SUBSTRING
topics.simple: SUBSTRING string ka slice nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: SUBSTRING(text FROM start FOR length) returns a one-indexed slice; a missing length returns the rest of the string.
points: Out-of-range slices return available characters or empty.

example.sql: SELECT SUBSTRING(name FROM 1 FOR 3) AS short FROM students;

topics.title: REPLACE
topics.simple: REPLACE matching text ko naye text se badalta hai.
topics.pro: REPLACE(text, from, to) replaces every occurrence of a substring and returns the original when no match exists.

example.sql: SELECT REPLACE(email, '@example.com', '@school.edu') AS school_email FROM students;

topics.title: POSITION and STRPOS
topics.simple: POSITION substring ka index batata hai.
topics.pro: POSITION(sub IN text) and STRPOS(text, sub) return the one-indexed position of the first match, or 0 when absent.

example.sql: SELECT name, POSITION('a' IN name) AS first_a FROM students;

topics.title: LEFT, RIGHT, LPAD and RPAD
topics.simple: LEFT/RIGHT slice karte hain; LPAD/RPAD padding add karte hain.
topics.pro: LEFT and RIGHT return a prefix or suffix, while LPAD and RPAD pad a string to a target length with a fill string.
points: LPAD/RPAD can truncate if the target is shorter.
Padding is useful for fixed-width codes.

example.sql: SELECT LEFT(name, 3) AS prefix, LPAD(id::text, 5, '0') AS padded_id FROM students;
example.output: A prefix and a zero-padded id.

topics.title: STRING_AGG and ARRAY_AGG
topics.simple: STRING_AGG values ko ek string me jodta hai; ARRAY_AGG array banata hai.
topics.pro: STRING_AGG concatenates values per group with a separator and optional ORDER BY, while ARRAY_AGG collects them into an array.
points: ORDER BY inside controls the order.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, STRING_AGG(c.title, ', ' ORDER BY c.title) AS courses FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id GROUP BY s.id, s.name;
example.output: One comma-separated course list per student.

topics.title: Date and Time Types
topics.simple: DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP aur INTERVAL alag concepts hain.
topics.pro: DATE stores a calendar date, TIME stores a time of day, TIMESTAMP stores date and time, TIMESTAMPTZ stores an instant with time zone, and INTERVAL stores a duration.

example.sql: SELECT enrolled_on, enrolled_on::timestamp AS at_midnight FROM enrollments;
example.output: A date and its timestamp form.

topics.title: Current Date and Time
topics.simple: CURRENT_DATE aur CURRENT_TIMESTAMP current values dete hain.
topics.pro: CURRENT_DATE returns the session date, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and NOW() return the transaction start time, and CURRENT_TIME returns the time of day.

example.sql: SELECT CURRENT_DATE AS today, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS now;
example.output: The session date and transaction timestamp.

topics.title: EXTRACT
topics.simple: EXTRACT date ke part ko number me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: EXTRACT(field FROM timestamp) returns a numeric component such as year, month, day, hour or epoch.

example.sql: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM enrolled_on) AS year, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM enrolled_on) AS month FROM enrollments;

topics.title: DATE_TRUNC
topics.simple: DATE_TRUNC date ko chosen unit ke start par le aata hai.
topics.pro: DATE_TRUNC('unit', value) truncates a timestamp to the beginning of the unit, which is the standard way to group by month, week or year.
points: Units include day, week, month, quarter and year.
It is ideal for GROUP BY.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

topics.title: Date Arithmetic and Intervals
topics.simple: Dates aur intervals ko add/subtract kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Date arithmetic adds or subtracts INTERVAL values, while subtracting two dates yields an integer day count and subtracting timestamps yields an interval.

example.sql: SELECT enrolled_on, enrolled_on + INTERVAL '30 days' AS due_on FROM enrollments;
example.output: A due date thirty days later.

topics.title: AGE and Duration
topics.simple: AGE do timestamps ka human-readable difference deta hai.
topics.pro: AGE(later, earlier) returns an interval broken into years, months and days, while AGE(timestamp) compares against the current date.
points: It is useful for tenure and age.

example.sql: SELECT AGE(DATE '2026-01-15', DATE '2025-01-15') AS duration;

topics.title: ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR and TRUNC
topics.simple: Rounding functions decimal ko nearest, up, down ya cut karte hain.
topics.pro: ROUND rounds to a scale, CEIL rounds up, FLOOR rounds down and TRUNC cuts toward zero without rounding.

example.sql: SELECT ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) AS rounded, CEIL(4.2) AS up, FLOOR(4.8) AS down, TRUNC(4.8) AS cut;

topics.title: ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT
topics.simple: Numeric helpers absolute value, remainder, power aur root dete hain.
topics.pro: ABS returns magnitude, MOD returns the remainder, POWER raises a number and SQRT returns the square root.
points: SQRT of a negative is an error.

example.sql: SELECT ABS(-5) AS distance, MOD(10, 3) AS remainder, POWER(2, 3) AS cubed, SQRT(16) AS root;

topics.title: CAST and Type Conversion
topics.simple: CAST value ko doosre type me badalta hai.
topics.pro: CAST(value AS type) and the :: shorthand convert between compatible types; invalid text raises an error rather than silently becoming NULL.

example.sql: SELECT CAST('42' AS INTEGER) AS number, '2026-01-15'::date AS day;

topics.title: Practical Reporting with Functions
topics.simple: Ab text, date aur numeric functions ko report me combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical report cleans text, formats dates, rounds numbers and handles NULL explicitly so the output is stable and readable.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(s.name), 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(s.name) FROM 2)) AS display_name, TO_CHAR(MIN(e.enrolled_on), 'DD Mon YYYY') AS first_enrolled, ROUND(AVG(s.marks), 2) AS average_marks FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name ORDER BY s.name;

learn.q: What does || do with NULL?
options: Returns NULL
Skips NULL
Treats NULL as empty
Raises an error
learn.answer: Returns NULL
learn.why: NULL propagation makes the whole concatenation NULL.

learn.q: Which function ignores NULL arguments when concatenating?
options: CONCAT
LENGTH
SUBSTRING
learn.answer: CONCAT
learn.why: CONCAT treats NULL as empty in PostgreSQL.

learn.q: What does LENGTH return?
options: The number of characters
The number of bytes
The number of rows
The number of bits
learn.answer: The number of characters
learn.why: OCTET_LENGTH and BIT_LENGTH count bytes and bits.

learn.q: What does UPPER do?
options: Converts text to uppercase
Converts text to lowercase
Removes spaces
Counts characters
learn.answer: Converts text to uppercase
learn.why: It changes letter case for the result.

learn.q: What does TRIM remove by default?
options: Spaces at both ends
All spaces
Digits
Newlines only
learn.answer: Spaces at both ends
learn.why: TRIM removes leading and trailing spaces by default.

learn.q: What is the first character position in SUBSTRING?
options: It depends on the column
learn.why: SQL string positions are one-indexed.

learn.q: What does REPLACE do?
options: Replaces every occurrence of a substring
Replaces only the first occurrence
Deletes a column
Sorts text
learn.answer: Replaces every occurrence of a substring
learn.why: All matching occurrences are replaced.

learn.q: What does POSITION return when there is no match?
options: NULL
An error
learn.why: No match is reported as position 0.

learn.q: What does LEFT(name, 3) return?
options: The first three characters
The last three characters
Three rows
The third character
learn.answer: The first three characters
learn.why: LEFT takes a prefix.

learn.q: What does STRING_AGG do?
options: Joins values into one string per group
Counts values
Splits a string
Sorts rows
learn.answer: Joins values into one string per group
learn.why: It concatenates values with a separator.

learn.q: Which type stores a calendar date without time?
options: DATE
TIMESTAMP
TIME
INTERVAL
learn.answer: DATE
learn.why: DATE has no time component.

learn.q: What does CURRENT_TIMESTAMP return?
options: The transaction start timestamp
The current row timestamp
A date only
An interval
learn.answer: The transaction start timestamp
learn.why: It is stable within a transaction.

learn.q: What does EXTRACT return?
options: A numeric component
A formatted string
A date
An interval
learn.answer: A numeric component
learn.why: It extracts a field such as year or month.

learn.q: What does DATE_TRUNC do?
options: Truncates to the start of a unit
Rounds to the nearest unit
Removes dates
Adds an interval
learn.answer: Truncates to the start of a unit
learn.why: It is used to group by month, week or year.

learn.q: What does DATE - DATE return?
options: An integer day count
An interval
A timestamp
A boolean
learn.answer: An integer day count
learn.why: PostgreSQL subtracts dates to days.

learn.q: What does AGE return?
options: An interval
An integer
A date
A string
learn.answer: An interval
learn.why: It expresses a calendar difference.

learn.q: What does CEIL(4.2) return?
learn.why: CEIL rounds up.

learn.q: What does FLOOR(4.8) return?
learn.why: FLOOR rounds down.

learn.q: What does MOD(10, 3) return?
learn.why: It is the remainder.

learn.q: What does CAST do with invalid text?
options: Raises an error
Returns NULL
Returns zero
Skips the row
learn.answer: Raises an error
learn.why: Invalid input syntax is an error.

interview.q: What is the difference between || and CONCAT?
interview.answer: || returns NULL if any operand is NULL; CONCAT ignores NULL arguments.

interview.q: What does LENGTH count?
interview.answer: Characters, not bytes.

interview.q: How do you make a case-insensitive comparison?
interview.answer: Compare LOWER(column) to LOWER(value), or use a case-insensitive collation.

interview.q: How do you remove both leading and trailing spaces?
interview.answer: Use TRIM(text).

interview.q: How do you extract the first three characters?
interview.answer: Use LEFT(text, 3) or SUBSTRING(text FROM 1 FOR 3).

interview.q: How do you replace part of a string?
interview.answer: Use REPLACE(text, from, to).

interview.q: How do you find a substring position?
interview.answer: Use POSITION(sub IN text) or STRPOS(text, sub).

interview.q: How do you concatenate values per group?
interview.answer: Use STRING_AGG(column, separator ORDER BY ...) with GROUP BY.

interview.q: What is the difference between DATE and TIMESTAMP?
interview.answer: DATE stores only a calendar date; TIMESTAMP stores date and time.

interview.q: What is TIMESTAMPTZ?
interview.answer: A timestamp with time zone that stores an instant.

interview.q: What is the difference between NOW() and CURRENT_DATE?
interview.answer: NOW() returns the transaction start timestamp; CURRENT_DATE returns the session date.

interview.q: How do you get the year from a date?
interview.answer: Use EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date).

interview.q: How do you group by month?
interview.answer: Use DATE_TRUNC('month', date_column) in GROUP BY.

interview.q: How do you add thirty days to a date?
interview.answer: Use date + INTERVAL '30 days'.

interview.q: What does timestamp subtraction return?
interview.answer: An interval.

interview.q: How do you calculate age or tenure?
interview.answer: Use AGE(later, earlier) or subtract the dates.

interview.q: What is the difference between ROUND and TRUNC?
interview.answer: ROUND changes the value to the nearest scale; TRUNC cuts digits without rounding.

interview.q: What does CEIL do?
interview.answer: Rounds up to the next integer or scale.

interview.q: How do you convert text to an integer?
interview.answer: Use CAST(text AS INTEGER) or text::integer.

interview.q: How do you format a date for display?
interview.answer: Use TO_CHAR(date, 'YYYY-MM-DD') or another format pattern.

logic.q: Why does || return NULL when one side is NULL?
logic.answer: NULL means unknown, so the concatenated result is unknown rather than partially known.

logic.q: Why is CONCAT useful for labels?
logic.answer: It ignores NULL arguments, so a missing field does not erase the whole label.

logic.q: Why use COALESCE before concatenation?
logic.answer: It gives a readable fallback and keeps the result non-null.

logic.q: Why can LOWER comparisons be slow?
logic.answer: A function on the column can prevent a plain index from being used; a functional or case-insensitive index may be needed.

logic.q: Why are SQL string positions one-indexed?
logic.answer: SQL follows a one-based convention for string positions.

logic.q: Why does DATE_TRUNC help grouping?
logic.answer: It maps every date in a month to the same timestamp, producing one group per month.

logic.q: Why is NOW() stable inside a transaction?
logic.answer: It returns the transaction start time, so multiple calls agree.

logic.q: Why does date subtraction return days?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL defines date minus date as an integer day difference.

logic.q: Why is timestamp subtraction an interval?
logic.answer: Timestamps have time-of-day precision, so the difference is a duration.

logic.q: Why use INTERVAL instead of adding 30?
logic.answer: Adding an integer to a date adds days, but INTERVAL makes the unit explicit and supports months, hours and minutes.

logic.q: Why can ROUND behave differently on double precision?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL’s two-argument ROUND requires numeric, so a double may need an explicit cast.

logic.q: Why is TRUNC different from ROUND?
logic.answer: TRUNC cuts digits; ROUND changes the value based on the next digit.

logic.q: Why can SQRT of a negative fail?
logic.answer: The square root of a negative real number is not defined in this numeric context.

logic.q: Why does CAST fail instead of returning NULL?
logic.answer: Invalid input is an error; silently returning NULL would hide bad data.

logic.q: Why format dates at the presentation layer?
logic.answer: Stored dates should stay typed; display formatting belongs in the report or UI.
