modules.title: Window Functions
modules.goal: Compute rankings, running totals and row comparisons without collapsing rows.

topics.title: Window Function Basics
topics.simple: Window functions har row ke saath related rows par calculate karte hain.
topics.pro: A window function computes across a set of related rows while keeping every row in the result.
points: The result can be ranked or accumulated.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, SUM(marks) OVER () AS total FROM students;
example.output: Every student plus the overall total.

topics.title: OVER Clause
topics.simple: OVER window ka shape batata hai.
topics.pro: OVER introduces the window specification and can include PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and a frame.
points: Empty OVER means the whole result.

example.sql: SELECT name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS rank FROM students;

topics.title: PARTITION BY
topics.simple: PARTITION BY rows ko independent groups me todta hai.
topics.pro: PARTITION BY restarts the window calculation for each group without removing rows.
points: It is like GROUP BY without collapsing.
Missing it makes one global window.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, student_id, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY course_id) AS enrolled FROM enrollments;
example.output: Enrollment count repeated per course row.

topics.title: ORDER BY in Windows
topics.simple: Window ORDER BY calculation ka sequence set karta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the row order used by ranking, lag and running calculations.
points: It is separate from final ORDER BY.

example.sql: SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC, id ASC) AS rn FROM students;

topics.title: ROW_NUMBER
topics.simple: ROW_NUMBER har row ko unique sequence number deta hai.
topics.pro: ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3 and so on in window order, even when values tie.
points: Ties are broken arbitrarily unless the ORDER BY is total.
It is useful for top-N per group.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC, id ASC) AS rn FROM students;

topics.title: RANK
topics.simple: RANK ties ko same rank deta hai aur gaps chhodta hai.
topics.pro: RANK assigns the same rank to tied rows and leaves gaps after a tie.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS rank FROM students;
example.output: Ties share a rank, then gaps.

topics.title: DENSE_RANK
topics.simple: DENSE_RANK ties ko same rank deta hai bina gaps ke.
topics.pro: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank but does not leave gaps.
points: It is useful for grade bands.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS rank FROM students;

topics.title: NTILE
topics.simple: NTILE rows ko N buckets me baantta hai.
topics.pro: NTILE(n) divides the ordered rows into n buckets, putting larger buckets first when the rows do not divide evenly.
points: Sizes differ by at most one.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS quartile FROM students;

topics.title: LAG
topics.simple: LAG previous row ki value deta hai.
topics.pro: LAG returns a value from an earlier row in the window, with an optional offset and default.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, LAG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS previous FROM students;

topics.title: LEAD
topics.simple: LEAD next row ki value deta hai.
topics.pro: LEAD returns a value from a later row in the window, with an optional offset and default.
points: It is useful for next-step analysis.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, LEAD(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_mark FROM students;

topics.title: FIRST_VALUE
topics.simple: FIRST_VALUE window ke first row ki value deta hai.
topics.pro: FIRST_VALUE returns the value from the first row of the window frame, which is often the group leader.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS top_name FROM students;
example.output: Every row shows the top name.

topics.title: LAST_VALUE
topics.simple: LAST_VALUE frame ke last row ki value deta hai.
topics.pro: LAST_VALUE returns the last row of the current frame; with the default frame that is often the current row, so an explicit full frame is usually needed.
points: The default frame ends at the current row.
Use UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for the true last row.

example.sql: SELECT name, LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_name FROM students;
example.output: Every row shows the lowest-ranked name.

topics.title: Running Totals
topics.simple: Running total current row tak accumulate karta hai.
topics.pro: A running total uses SUM with an ordered frame from the start of the partition to the current row.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running FROM students;

topics.title: Moving Averages
topics.simple: Moving average nearby rows ka average deta hai.
topics.pro: A moving average uses a bounded frame such as two preceding rows through the current row.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg FROM students;

topics.title: Window Frames
topics.simple: Frame batata hai kaunse rows current calculation me shaamil hain.
topics.pro: A frame clause defines the start and end boundaries inside the partition, using ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS nearby FROM students;

topics.title: ROWS vs RANGE
topics.simple: ROWS physical rows ginata hai; RANGE value ranges par kaam karta hai.
topics.pro: ROWS addresses physical row offsets, while RANGE groups peers with equal ORDER BY values before applying the boundary.
points: ROWS is precise for row counts.

example.sql: SELECT marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative FROM students;
example.output: Peers receive the same cumulative value.

topics.title: Named Windows
topics.simple: WINDOW clause ek window ko naam dekar reuse karta hai.
topics.pro: A named window defined in WINDOW can be reused by several window functions in the same query.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, student_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn FROM enrollments WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY course_id ORDER BY student_id);

topics.title: Window vs GROUP BY
topics.simple: GROUP BY rows collapse karta hai; window rows preserve karta hai.
topics.pro: GROUP BY returns one row per group, while a window function returns one row per input row with the group calculation attached.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY course_id) AS enrolled FROM enrollments;
example.output: Every enrollment row with its course count.

topics.title: Window Performance
topics.simple: Window functions sort aur memory use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Window execution often requires sorting by partition and order keys, so matching indexes and narrow frames reduce the cost.
points: Index the partition and order keys.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) FROM students;
example.output: A plan with a WindowAgg and Sort.

topics.title: Practical Window Report
topics.simple: Windows se ranking, running totals aur per-group top N banao.
topics.pro: A practical report combines a partition, an order, a ranking function and an outer filter on the rank alias.
points: Rank in a CTE or subquery.

example.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT course_id, student_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY course_id ORDER BY student_id) AS rn FROM enrollments) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;
example.output: The first three students per course.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Window Function Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A window function computes across a set of related rows while keeping every row in the result. Key rules: OVER defines the window. Rows are not collapsed. The result can be ranked or accumulated.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain OVER Clause in a production query.
interview.answer: OVER introduces the window specification and can include PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and a frame. Key rules: OVER is mandatory. Empty OVER means the whole result. It follows the function call.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain PARTITION BY in a production query.
interview.answer: PARTITION BY restarts the window calculation for each group without removing rows. Key rules: Each partition is independent. It is like GROUP BY without collapsing. Missing it makes one global window.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain ORDER BY in Windows in a production query.
interview.answer: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the row order used by ranking, lag and running calculations. Key rules: It is separate from final ORDER BY. It controls the frame direction. Ties need a deterministic key.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain ROW_NUMBER in a production query.
interview.answer: ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3 and so on in window order, even when values tie. Key rules: It is unique per partition. Ties are broken arbitrarily unless the ORDER BY is total. It is useful for top-N per group.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain RANK in a production query.
interview.answer: RANK assigns the same rank to tied rows and leaves gaps after a tie. Key rules: Ties share a rank. Gaps appear after ties. It follows competition ranking.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain DENSE_RANK in a production query.
interview.answer: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank but does not leave gaps. Key rules: Ties share a rank. No gaps appear. It is useful for grade bands.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain NTILE in a production query.
interview.answer: NTILE(n) divides the ordered rows into n buckets, putting larger buckets first when the rows do not divide evenly. Key rules: Buckets are numbered 1 to n. Rows are ordered first. Sizes differ by at most one.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain LAG in a production query.
interview.answer: LAG returns a value from an earlier row in the window, with an optional offset and default. Key rules: Offset defaults to 1. The default is NULL. It is useful for deltas.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain LEAD in a production query.
interview.answer: LEAD returns a value from a later row in the window, with an optional offset and default. Key rules: Offset defaults to 1. The last row gets NULL. It is useful for next-step analysis.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain FIRST_VALUE in a production query.
interview.answer: FIRST_VALUE returns the value from the first row of the window frame, which is often the group leader. Key rules: It respects the frame. It can be partitioned. It is useful for comparisons.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain LAST_VALUE in a production query.
interview.answer: LAST_VALUE returns the last row of the current frame; with the default frame that is often the current row, so an explicit full frame is usually needed. Key rules: The default frame ends at the current row. Use UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for the true last row. It respects PARTITION BY.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Running Totals in a production query.
interview.answer: A running total uses SUM with an ordered frame from the start of the partition to the current row. Key rules: Order the rows. Use an unbounded preceding frame. Partition to restart per group.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Moving Averages in a production query.
interview.answer: A moving average uses a bounded frame such as two preceding rows through the current row. Key rules: Choose the frame width. Order by a stable key. Partition when averages restart.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Window Frames in a production query.
interview.answer: A frame clause defines the start and end boundaries inside the partition, using ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS. Key rules: Frames apply to ordered windows. ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE counts value ranges.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain ROWS vs RANGE in a production query.
interview.answer: ROWS addresses physical row offsets, while RANGE groups peers with equal ORDER BY values before applying the boundary. Key rules: ROWS is precise for row counts. RANGE includes peer rows. Duplicates behave differently.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Named Windows in a production query.
interview.answer: A named window defined in WINDOW can be reused by several window functions in the same query. Key rules: Define it after FROM. Reference it in OVER. It reduces repetition.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Window vs GROUP BY in a production query.
interview.answer: GROUP BY returns one row per group, while a window function returns one row per input row with the group calculation attached. Key rules: GROUP BY changes the grain. Windows preserve the grain. Both can use partitions.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Window Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Window execution often requires sorting by partition and order keys, so matching indexes and narrow frames reduce the cost. Key rules: Index the partition and order keys. Narrow the frame when possible. Read EXPLAIN for WindowAgg.

interview.q: Module 15 · Explain Practical Window Report in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical report combines a partition, an order, a ranking function and an outer filter on the rank alias. Key rules: Rank in a CTE or subquery. Filter the rank outside. State the result grain.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does OVER Clause matter?
logic.answer: OVER introduces the window specification and can include PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and a frame. OVER is mandatory. Empty OVER means the whole result. It follows the function call.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does PARTITION BY matter?
logic.answer: PARTITION BY restarts the window calculation for each group without removing rows. Each partition is independent. It is like GROUP BY without collapsing. Missing it makes one global window.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does ORDER BY in Windows matter?
logic.answer: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the row order used by ranking, lag and running calculations. It is separate from final ORDER BY. It controls the frame direction. Ties need a deterministic key.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does ROW_NUMBER matter?
logic.answer: ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3 and so on in window order, even when values tie. It is unique per partition. Ties are broken arbitrarily unless the ORDER BY is total. It is useful for top-N per group.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does RANK matter?
logic.answer: RANK assigns the same rank to tied rows and leaves gaps after a tie. Ties share a rank. Gaps appear after ties. It follows competition ranking.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does DENSE_RANK matter?
logic.answer: DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank but does not leave gaps. Ties share a rank. No gaps appear. It is useful for grade bands.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does NTILE matter?
logic.answer: NTILE(n) divides the ordered rows into n buckets, putting larger buckets first when the rows do not divide evenly. Buckets are numbered 1 to n. Rows are ordered first. Sizes differ by at most one.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does LAG matter?
logic.answer: LAG returns a value from an earlier row in the window, with an optional offset and default. Offset defaults to 1. The default is NULL. It is useful for deltas.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does LEAD matter?
logic.answer: LEAD returns a value from a later row in the window, with an optional offset and default. Offset defaults to 1. The last row gets NULL. It is useful for next-step analysis.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does FIRST_VALUE matter?
logic.answer: FIRST_VALUE returns the value from the first row of the window frame, which is often the group leader. It respects the frame. It can be partitioned. It is useful for comparisons.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does LAST_VALUE matter?
logic.answer: LAST_VALUE returns the last row of the current frame; with the default frame that is often the current row, so an explicit full frame is usually needed. The default frame ends at the current row. Use UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for the true last row. It respects PARTITION BY.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does Running Totals matter?
logic.answer: A running total uses SUM with an ordered frame from the start of the partition to the current row. Order the rows. Use an unbounded preceding frame. Partition to restart per group.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does Moving Averages matter?
logic.answer: A moving average uses a bounded frame such as two preceding rows through the current row. Choose the frame width. Order by a stable key. Partition when averages restart.

logic.q: Module 15 · Why does Window Frames matter?
logic.answer: A frame clause defines the start and end boundaries inside the partition, using ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS. Frames apply to ordered windows. ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE counts value ranges.

modules.title: Advanced Window Functions and Frames
modules.goal: Use ranking, frames and distribution functions for serious analytical queries.

topics.title: Ranking vs Row Number
topics.simple: Ranking ties ko same number deta hai; row number unique rehta hai.
topics.pro: RANK shares numbers across ties and leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK shares without gaps, and ROW_NUMBER is unique but arbitrary on ties.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS r, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS d, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC, id) AS rn FROM students;

topics.title: Top N per Group
topics.simple: Partitioned row numbers se har group ka top N nikaalo.
topics.pro: Top-N per group ranks rows inside each partition and filters the rank in an outer query.

example.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT course_id, student_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY course_id ORDER BY student_id) AS rn FROM enrollments) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

topics.title: Running Totals
topics.simple: Running total ordered rows ko accumulate karta hai.
topics.pro: A running total uses SUM with an unbounded preceding frame and restarts per partition.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running FROM students;

topics.title: Moving Averages
topics.simple: Moving average window ke andar ke rows ka average deta hai.
topics.pro: A moving average uses a bounded frame and a stable order so each row sees the same number of neighbors.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg FROM students;

topics.title: Frame Boundaries
topics.simple: Frame ka start aur end explicitly set karo.
topics.pro: Frame boundaries use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
points: The default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS nearby FROM students;

topics.title: ROWS Frame
topics.simple: ROWS physical row offsets par kaam karta hai.
topics.pro: ROWS counts actual rows, so duplicate ORDER BY values are still separate frame positions.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg2 FROM students;

topics.title: RANGE Frame
topics.simple: RANGE ORDER BY values ke ranges par kaam karta hai.
topics.pro: RANGE includes peer rows with equal ORDER BY values, so duplicates move through the frame together.

example.sql: SELECT marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative FROM students;
example.output: Tied marks receive the same cumulative value.

topics.title: GROUPS Frame
topics.simple: GROUPS peer groups ke offsets par kaam karta hai.
topics.pro: GROUPS counts peer groups rather than physical rows, which is useful when ties should be one unit.
points: It sits between ROWS and RANGE.

example.sql: SELECT marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS grouped_avg FROM students;
example.output: Averages over the previous peer group and the current group.

topics.title: EXCLUDE Clause
topics.simple: EXCLUDE current row ya peers ko frame se hataata hai.
topics.pro: EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, EXCLUDE GROUP and EXCLUDE TIES remove rows from the frame for calculations such as leave-one-out averages.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW) AS neighbor_avg FROM students;

topics.title: LAG and LEAD
topics.simple: LAG previous aur LEAD next row deta hai.
topics.pro: LAG and LEAD compare a row with an earlier or later row using an offset and optional default.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, marks - LAG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS delta FROM students;
example.output: The change from the previous mark.

topics.title: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE
topics.simple: Frame ke first aur last value dete hain.
topics.pro: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return boundary values from the frame, so the frame definition determines the result.
points: LAST_VALUE needs a full frame for the last row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY marks ORDER BY id) AS first_peer FROM students;
example.output: The first student at each mark.

topics.title: NTH_VALUE
topics.simple: NTH_VALUE frame ka Nth row deta hai.
topics.pro: NTH_VALUE returns the value at a one-based position inside the frame, with an optional direction.
points: The frame must include the row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS second_name FROM students;
example.output: The second-highest name on every row.

topics.title: PERCENT_RANK
topics.simple: PERCENT_RANK relative percentile rank deta hai.
topics.pro: PERCENT_RANK returns (rank - 1) / (rows - 1), giving a value from 0 to 1 for ordered rows.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks) AS pct FROM students;

topics.title: CUME_DIST
topics.simple: CUME_DIST cumulative distribution deta hai.
topics.pro: CUME_DIST returns the fraction of rows at or below the current peer group, always greater than zero and at most one.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY marks) AS cume FROM students;

topics.title: NTILE Buckets
topics.simple: NTILE ordered rows ko equal buckets me baantta hai.
topics.pro: NTILE(n) assigns bucket numbers from 1 to n, with earlier buckets taking the extra rows.
points: Buckets differ by at most one.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS quartile FROM students;

topics.title: Percent of Total
topics.simple: Window sum se row ka percent of total nikaalo.
topics.pro: Dividing a row value by SUM over an empty window produces its share of the total without a separate aggregate query.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks, ROUND(100.0 * marks / SUM(marks) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM students;
example.output: Each mark as a percentage of the total.

topics.title: Difference from Previous
topics.simple: LAG se previous value ka difference nikaalo.
topics.pro: Subtracting LAG from the current value gives a row-to-row delta, with NULL for the first row.

example.sql: SELECT id, marks, marks - LAG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS delta FROM students;
example.output: The change from the prior row.

topics.title: Median with PERCENTILE_CONT
topics.simple: PERCENTILE_CONT continuous percentile deta hai.
topics.pro: PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between values to return a continuous percentile, commonly the median at 0.5.
points: It returns one row per group.

example.sql: SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY marks) AS median FROM students;

topics.title: Mode with MODE
topics.simple: MODE sabse frequent value deta hai.
topics.pro: MODE() WITHIN GROUP returns the most frequent input value, and PostgreSQL picks the first one when there is a tie.

example.sql: SELECT MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY marks) AS mode FROM students;

topics.title: Practical Ranking Report
topics.simple: Ranking, percent of total aur top N ko report me combine karo.
topics.pro: A production ranking report uses a CTE for window calculations, filters the rank outside and presents a stable order.

example.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS r, ROUND(100.0 * marks / SUM(marks) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM students) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 5 ORDER BY r;
example.output: Top five with rank and share.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Ranking vs Row Number in a production query.
interview.answer: RANK shares numbers across ties and leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK shares without gaps, and ROW_NUMBER is unique but arbitrary on ties. Key rules: Choose by tie semantics. ROW_NUMBER needs a total order. DENSE_RANK is compact.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Top N per Group in a production query.
interview.answer: Top-N per group ranks rows inside each partition and filters the rank in an outer query. Key rules: Partition by the group. Order by the ranking key. Filter the rank outside.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Running Totals in a production query.
interview.answer: A running total uses SUM with an unbounded preceding frame and restarts per partition. Key rules: Order by a stable key. Use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING. Partition for group totals.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Moving Averages in a production query.
interview.answer: A moving average uses a bounded frame and a stable order so each row sees the same number of neighbors. Key rules: Pick the frame width. Use ROWS for exact counts. Use RANGE for date windows.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Frame Boundaries in a production query.
interview.answer: Frame boundaries use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Key rules: Start must not follow end. The default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW. Frames require ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain ROWS Frame in a production query.
interview.answer: ROWS counts actual rows, so duplicate ORDER BY values are still separate frame positions. Key rules: Exact row counts. Duplicates are separate. Good for moving averages.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain RANGE Frame in a production query.
interview.answer: RANGE includes peer rows with equal ORDER BY values, so duplicates move through the frame together. Key rules: Peers share a frame. Good for value ranges. Date ranges use intervals.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain GROUPS Frame in a production query.
interview.answer: GROUPS counts peer groups rather than physical rows, which is useful when ties should be one unit. Key rules: Groups are peer sets. It sits between ROWS and RANGE. It needs ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain EXCLUDE Clause in a production query.
interview.answer: EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, EXCLUDE GROUP and EXCLUDE TIES remove rows from the frame for calculations such as leave-one-out averages. Key rules: It applies after the frame. PostgreSQL supports it. It is useful for comparisons.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain LAG and LEAD in a production query.
interview.answer: LAG and LEAD compare a row with an earlier or later row using an offset and optional default. Key rules: Offset defaults to 1. Order must be deterministic. Partition for group-local comparisons.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in a production query.
interview.answer: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return boundary values from the frame, so the frame definition determines the result. Key rules: They respect the frame. LAST_VALUE needs a full frame for the last row. Partition for group boundaries.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain NTH_VALUE in a production query.
interview.answer: NTH_VALUE returns the value at a one-based position inside the frame, with an optional direction. Key rules: Position is one-based. The frame must include the row. It returns NULL when absent.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain PERCENT_RANK in a production query.
interview.answer: PERCENT_RANK returns (rank - 1) / (rows - 1), giving a value from 0 to 1 for ordered rows. Key rules: It uses RANK semantics. The best row is 0. The worst row is 1.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain CUME_DIST in a production query.
interview.answer: CUME_DIST returns the fraction of rows at or below the current peer group, always greater than zero and at most one. Key rules: It includes peers. It is cumulative. It differs from PERCENT_RANK.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain NTILE Buckets in a production query.
interview.answer: NTILE(n) assigns bucket numbers from 1 to n, with earlier buckets taking the extra rows. Key rules: It needs an order. Buckets differ by at most one. It is good for quartiles.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Percent of Total in a production query.
interview.answer: Dividing a row value by SUM over an empty window produces its share of the total without a separate aggregate query. Key rules: Use SUM(...) OVER (). Guard against zero. Round at display time.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Difference from Previous in a production query.
interview.answer: Subtracting LAG from the current value gives a row-to-row delta, with NULL for the first row. Key rules: Order by the event key. Handle the first NULL. Partition for restarts.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Median with PERCENTILE_CONT in a production query.
interview.answer: PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between values to return a continuous percentile, commonly the median at 0.5. Key rules: It uses WITHIN GROUP. It interpolates. It returns one row per group.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Mode with MODE in a production query.
interview.answer: MODE() WITHIN GROUP returns the most frequent input value, and PostgreSQL picks the first one when there is a tie. Key rules: It uses WITHIN GROUP. It ignores NULL. Ties are resolved arbitrarily.

interview.q: Module 16 · Explain Practical Ranking Report in a production query.
interview.answer: A production ranking report uses a CTE for window calculations, filters the rank outside and presents a stable order. Key rules: Calculate windows in a CTE. Filter in the outer query. Order the final report.

labs.title: Ranking vs Row Number
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Ranking vs Row Number.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS r, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS d, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC, id) AS rn FROM students;

labs.title: Top N per Group
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Top N per Group.
labs.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT course_id, student_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY course_id ORDER BY student_id) AS rn FROM enrollments) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

labs.title: Running Totals
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Running Totals.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running FROM students;

labs.title: Moving Averages
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Moving Averages.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg FROM students;

labs.title: Frame Boundaries
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Frame Boundaries.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS nearby FROM students;

labs.title: ROWS Frame
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates ROWS Frame.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg2 FROM students;

labs.title: RANGE Frame
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates RANGE Frame.
labs.solution: SELECT marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative FROM students;
labs.expected: Tied marks receive the same cumulative value.

labs.title: GROUPS Frame
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates GROUPS Frame.
labs.solution: SELECT marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS grouped_avg FROM students;
labs.expected: Averages over the previous peer group and the current group.

labs.title: EXCLUDE Clause
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates EXCLUDE Clause.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, AVG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW) AS neighbor_avg FROM students;

labs.title: LAG and LEAD
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates LAG and LEAD.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, marks - LAG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS delta FROM students;
labs.expected: The change from the previous mark.

labs.title: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY marks ORDER BY id) AS first_peer FROM students;
labs.expected: The first student at each mark.

labs.title: NTH_VALUE
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates NTH_VALUE.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS second_name FROM students;
labs.expected: The second-highest name on every row.

labs.title: PERCENT_RANK
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates PERCENT_RANK.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks) AS pct FROM students;

labs.title: CUME_DIST
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates CUME_DIST.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY marks) AS cume FROM students;

labs.title: NTILE Buckets
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates NTILE Buckets.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS quartile FROM students;

labs.title: Percent of Total
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Percent of Total.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks, ROUND(100.0 * marks / SUM(marks) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM students;
labs.expected: Each mark as a percentage of the total.

labs.title: Difference from Previous
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Difference from Previous.
labs.solution: SELECT id, marks, marks - LAG(marks) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS delta FROM students;
labs.expected: The change from the prior row.

labs.title: Median with PERCENTILE_CONT
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Median with PERCENTILE_CONT.
labs.solution: SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY marks) AS median FROM students;

labs.title: Mode with MODE
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Mode with MODE.
labs.solution: SELECT MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY marks) AS mode FROM students;

labs.title: Practical Ranking Report
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Practical Ranking Report.
labs.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS r, ROUND(100.0 * marks / SUM(marks) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM students) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 5 ORDER BY r;
labs.expected: Top five with rank and share.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does Ranking vs Row Number matter?
logic.answer: RANK shares numbers across ties and leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK shares without gaps, and ROW_NUMBER is unique but arbitrary on ties. Choose by tie semantics. ROW_NUMBER needs a total order. DENSE_RANK is compact.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does Top N per Group matter?
logic.answer: Top-N per group ranks rows inside each partition and filters the rank in an outer query. Partition by the group. Order by the ranking key. Filter the rank outside.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does Running Totals matter?
logic.answer: A running total uses SUM with an unbounded preceding frame and restarts per partition. Order by a stable key. Use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING. Partition for group totals.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does Moving Averages matter?
logic.answer: A moving average uses a bounded frame and a stable order so each row sees the same number of neighbors. Pick the frame width. Use ROWS for exact counts. Use RANGE for date windows.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does Frame Boundaries matter?
logic.answer: Frame boundaries use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Start must not follow end. The default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW. Frames require ORDER BY.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does ROWS Frame matter?
logic.answer: ROWS counts actual rows, so duplicate ORDER BY values are still separate frame positions. Exact row counts. Duplicates are separate. Good for moving averages.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does RANGE Frame matter?
logic.answer: RANGE includes peer rows with equal ORDER BY values, so duplicates move through the frame together. Peers share a frame. Good for value ranges. Date ranges use intervals.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does GROUPS Frame matter?
logic.answer: GROUPS counts peer groups rather than physical rows, which is useful when ties should be one unit. Groups are peer sets. It sits between ROWS and RANGE. It needs ORDER BY.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does EXCLUDE Clause matter?
logic.answer: EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, EXCLUDE GROUP and EXCLUDE TIES remove rows from the frame for calculations such as leave-one-out averages. It applies after the frame. PostgreSQL supports it. It is useful for comparisons.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does LAG and LEAD matter?
logic.answer: LAG and LEAD compare a row with an earlier or later row using an offset and optional default. Offset defaults to 1. Order must be deterministic. Partition for group-local comparisons.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE matter?
logic.answer: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return boundary values from the frame, so the frame definition determines the result. They respect the frame. LAST_VALUE needs a full frame for the last row. Partition for group boundaries.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does NTH_VALUE matter?
logic.answer: NTH_VALUE returns the value at a one-based position inside the frame, with an optional direction. Position is one-based. The frame must include the row. It returns NULL when absent.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does PERCENT_RANK matter?
logic.answer: PERCENT_RANK returns (rank - 1) / (rows - 1), giving a value from 0 to 1 for ordered rows. It uses RANK semantics. The best row is 0. The worst row is 1.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does CUME_DIST matter?
logic.answer: CUME_DIST returns the fraction of rows at or below the current peer group, always greater than zero and at most one. It includes peers. It is cumulative. It differs from PERCENT_RANK.

logic.q: Module 16 · Why does NTILE Buckets matter?
logic.answer: NTILE(n) assigns bucket numbers from 1 to n, with earlier buckets taking the extra rows. It needs an order. Buckets differ by at most one. It is good for quartiles.

modules.title: Views and Materialized Views
modules.goal: Package queries behind stable relations and choose between live and materialized results.

topics.title: What Is a View?
topics.simple: View ek saved query hai jo table ki tarah query hoti hai.
topics.pro: A view is a named stored query; it has no independent rows and is evaluated when queried.
points: Views store the query, not the data.
They can restrict columns and rows.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

topics.title: CREATE VIEW
topics.simple: CREATE VIEW se named query banao.
topics.pro: CREATE VIEW name AS query defines a view over one or more relations.
points: Column names come from the select list.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: Querying a View
topics.simple: View ko normal table ki tarah SELECT karo.
topics.pro: A view can be used in SELECT, JOIN, WHERE and most places a table is allowed.
points: Its columns are the select-list columns.
The underlying query runs each time.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM student_names ORDER BY name;

topics.title: View as Abstraction
topics.simple: View complex joins ko simple interface deta hai.
topics.pro: A view hides join and filter details behind a stable name, so consumers do not repeat fragile SQL.
points: Change the view instead of every caller.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW course_roster AS SELECT c.title, s.name FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id;

topics.title: Updatable Views
topics.simple: Simple views ko INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE kiya ja sakta hai.
topics.pro: A view is automatically updatable when it maps rows one-to-one to a base table without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations.
points: Use INSTEAD OF triggers for complex views.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: WITH CHECK OPTION
topics.simple: WITH CHECK OPTION view ke filter ke bahar writes rokta hai.
topics.pro: WITH CHECK OPTION rejects inserts or updates that would make a row invisible through the view predicate.
points: It can be LOCAL or CASCADED.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW passing AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 WITH CHECK OPTION;

topics.title: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
topics.simple: Existing view ko replace karne ke liye OR REPLACE use karo.
topics.pro: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the query in place, but cannot change existing column names, order or types.
points: Use DROP and CREATE for a redesign.

example.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name, email FROM students;

topics.title: Dropping Views
topics.simple: DROP VIEW view ko remove karta hai.
topics.pro: DROP VIEW removes the named query; CASCADE also drops dependent objects, while RESTRICT refuses if dependencies exist.
points: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS is safe for scripts.

example.sql: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS student_names;

topics.title: View Dependencies
topics.simple: Views doosri views aur tables par depend kar sakti hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping a referenced object may require CASCADE or fail with a dependency error.

example.sql: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = 'public';

topics.title: Materialized Views
topics.simple: Materialized view result ko disk par store karta hai.
topics.pro: A materialized view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but can be stale until refreshed.

example.sql: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts AS SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

topics.title: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
topics.simple: Refresh stored result ko dobara compute karta hai.
topics.pro: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW reruns the query and replaces the stored rows.
points: It locks the view by default.

example.sql: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts;

topics.title: Concurrent Refresh
topics.simple: CONCURRENTLY refresh ke dauraan reads allow karta hai.
topics.pro: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and avoids blocking readers, at the cost of more work.
points: Cannot run inside a transaction block.

example.sql:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX course_counts_course_id ON course_counts (course_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY course_counts;

topics.title: Indexing Materialized Views
topics.simple: Materialized view par index laga sakte hain.
topics.pro: Because a materialized view stores rows, it supports ordinary indexes for lookup and uniqueness.
points: A unique index enables concurrent refresh.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX course_counts_total ON course_counts (total DESC);

topics.title: View vs Materialized View
topics.simple: View live hota hai; materialized view cached hota hai.
topics.pro: A view always reflects current base data, while a materialized view reflects the last refresh and can be stale.
points: Materialized views trade freshness for speed.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM course_counts;

topics.title: Security with Views
topics.simple: View se column-level access restrict kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Granting access to a view can expose only selected columns and rows without granting the base table.
points: Views do not bypass underlying privileges unless security definer is used.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON student_names TO app_role;

topics.title: Performance of Views
topics.simple: View apne aap me optimization cache nahi hai.
topics.pro: A plain view is expanded into the caller query and optimized with it; it does not store results or guarantee a fixed plan.
points: The planner sees through simple views.
Complex views can still be expensive.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM high_scorers;
example.output: A plan over the students table.

topics.title: Common View Errors
topics.simple: Duplicate columns, bad replacements aur stale materialized data common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are duplicate output names, replacing a view with an incompatible shape, refreshing without a unique index and forgetting that a materialized view is stale.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id AS student_id, c.id AS course_id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;

topics.title: Practical Reporting View
topics.simple: Reporting view stable columns aur filters deta hai.
topics.pro: A reporting view joins and labels data once, giving dashboards a stable interface over changing tables.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW enrollment_report AS SELECT c.title AS course, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

topics.title: Column Aliases in Views
topics.simple: View columns ko explicit names do.
topics.pro: Explicit aliases prevent duplicate names and keep the view contract stable when the underlying query changes.
points: Column order is part of the contract.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_labels AS SELECT id AS student_id, name AS display_name FROM students;

topics.title: View Maintenance
topics.simple: Views ko schema changes ke saath maintain karo.
topics.pro: Review dependencies, test replacements and refresh materialized views after data changes.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_depend WHERE refobjid = 'students'::regclass;

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain What Is a View? in a production query.
interview.answer: A view is a named stored query; it has no independent rows and is evaluated when queried. Key rules: Views store the query, not the data. They simplify complex SQL. They can restrict columns and rows.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain CREATE VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE VIEW name AS query defines a view over one or more relations. Key rules: Name the view. The query follows AS. Column names come from the select list.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Querying a View in a production query.
interview.answer: A view can be used in SELECT, JOIN, WHERE and most places a table is allowed. Key rules: Query it by name. Its columns are the select-list columns. The underlying query runs each time.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View as Abstraction in a production query.
interview.answer: A view hides join and filter details behind a stable name, so consumers do not repeat fragile SQL. Key rules: Centralize reusable logic. Expose only needed columns. Change the view instead of every caller.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Updatable Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A view is automatically updatable when it maps rows one-to-one to a base table without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations. Key rules: Simple projections are updatable. Aggregates block updates. Use INSTEAD OF triggers for complex views.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain WITH CHECK OPTION in a production query.
interview.answer: WITH CHECK OPTION rejects inserts or updates that would make a row invisible through the view predicate. Key rules: It protects the view contract. It applies to writes. It can be LOCAL or CASCADED.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the query in place, but cannot change existing column names, order or types. Key rules: It keeps dependencies. Column shape must stay compatible. Use DROP and CREATE for a redesign.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Dropping Views in a production query.
interview.answer: DROP VIEW removes the named query; CASCADE also drops dependent objects, while RESTRICT refuses if dependencies exist. Key rules: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS is safe for scripts. CASCADE can remove dependents. The base tables remain.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View Dependencies in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping a referenced object may require CASCADE or fail with a dependency error. Key rules: Check dependencies before dropping. CASCADE is destructive. information_schema.views lists definitions.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Materialized Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A materialized view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but can be stale until refreshed. Key rules: It stores rows. It must be refreshed. It can have indexes.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW reruns the query and replaces the stored rows. Key rules: It can be expensive. It locks the view by default. CONCURRENTLY reduces blocking.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Concurrent Refresh in a production query.
interview.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and avoids blocking readers, at the cost of more work. Key rules: Requires a unique index. Cannot run inside a transaction block. It may be slower.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Indexing Materialized Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Because a materialized view stores rows, it supports ordinary indexes for lookup and uniqueness. Key rules: Index the refreshed rows. A unique index enables concurrent refresh. Refresh maintains the indexes.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View vs Materialized View in a production query.
interview.answer: A view always reflects current base data, while a materialized view reflects the last refresh and can be stale. Key rules: Views have no refresh cost. Materialized views trade freshness for speed. Choose by freshness requirements.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Security with Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Granting access to a view can expose only selected columns and rows without granting the base table. Key rules: Grant on the view. Do not expose sensitive columns. Views do not bypass underlying privileges unless security definer is used.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Performance of Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A plain view is expanded into the caller query and optimized with it; it does not store results or guarantee a fixed plan. Key rules: The planner sees through simple views. Complex views can still be expensive. Materialize only when needed.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Common View Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are duplicate output names, replacing a view with an incompatible shape, refreshing without a unique index and forgetting that a materialized view is stale. Key rules: Alias duplicate columns. Keep replacement shapes compatible. Refresh materialized views.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Practical Reporting View in a production query.
interview.answer: A reporting view joins and labels data once, giving dashboards a stable interface over changing tables. Key rules: Name columns explicitly. Keep the grain clear. Document refresh expectations.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Column Aliases in Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Explicit aliases prevent duplicate names and keep the view contract stable when the underlying query changes. Key rules: Alias expressions. Alias duplicate names. Column order is part of the contract.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Review dependencies, test replacements and refresh materialized views after data changes. Key rules: Track dependent views. Test CREATE OR REPLACE. Schedule refreshes.

debug.title: Duplicate view columns
debug.broken: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id, c.id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;
debug.fix: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id AS student_id, c.id AS course_id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;
debug.error: column "id" specified more than once
debug.expected: A view with two distinct columns.

debug.title: View already exists
debug.broken: CREATE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.fix: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.error: relation "high_scorers" already exists

debug.title: Aggregate view update
debug.broken: UPDATE course_counts SET total = 0;
debug.fix: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts;
debug.error: cannot update view "course_counts"

debug.title: Concurrent refresh without index
debug.broken: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY course_counts;
debug.fix:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX course_counts_course_id ON course_counts (course_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY course_counts;
debug.error: cannot refresh materialized view "course_counts" concurrently

debug.title: Drop with dependency
debug.broken: DROP VIEW student_names;
debug.fix: DROP VIEW student_names CASCADE;
debug.error: cannot drop view because other objects depend on it
debug.expected: The view and dependents are removed.

debug.title: Check option violation
debug.broken:
CREATE VIEW passing AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 WITH CHECK OPTION;
INSERT INTO passing (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 40);
debug.fix: INSERT INTO passing (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 75);
debug.error: new row violates check option for view "passing"

debug.fix:

modules.title: Indexes and Query Plans
modules.goal: Choose indexes from real query shapes and read plans before adding more.

topics.title: What Is an Index?
topics.simple: Index lookup ko fast karta hai, writes ko mehnga.
topics.pro: An index is an auxiliary structure that speeds selected reads at the cost of storage and write maintenance.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks);

topics.title: B-tree Index
topics.simple: B-tree default index hai equality aur range ke liye.
topics.pro: A B-tree supports equality, ordering and range predicates and is the default PostgreSQL index type.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks DESC);

topics.title: CREATE INDEX
topics.simple: CREATE INDEX se index banao.
topics.pro: CREATE INDEX name ON table (columns) builds an index for the chosen key.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student ON enrollments (student_id);

topics.title: Unique Index
topics.simple: Unique index duplicate values rokta hai.
topics.pro: A unique index enforces uniqueness and also speeds equality lookups.
points: It can back a primary key.

example.sql: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email);

topics.title: Composite Index
topics.simple: Composite index multiple columns ko ek order me index karta hai.
topics.pro: A composite index keys on several columns and supports predicates that use a left-hand prefix of that key.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student_course ON enrollments (student_id, course_id);

topics.title: Index Column Order
topics.simple: Composite index ka column order usability decide karta hai.
topics.pro: The first column is the primary navigation key; putting a low-selectivity column first weakens common filters on later columns.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_course_student ON enrollments (course_id, student_id);

topics.title: Covering Index
topics.simple: INCLUDE columns se index-only scan possible hota hai.
topics.pro: INCLUDE adds payload columns to a B-tree so a query can be answered from the index without visiting the heap.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_name ON students (marks) INCLUDE (name);

topics.title: Partial Index
topics.simple: Partial index sirf matching rows ko index karta hai.
topics.pro: A partial index has a WHERE predicate, so it is smaller and cheaper when only a subset is queried.
points: The query predicate must imply it.
It is ideal for rare statuses.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_known_marks ON students (marks) WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: Expression Index
topics.simple: Expression index function ke result ko index karta hai.
topics.pro: An expression index stores a computed key such as LOWER(name), matching queries that use the same expression.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_lower_name ON students (LOWER(name));

topics.title: Hash Index
topics.simple: Hash index equality ke liye hota hai, range ke liye nahi.
topics.pro: A hash index supports equality comparisons only and is rarely preferable to B-tree in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_email_hash ON students USING hash (email);

topics.title: GIN Index
topics.simple: GIN composite values jaise arrays aur JSONB ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GIN indexes inverted lists and is used for arrays, JSONB and full-text search.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_email_gin ON students USING gin (to_tsvector('simple', email));

topics.title: GiST Index
topics.simple: GiST geometric aur range data ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GiST supports extensible tree searches for geometric, range and nearest-neighbor queries.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date_gist ON enrollments USING gist (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Index Selectivity
topics.simple: High selectivity wale predicates index ke liye best hain.
topics.pro: Selectivity measures how many rows a predicate removes; an index helps most when the query returns a small fraction of the table.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT course_id)::numeric / COUNT(*) AS selectivity FROM enrollments;

topics.title: EXPLAIN
topics.simple: EXPLAIN plan dikhata hai bina query chalaye.
topics.pro: EXPLAIN shows the planner’s chosen access paths, join order and estimated costs without executing the statement.
points: It does not run the query.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
example.output: An Index Scan or Seq Scan plan.

topics.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
topics.simple: EXPLAIN ANALYZE query chala kar actual timing deta hai.
topics.pro: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual rows, loops and timing alongside estimates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;

topics.title: Seq Scan vs Index Scan
topics.simple: Seq scan poora table padhta hai; index scan selected rows.
topics.pro: A sequential scan reads the heap linearly, while an index scan follows the index and fetches matching heap rows.
points: Seq scan is fine for large fractions.
Index scan wins for selective filters.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;
example.output: An Index Scan for the primary key.

topics.title: Bitmap Scan
topics.simple: Bitmap scan index matches ko batch me heap se laata hai.
topics.pro: A bitmap heap scan builds a bitmap from one or more indexes and visits heap pages in physical order.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 70;

topics.title: Index Maintenance
topics.simple: Indexes bloat hote hain aur rebuild karne pad sakte hain.
topics.pro: Updates create index bloat; REINDEX rebuilds an index, and VACUUM helps the planner and heap health.

example.sql: REINDEX INDEX idx_students_marks;

topics.title: Common Index Mistakes
topics.simple: Unused, duplicate aur wrong-order indexes common mistakes hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are indexing low-selectivity columns, duplicating an existing prefix, and expecting an index to help every query.

example.sql: SELECT indexrelid::regclass, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;

topics.title: Practical Tuning
topics.simple: Query, plan, index, measure — phir repeat.
topics.pro: Tuning starts from a slow query and its plan, adds the smallest useful index, and re-measures rather than guessing.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10;
example.output: A plan with buffer and timing detail.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain What Is an Index? in a production query.
interview.answer: An index is an auxiliary structure that speeds selected reads at the cost of storage and write maintenance. Key rules: Indexes speed reads. They slow writes. They consume space.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain B-tree Index in a production query.
interview.answer: A B-tree supports equality, ordering and range predicates and is the default PostgreSQL index type. Key rules: Default type. Supports ranges. Supports ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain CREATE INDEX in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE INDEX name ON table (columns) builds an index for the chosen key. Key rules: Name indexes clearly. Choose columns from real predicates. Build concurrently on live tables.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Unique Index in a production query.
interview.answer: A unique index enforces uniqueness and also speeds equality lookups. Key rules: It enforces a rule. NULLs are allowed by default. It can back a primary key.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Composite Index in a production query.
interview.answer: A composite index keys on several columns and supports predicates that use a left-hand prefix of that key. Key rules: Order columns deliberately. The leftmost column matters most. It can cover multiple filters.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Index Column Order in a production query.
interview.answer: The first column is the primary navigation key; putting a low-selectivity column first weakens common filters on later columns. Key rules: Put equality columns first. Put range columns later. Match the query predicate.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Covering Index in a production query.
interview.answer: INCLUDE adds payload columns to a B-tree so a query can be answered from the index without visiting the heap. Key rules: INCLUDE is not a key. It increases index size. It can enable index-only scans.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Partial Index in a production query.
interview.answer: A partial index has a WHERE predicate, so it is smaller and cheaper when only a subset is queried. Key rules: Add a WHERE clause. The query predicate must imply it. It is ideal for rare statuses.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Expression Index in a production query.
interview.answer: An expression index stores a computed key such as LOWER(name), matching queries that use the same expression. Key rules: Match the expression exactly. Use it for case-insensitive lookup. It costs write time.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Hash Index in a production query.
interview.answer: A hash index supports equality comparisons only and is rarely preferable to B-tree in PostgreSQL. Key rules: Equality only. No ordering. Usually choose B-tree.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain GIN Index in a production query.
interview.answer: GIN indexes inverted lists and is used for arrays, JSONB and full-text search. Key rules: Good for containment. Large and slower to update. Use the matching operator class.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain GiST Index in a production query.
interview.answer: GiST supports extensible tree searches for geometric, range and nearest-neighbor queries. Key rules: Good for ranges and geometry. Supports exclusion constraints. Choose an operator class.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Index Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: Selectivity measures how many rows a predicate removes; an index helps most when the query returns a small fraction of the table. Key rules: Unique keys are highly selective. Low-selectivity filters may prefer scans. Statistics drive the choice.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain EXPLAIN in a production query.
interview.answer: EXPLAIN shows the planner’s chosen access paths, join order and estimated costs without executing the statement. Key rules: It does not run the query. Estimates come from statistics. Look for scans and sorts.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a production query.
interview.answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual rows, loops and timing alongside estimates. Key rules: It runs the query. Use it on safe statements. Compare estimated and actual rows.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Seq Scan vs Index Scan in a production query.
interview.answer: A sequential scan reads the heap linearly, while an index scan follows the index and fetches matching heap rows. Key rules: Seq scan is fine for large fractions. Index scan wins for selective filters. Random I/O matters.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Bitmap Scan in a production query.
interview.answer: A bitmap heap scan builds a bitmap from one or more indexes and visits heap pages in physical order. Key rules: Good for medium selectivity. Combines multiple indexes. It loses exact ordering.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Index Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Updates create index bloat; REINDEX rebuilds an index, and VACUUM helps the planner and heap health. Key rules: Monitor bloat. REINDEX can lock. VACUUM regularly.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Common Index Mistakes in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are indexing low-selectivity columns, duplicating an existing prefix, and expecting an index to help every query. Key rules: Check actual queries. Avoid duplicate indexes. Verify with EXPLAIN.

interview.q: Module 18 · Explain Practical Tuning in a production query.
interview.answer: Tuning starts from a slow query and its plan, adds the smallest useful index, and re-measures rather than guessing. Key rules: Capture the query. Read the plan. Add one index. Measure again.

debug.title: Function mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON students (LOWER(name));
SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = 'aarav';
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE LOWER(name) = LOWER('aarav');
debug.error: The plain name predicate cannot use the expression index

debug.title: Wrong composite prefix
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_course_student ON enrollments (course_id, student_id);
SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE student_id = 1;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student_course ON enrollments (student_id, course_id);
debug.error: The query does not use the leftmost column

debug.title: Duplicate index
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks);
CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_again ON students (marks);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks);
debug.error: Two indexes with the same key waste writes and space

debug.title: Unique index duplicates
debug.broken: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.fix:
DELETE FROM students a USING students b WHERE a.id > b.id AND a.email = b.email;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.error: could not create unique index

debug.title: Concurrent in transaction
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_marks ON students (marks);
debug.error: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block

debug.title: Partial predicate mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_known ON students (marks) WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90 OR marks IS NULL;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: The OR predicate does not imply the partial index condition

debug.title: EXPLAIN without analyze
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: Estimates only, no actual timing

debug.title: Stale statistics
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix:
ANALYZE students;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: The planner may choose a plan from stale estimates

debug.title: Too many indexes
debug.fix: Keep only indexes justified by real queries and verify with pg_stat_user_indexes.
debug.error: Every write maintains all three indexes

debug.title: Nullable unique confusion
debug.broken: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.fix: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
debug.error: Multiple NULL emails are still allowed

modules.title: Transactions and Concurrency
modules.goal: Make multi-step changes atomic and reason about isolation and locks.

topics.title: Transaction Basics
topics.simple: Transaction multiple statements ko ek unit banata hai.
topics.pro: A transaction groups statements so they commit together or roll back together.
points: It ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

topics.title: BEGIN
topics.simple: BEGIN transaction start karta hai.
topics.pro: BEGIN starts an explicit transaction block and disables autocommit until the block ends.
points: It can be implicit in some clients.

example.sql: BEGIN;

topics.title: COMMIT
topics.simple: COMMIT changes ko permanent karta hai.
topics.pro: COMMIT makes the transaction’s changes visible and durable, then ends the block.

topics.title: ROLLBACK
topics.simple: ROLLBACK changes ko undo karta hai.
topics.pro: ROLLBACK discards all changes in the transaction and releases its locks.
points: It cannot undo a committed transaction.

topics.title: ACID
topics.simple: ACID atomicity, consistency, isolation aur durability deta hai.
topics.pro: ACID describes atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the guarantees that make transactions trustworthy.

topics.title: Isolation Levels
topics.simple: Isolation level concurrent transactions ke visibility rules set karta hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL supports Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable, each trading concurrency for stronger guarantees.

example.sql: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

topics.title: Read Committed
topics.simple: Read Committed har statement ko naya snapshot deta hai.
topics.pro: Read Committed sees data committed before each statement starts, so the same query can see different rows within one transaction.

topics.title: Repeatable Read
topics.simple: Repeatable Read transaction ke snapshot ko stable rakhta hai.
topics.pro: Repeatable Read uses one snapshot for the whole transaction, preventing non-repeatable reads but allowing serialization failures on write conflicts.
points: Writes can fail with serialization errors.

topics.title: Serializable
topics.simple: Serializable strongest isolation deta hai.
topics.pro: Serializable makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, aborting when a serialization conflict is detected.

topics.title: Dirty Read
topics.simple: Dirty read uncommitted data dikhata hai.
topics.pro: A dirty read sees another transaction’s uncommitted changes; PostgreSQL does not allow it at any isolation level.

example.output: The other session sees the old value.

topics.title: Non-repeatable Read
topics.simple: Non-repeatable read same row ko do baar different dikhata hai.
topics.pro: A non-repeatable read occurs when a row changes between two reads in the same transaction; Read Committed allows it, Repeatable Read prevents it.

example.output: Both reads see the same snapshot.

topics.title: Phantom Read
topics.simple: Phantom read naye rows ko dobara query me dikhata hai.
topics.pro: A phantom read occurs when a re-run query sees new rows that match the predicate; stronger isolation prevents it.

topics.title: Row Locks
topics.simple: Row locks competing updates ko serialize karte hain.
topics.pro: UPDATE and DELETE take row-level locks that block conflicting writes until the transaction ends.

example.output: The row is locked until commit.

topics.title: SELECT FOR UPDATE

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Transaction Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A transaction groups statements so they commit together or roll back together. Key rules: All-or-nothing. It protects multi-step changes. It ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain BEGIN in a production query.
interview.answer: BEGIN starts an explicit transaction block and disables autocommit until the block ends. Key rules: It starts the unit. It can be implicit in some clients. Nested BEGIN warns.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain COMMIT in a production query.
interview.answer: COMMIT makes the transaction’s changes visible and durable, then ends the block. Key rules: It makes changes permanent. It releases locks. It cannot be undone afterward.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain ROLLBACK in a production query.
interview.answer: ROLLBACK discards all changes in the transaction and releases its locks. Key rules: It undoes the block. It works after errors. It cannot undo a committed transaction.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain ACID in a production query.
interview.answer: ACID describes atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the guarantees that make transactions trustworthy. Key rules: Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: rules hold. Isolated: concurrent work is controlled. Durable: committed data survives.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Isolation Levels in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL supports Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable, each trading concurrency for stronger guarantees. Key rules: Read Committed is the default. Repeatable Read is snapshot-based. Serializable can abort transactions.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Read Committed in a production query.
interview.answer: Read Committed sees data committed before each statement starts, so the same query can see different rows within one transaction. Key rules: Default level. Statement-level snapshot. Non-repeatable reads are possible.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Repeatable Read in a production query.
interview.answer: Repeatable Read uses one snapshot for the whole transaction, preventing non-repeatable reads but allowing serialization failures on write conflicts. Key rules: Stable snapshot. No non-repeatable reads. Writes can fail with serialization errors.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Serializable in a production query.
interview.answer: Serializable makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, aborting when a serialization conflict is detected. Key rules: Strongest guarantee. Retries are required. It can reduce concurrency.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Dirty Read in a production query.
interview.answer: A dirty read sees another transaction’s uncommitted changes; PostgreSQL does not allow it at any isolation level. Key rules: Uncommitted data. Not possible in PostgreSQL. It would break atomicity.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Non-repeatable Read in a production query.
interview.answer: A non-repeatable read occurs when a row changes between two reads in the same transaction; Read Committed allows it, Repeatable Read prevents it. Key rules: Same row, different value. Read Committed allows it. Repeatable Read blocks it.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Phantom Read in a production query.
interview.answer: A phantom read occurs when a re-run query sees new rows that match the predicate; stronger isolation prevents it. Key rules: New matching rows. Repeatable Read prevents most cases. Serializable prevents anomalies.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Row Locks in a production query.
interview.answer: UPDATE and DELETE take row-level locks that block conflicting writes until the transaction ends. Key rules: Locks are held to commit. Readers usually do not block. Long transactions hold locks longer.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain SELECT FOR UPDATE in a production query.
interview.answer: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks selected rows so another transaction cannot change them before you do. Key rules: Use inside a transaction. It blocks competing writers. It can deadlock.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Deadlocks in a production query.
interview.answer: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on each other’s locks; PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one transaction. Key rules: Avoid inconsistent lock order. Keep transactions short. Retry the aborted transaction.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Savepoints in a production query.
interview.answer: SAVEPOINT marks a point inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO undoes work after it without ending the whole block. Key rules: Create with SAVEPOINT. Roll back to the name. Release when done.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Autocommit in a production query.
interview.answer: With autocommit on, each statement commits immediately; an explicit BEGIN groups statements until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Key rules: Default in many clients. BEGIN disables it temporarily. Multi-step work needs a block.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Long Transactions in a production query.
interview.answer: Long-running transactions hold locks, retain snapshots and delay vacuum cleanup, so keep them short. Key rules: Short blocks are safer. Avoid user think-time. Monitor pg_stat_activity.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Common Transaction Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are forgetting to commit, assuming ROLLBACK works after commit, and not retrying serialization or deadlock failures. Key rules: End every block. Retry transient failures. Do not hold locks during UI waits.

interview.q: Module 19 · Explain Practical Transaction Pattern in a production query.
interview.answer: A safe write transaction previews the target, performs the change, verifies affected rows and commits only when the result is correct. Key rules: Preview first. Check the row count. Commit or roll back explicitly. Handle retries.
