modules.title: Constraints and Data Integrity
modules.goal: Enforce correctness in the database instead of relying only on application code.

topics.title: Constraints Overview
topics.simple: Constraints database me rules enforce karte hain.
topics.pro: Constraints reject invalid data at write time, protecting every application that shares the database.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: NOT NULL
topics.simple: NOT NULL missing values rokta hai.
topics.pro: NOT NULL requires a value on every row and is the only direct way to require presence.
points: It does not reject empty strings.
Add it after cleaning existing NULLs.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ALTER COLUMN name SET NOT NULL;

topics.title: UNIQUE
topics.simple: UNIQUE duplicate values rokta hai.
topics.pro: A unique constraint enforces distinct key values and creates a supporting unique index.
points: It allows multiple NULLs by default.
It is a constraint and an index.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE (email);

topics.title: PRIMARY KEY
topics.simple: Primary key row ko uniquely identify karta hai.
topics.pro: A primary key is a unique, not-null constraint that identifies each row and is usually referenced by foreign keys.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id);

topics.title: FOREIGN KEY
topics.simple: Foreign key child rows ko parent se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A foreign key requires child values to exist in the parent key, preserving referential integrity.
points: The parent key must be unique.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD CONSTRAINT enrollments_student_fk FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id);

topics.title: CHECK
topics.simple: CHECK row-level boolean rule enforce karta hai.
topics.pro: A CHECK constraint rejects rows where the expression is FALSE; UNKNOWN from NULL passes, so pair it with NOT NULL when needed.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: DEFAULT
topics.simple: DEFAULT missing value ke liye fallback deta hai.
topics.pro: A default supplies a value when an INSERT omits the column; it does not replace an explicit NULL.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments ALTER COLUMN enrolled_on SET DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE;

topics.title: ON DELETE CASCADE
topics.simple: Parent delete par child rows bhi delete hoti hain.
topics.pro: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically removes child rows when the referenced parent is deleted.
points: It can delete more than expected.

example.sql:
ALTER TABLE enrollments DROP CONSTRAINT enrollments_student_fk;
ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD CONSTRAINT enrollments_student_fk FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE;

topics.title: ON UPDATE CASCADE
topics.simple: Parent key update child me propagate hota hai.
topics.pro: ON UPDATE CASCADE updates child foreign keys when the parent key changes, which is useful for natural keys.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD CONSTRAINT enrollments_student_fk FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id) ON UPDATE CASCADE;

topics.title: Deferrable Constraints
topics.simple: Deferrable constraint transaction ke end tak wait kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: A DEFERRABLE constraint can be checked at statement end or transaction end, which helps circular references.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD CONSTRAINT enrollments_student_fk FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;

topics.title: VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
topics.simple: NOT VALID constraint ko baad me validate karo.
topics.pro: Adding a foreign key or check with NOT VALID avoids a long initial scan; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT then checks existing rows.
points: NOT VALID applies to new rows.

example.sql:
ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE students VALIDATE CONSTRAINT marks_range;

topics.title: Adding Constraints Safely
topics.simple: Existing data clean karke constraint add karo.
topics.pro: Adding a constraint fails if existing rows violate it, so clean or quarantine bad rows first.
points: Use NOT VALID for large tables.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks < 0 OR marks > 100;

topics.title: Dropping Constraints
topics.simple: Constraint drop karne se rule hat jaata hai.
topics.pro: ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT removes the rule; dropping a unique or primary key also removes its backing index.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students DROP CONSTRAINT marks_range;

topics.title: Unique NULLs
topics.simple: UNIQUE default multiple NULLs allow karta hai.
topics.pro: A regular unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct; PostgreSQL 15+ can use NULLS NOT DISTINCT to allow only one NULL.
points: Multiple NULLs are allowed by default.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (email);

topics.title: Exclusion Constraints
topics.simple: Exclusion constraint overlapping ranges rokta hai.
topics.pro: An exclusion constraint uses a GiST index to reject rows whose values conflict under a chosen operator, such as overlapping date ranges.
points: It needs btree_gist for equality columns.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);

topics.title: Domain Constraints
topics.simple: Domain reusable constraint set deta hai.
topics.pro: A domain packages a base type with CHECK and NOT NULL rules that can be reused across columns.
points: It can add NOT NULL and CHECK.

example.sql: CREATE DOMAIN mark AS INTEGER CHECK (VALUE BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: Constraint Naming
topics.simple: Constraints ko clear names do.
topics.pro: Explicit names make errors, migrations and drops predictable instead of relying on generated names.
points: Name primary keys and foreign keys.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_marks_check CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: Common Constraint Errors
topics.simple: NULL, duplicates aur orphan rows common failures hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are NOT NULL violations, duplicate unique keys, foreign-key orphans and CHECK expressions that silently pass NULL.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 101);

topics.title: Application vs Database Validation
topics.simple: Critical rules database me rakho.
topics.pro: Application validation improves UX, but database constraints are the final guard shared by every writer.
points: Enforce critical rules in the DB.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: Practical Integrity Design
topics.simple: Keys, foreign keys aur checks ko schema design me plan karo.
topics.pro: A reliable schema combines primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, CHECK and deliberate cascade actions.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Constraints Overview in a production query.
interview.answer: Constraints reject invalid data at write time, protecting every application that shares the database. Key rules: They enforce rules centrally. They run on writes. They make assumptions explicit.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain NOT NULL in a production query.
interview.answer: NOT NULL requires a value on every row and is the only direct way to require presence. Key rules: It rejects NULL. It does not reject empty strings. Add it after cleaning existing NULLs.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain UNIQUE in a production query.
interview.answer: A unique constraint enforces distinct key values and creates a supporting unique index. Key rules: It allows multiple NULLs by default. It supports composite keys. It is a constraint and an index.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain PRIMARY KEY in a production query.
interview.answer: A primary key is a unique, not-null constraint that identifies each row and is usually referenced by foreign keys. Key rules: Unique and not null. One per table. It creates an index.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain FOREIGN KEY in a production query.
interview.answer: A foreign key requires child values to exist in the parent key, preserving referential integrity. Key rules: The parent key must be unique. It can cascade actions. It blocks orphan rows.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain CHECK in a production query.
interview.answer: A CHECK constraint rejects rows where the expression is FALSE; UNKNOWN from NULL passes, so pair it with NOT NULL when needed. Key rules: It rejects FALSE. NULL passes as UNKNOWN. It can use multiple columns.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain DEFAULT in a production query.
interview.answer: A default supplies a value when an INSERT omits the column; it does not replace an explicit NULL. Key rules: It applies on omission. It can call functions. It does not enforce presence.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain ON DELETE CASCADE in a production query.
interview.answer: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically removes child rows when the referenced parent is deleted. Key rules: Use with care. It can delete more than expected. RESTRICT is the safer default.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain ON UPDATE CASCADE in a production query.
interview.answer: ON UPDATE CASCADE updates child foreign keys when the parent key changes, which is useful for natural keys. Key rules: It follows key changes. It avoids orphans. Surrogate keys reduce the need.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Deferrable Constraints in a production query.
interview.answer: A DEFERRABLE constraint can be checked at statement end or transaction end, which helps circular references. Key rules: INITIALLY IMMEDIATE is the default. SET CONSTRAINTS changes timing. Only some constraints are deferrable.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a production query.
interview.answer: Adding a foreign key or check with NOT VALID avoids a long initial scan; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT then checks existing rows. Key rules: NOT VALID applies to new rows. VALIDATE checks old rows. It takes a lighter lock.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Adding Constraints Safely in a production query.
interview.answer: Adding a constraint fails if existing rows violate it, so clean or quarantine bad rows first. Key rules: Find violations first. Use NOT VALID for large tables. Validate after the backfill.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Dropping Constraints in a production query.
interview.answer: ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT removes the rule; dropping a unique or primary key also removes its backing index. Key rules: Know the constraint name. CASCADE can remove dependents. Re-adding may require a scan.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Unique NULLs in a production query.
interview.answer: A regular unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct; PostgreSQL 15+ can use NULLS NOT DISTINCT to allow only one NULL. Key rules: Multiple NULLs are allowed by default. NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that. It is a data-model decision.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Exclusion Constraints in a production query.
interview.answer: An exclusion constraint uses a GiST index to reject rows whose values conflict under a chosen operator, such as overlapping date ranges. Key rules: It needs btree_gist for equality columns. It prevents overlaps. It is advanced but powerful.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Domain Constraints in a production query.
interview.answer: A domain packages a base type with CHECK and NOT NULL rules that can be reused across columns. Key rules: Create once, reuse often. It can add NOT NULL and CHECK. It keeps rules consistent.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Constraint Naming in a production query.
interview.answer: Explicit names make errors, migrations and drops predictable instead of relying on generated names. Key rules: Name primary keys and foreign keys. Use table_column_suffix. Document the rule.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Common Constraint Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are NOT NULL violations, duplicate unique keys, foreign-key orphans and CHECK expressions that silently pass NULL. Key rules: Read the constraint name. Fix data before re-adding. Remember NULL passes CHECK.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Application vs Database Validation in a production query.
interview.answer: Application validation improves UX, but database constraints are the final guard shared by every writer. Key rules: Validate early in the app. Enforce critical rules in the DB. Do not duplicate contradictory rules.

interview.q: Module 20 · Explain Practical Integrity Design in a production query.
interview.answer: A reliable schema combines primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, CHECK and deliberate cascade actions. Key rules: Start with keys. Add foreign keys. Add checks for domain rules. Choose cascade behaviour explicitly.

debug.title: NOT NULL violation
debug.broken: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (NULL);
debug.fix: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Zara');
debug.error: null value in column "name" violates not-null constraint

debug.title: Unique violation
debug.broken: INSERT INTO students (email) VALUES ('a@example.com'), ('a@example.com');
debug.fix: INSERT INTO students (email) VALUES ('a@example.com'), ('b@example.com');
debug.error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint

debug.title: Foreign key orphan
debug.broken: INSERT INTO enrollments (student_id, course_id) VALUES (999, 10);
debug.fix: INSERT INTO enrollments (student_id, course_id) VALUES (1, 10);
debug.error: violates foreign key constraint

debug.title: CHECK violation
debug.broken: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 101);
debug.fix: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 99);
debug.error: violates check constraint

debug.title: Cascade surprise
debug.broken: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1;
debug.fix: Review the ON DELETE action before deleting, or use RESTRICT for protected parents.
debug.error: Child enrollments are deleted automatically

debug.title: NOT VALID not validated
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100) NOT VALID;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students VALIDATE CONSTRAINT marks_range;
debug.error: Existing violating rows are not checked yet

debug.title: Duplicate constraint name
debug.broken:
ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks >= 0);
ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks <= 100);
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);
debug.error: constraint "marks_range" for relation "students" already exists

debug.title: Drop wrong table
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE courses DROP CONSTRAINT marks_range;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students DROP CONSTRAINT marks_range;
debug.error: constraint "marks_range" of relation "courses" does not exist

debug.title: Unique NULL assumption
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE (email);
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (email);
debug.error: Multiple NULL emails are still allowed

debug.title: Deferrable misuse
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE (email) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT students_email_key UNIQUE (email);
debug.error: This unique constraint does not need deferral

modules.title: Database Design and Normalization
modules.goal: Model entities and relationships so the schema stays correct as it grows.

topics.title: Data Modeling Basics
topics.simple: Schema design entities, attributes aur relationships se shuru hota hai.
topics.pro: Data modeling identifies the nouns, their attributes and the relationships before tables are written.

example.sql: -- students, courses and enrollments are the core entities

topics.title: Entities
topics.simple: Entity ek real-world object ya concept hai.
topics.pro: An entity becomes a table, with each row representing one instance of that concept.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Attributes
topics.simple: Attributes entity ke properties hote hain.
topics.pro: Attributes become columns with a type, nullability and constraints that reflect the domain.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT UNIQUE, marks INTEGER CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100));

topics.title: Keys
topics.simple: Keys rows ko identify aur relate karte hain.
topics.pro: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key references another table’s key and enforces the relationship.
points: Primary key is unique and not null.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Relationships
topics.simple: Relationships cardinality batate hain.
topics.pro: Relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; the cardinality determines where keys live.
points: 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: One-to-One
topics.simple: 1:1 relationship me har row ka ek partner hota hai.
topics.pro: A one-to-one relationship uses a unique foreign key or a shared primary key, often to split optional or sensitive data.
points: Sharing the primary key is common.
Do not use it for unrelated data.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE student_profiles (student_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES students(id), bio TEXT);

topics.title: One-to-Many
topics.simple: 1:N relationship me parent ke multiple children hote hain.
topics.pro: The foreign key lives on the many side, pointing back to the one parent.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Many-to-Many
topics.simple: M:N relationship ke liye junction table chahiye.
topics.pro: A junction table stores one row per pair and can carry relationship attributes such as enrollment date.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Normalization
topics.simple: Normalization duplication aur update anomalies kam karta hai.
topics.pro: Normalization organizes data into related tables so each fact is stored once and updated in one place.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: First Normal Form
topics.simple: 1NF atomic values aur repeating groups hataata hai.
topics.pro: First normal form requires atomic column values and no repeating groups or arrays masquerading as columns.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Second Normal Form
topics.simple: 2NF partial dependencies hataata hai.
topics.pro: Second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, grade TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Third Normal Form
topics.simple: 3NF transitive dependencies hataata hai.
topics.pro: Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: BCNF
topics.simple: BCNF strong normal form hai.
topics.pro: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_rooms (course_id INTEGER, room TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (course_id, room));

topics.title: Denormalization
topics.simple: Denormalization performance ke liye duplication add karta hai.
topics.pro: Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE courses ADD COLUMN enrolled_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

topics.title: Surrogate vs Natural Keys
topics.simple: Surrogate key generated hota hai; natural key business value hai.
topics.pro: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact.
points: Keep a unique natural key when needed.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE);

topics.title: Junction Tables
topics.simple: Junction table M:N relationship ko rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: A junction table has foreign keys to both sides and usually a composite primary key over the pair.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Audit Columns
topics.simple: Audit columns created/updated timestamps rakhte hain.
topics.pro: created_at and updated_at columns make data changes observable and support debugging and reporting.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();

topics.title: Soft Deletes
topics.simple: Soft delete row ko flag karta hai, remove nahi.
topics.pro: A deleted_at timestamp hides rows without physically removing them, but every query must filter it.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ;

topics.title: Schema Naming
topics.simple: Clear names schema ko understandable banate hain.
topics.pro: Consistent table, column and constraint names reduce mistakes and make migrations predictable.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Practical School Schema
topics.simple: Students, courses aur enrollments ka clean schema banao.
topics.pro: A school schema uses students and courses as entities and enrollments as the many-to-many junction with its own attributes.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Data Modeling Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: Data modeling identifies the nouns, their attributes and the relationships before tables are written. Key rules: Find entities. List attributes. Define relationships.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Entities in a production query.
interview.answer: An entity becomes a table, with each row representing one instance of that concept. Key rules: Students are an entity. Courses are an entity. Enrollments connect them.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Attributes in a production query.
interview.answer: Attributes become columns with a type, nullability and constraints that reflect the domain. Key rules: Choose precise types. Mark required attributes. Avoid overloaded columns.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key references another table’s key and enforces the relationship. Key rules: Primary key is unique and not null. Foreign keys enforce relationships. Keys should be stable.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Relationships in a production query.
interview.answer: Relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; the cardinality determines where keys live. Key rules: 1:1 shares a key. 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side. M:N needs a junction table.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain One-to-One in a production query.
interview.answer: A one-to-one relationship uses a unique foreign key or a shared primary key, often to split optional or sensitive data. Key rules: Use a unique foreign key. Sharing the primary key is common. Do not use it for unrelated data.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain One-to-Many in a production query.
interview.answer: The foreign key lives on the many side, pointing back to the one parent. Key rules: Parent key is referenced. Child holds the foreign key. Index the foreign key.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Many-to-Many in a production query.
interview.answer: A junction table stores one row per pair and can carry relationship attributes such as enrollment date. Key rules: Two foreign keys. Composite primary key. Relationship attributes live here.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Normalization in a production query.
interview.answer: Normalization organizes data into related tables so each fact is stored once and updated in one place. Key rules: Reduce duplication. Avoid update anomalies. Normalize first, denormalize deliberately.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain First Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: First normal form requires atomic column values and no repeating groups or arrays masquerading as columns. Key rules: One value per cell. No repeating columns. Give each row a key.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Second Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: Second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key. Key rules: Start with 1NF. Check composite keys. Move partial dependencies out.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Third Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes. Key rules: Start with 2NF. Move derived facts out. Keep each fact once.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain BCNF in a production query.
interview.answer: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys. Key rules: Stronger than 3NF. Check all determinants. Split overlapping keys.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Denormalization in a production query.
interview.answer: Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity. Key rules: Measure first. Document the duplication. Keep it synchronized.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Surrogate vs Natural Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact. Key rules: Surrogates are stable. Natural keys can change. Keep a unique natural key when needed.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Junction Tables in a production query.
interview.answer: A junction table has foreign keys to both sides and usually a composite primary key over the pair. Key rules: One row per relationship. Add relationship attributes. Index both foreign keys.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Audit Columns in a production query.
interview.answer: created_at and updated_at columns make data changes observable and support debugging and reporting. Key rules: Default created_at to now. Update updated_at deliberately. Store timestamps with time zone.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Soft Deletes in a production query.
interview.answer: A deleted_at timestamp hides rows without physically removing them, but every query must filter it. Key rules: Add deleted_at. Filter in queries or views. Hard-delete when policy requires.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Schema Naming in a production query.
interview.answer: Consistent table, column and constraint names reduce mistakes and make migrations predictable. Key rules: Use snake_case. Plural table names are common. Name keys and constraints explicitly.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Practical School Schema in a production query.
interview.answer: A school schema uses students and courses as entities and enrollments as the many-to-many junction with its own attributes. Key rules: Keys first. Foreign keys next. Constraints last. Index relationship columns.

logic.answer: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys. Stronger than 3NF. Check all determinants. Split overlapping keys.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Denormalization matter?
logic.answer: Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity. Measure first. Document the duplication. Keep it synchronized.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Surrogate vs Natural Keys matter?
logic.answer: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact. Surrogates are stable. Natural keys can change. Keep a unique natural key when needed.

modules.title: JSON and JSONB
modules.goal: Store, query, index and update semi-structured data without losing relational discipline.

topics.title: JSON vs JSONB
topics.simple: JSON text hai; JSONB parsed binary hai.
topics.pro: JSON stores the original text, while JSONB parses it into a binary form that supports indexing and efficient operators.
points: JSONB is usually the better default.
JSONB loses key order and duplicates.

example.sql: SELECT '{"name":"Aarav"}'::jsonb AS data;

topics.title: JSON Literals
topics.simple: JSON literal quoted object ya array hota hai.
topics.pro: A JSON literal is cast with ::json or ::jsonb and can contain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
points: Use single quotes around the literal.
JSON null is not SQL NULL.

example.sql: SELECT '{"name":"Aarav","marks":90}'::jsonb AS student;

topics.title: Storing JSONB
topics.simple: JSONB column semi-structured data ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: A jsonb column stores flexible attributes while the table keeps relational keys and constraints.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, payload JSONB NOT NULL);

topics.title: Arrow Operator
topics.simple: -> JSON value ko JSON ke roop me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: The -> operator returns a JSONB value, preserving quotes and structure for chaining.
points: Works with object keys and array indexes.

example.sql: SELECT payload->'name' AS name_json FROM events;

topics.title: Text Arrow Operator
topics.simple: ->> JSON value ko text me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: The ->> operator returns text, which is what you usually want for comparisons and display.
points: Casts numbers and booleans to text.
Use it in WHERE and ORDER BY.

example.sql: SELECT payload->>'name' AS name FROM events;

topics.title: Path Operators
topics.simple: #> and #>> nested paths nikaalte hain.
topics.pro: #> returns a JSONB value at a path array and #>> returns text at that path.
points: The path is a text array.

example.sql: SELECT payload#>'{address,city}' AS city_json, payload#>>'{address,city}' AS city FROM events;
example.output: The nested city value and text.

topics.title: JSONB Operators
topics.simple: JSONB mein containment, existence aur deletion operators hote hain.
topics.pro: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents.

example.sql: SELECT payload || '{"active":true}'::jsonb AS merged FROM events;

topics.title: Containment
topics.simple: @> check karta hai ki JSONB doosre ko contain karta hai.
topics.pro: The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"active":true}'::jsonb;

topics.title: Key Existence
topics.simple: ? operator key ya array element ki existence check karta hai.
topics.pro: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload ? 'email';

topics.title: jsonb_each
topics.simple: jsonb_each object ko key/value rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys.
points: Use it in a lateral join.

example.sql: SELECT key, value FROM events, LATERAL jsonb_each(payload);

topics.title: jsonb_array_elements
topics.simple: jsonb_array_elements array ko rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items.

example.sql: SELECT value FROM events, LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(payload->'tags');

topics.title: Building JSON
topics.simple: jsonb_build_object aur jsonb_build_array JSON banate hain.
topics.pro: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array.

example.sql: SELECT jsonb_build_object('name', name, 'marks', marks) AS student FROM students;

topics.title: Updating JSONB
topics.simple: jsonb_set nested value update karta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag.
points: The path is a text array.
Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

example.sql: UPDATE events SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{active}', 'true'::jsonb) WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Deleting Keys
topics.simple: Minus operator key ya array element hataata hai.
topics.pro: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path.

example.sql: UPDATE events SET payload = payload - 'email' WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: JSON Path
topics.simple: jsonb_path_query JSONPath expressions chalata hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent.

example.sql: SELECT jsonb_path_query(payload, '$.tags[*]') FROM events;

topics.title: Indexing JSONB
topics.simple: GIN index JSONB containment aur existence ko fast karta hai.
topics.pro: A GIN index on a jsonb column accelerates @>, ?, ?| and ?& queries.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload ON events USING gin (payload);

topics.title: JSON vs Relational
topics.simple: Stable fields columns me rakho; flexible fields JSONB me.
topics.pro: Relational columns give typed constraints and joins, while JSONB gives flexibility for sparse or evolving attributes.
points: Do not hide core keys in JSON.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL);

topics.title: Validation
topics.simple: JSONB type aur shape ko CHECK se validate karo.
topics.pro: A CHECK constraint can require an object or a specific key, but deep schema validation often belongs in the application or a JSON schema validator.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE events ADD CONSTRAINT payload_object CHECK (jsonb_typeof(payload) = 'object');

topics.title: Common JSON Errors
topics.simple: Missing casts, wrong arrows aur array assumptions common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are comparing jsonb to text, using -> when ->> is needed, and calling array functions on a non-array.

example.sql: SELECT payload->>'name' FROM events WHERE payload->>'active' = 'true';

topics.title: Practical API Data
topics.simple: JSONB ko API payload, audit metadata aur flexible settings ke liye use karo.
topics.pro: A practical JSONB design keeps identity and relationships relational and stores the flexible payload with a GIN index for the queries that matter.

example.sql:
CREATE TABLE api_events (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW());
CREATE INDEX api_events_payload_gin ON api_events USING gin (payload);

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON vs JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: JSON stores the original text, while JSONB parses it into a binary form that supports indexing and efficient operators. Key rules: JSON preserves formatting. JSONB is usually the better default. JSONB loses key order and duplicates.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON Literals in a production query.
interview.answer: A JSON literal is cast with ::json or ::jsonb and can contain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Key rules: Use single quotes around the literal. Cast to jsonb. JSON null is not SQL NULL.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Storing JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: A jsonb column stores flexible attributes while the table keeps relational keys and constraints. Key rules: Use jsonb for queryable documents. Keep stable fields as columns. Add a CHECK for jsonb_typeof.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Arrow Operator in a production query.
interview.answer: The -> operator returns a JSONB value, preserving quotes and structure for chaining. Key rules: Returns jsonb. Works with object keys and array indexes. Chain it for nested values.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Text Arrow Operator in a production query.
interview.answer: The ->> operator returns text, which is what you usually want for comparisons and display. Key rules: Returns text. Casts numbers and booleans to text. Use it in WHERE and ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Path Operators in a production query.
interview.answer: #> returns a JSONB value at a path array and #>> returns text at that path. Key rules: The path is a text array. Use braces in a literal. Chain arrows for simple paths.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSONB Operators in a production query.
interview.answer: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents. Key rules: @> tests containment. ? tests key existence. || merges objects.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Containment in a production query.
interview.answer: The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements. Key rules: It is indexable with GIN. Objects match by key/value. Arrays match elements.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Key Existence in a production query.
interview.answer: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys. Key rules: ? tests one key. ?| tests any key. ?& tests all keys.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain jsonb_each in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys. Key rules: It returns key and value. jsonb_each_text returns text. Use it in a lateral join.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain jsonb_array_elements in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items. Key rules: It requires an array. Use WITH ORDINALITY for positions. It can multiply rows.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Building JSON in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array. Key rules: Build objects from key/value pairs. Build arrays from values. Aggregate rows with jsonb_agg.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Updating JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag. Key rules: The path is a text array. The new value is JSONB. Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Deleting Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path. Key rules: - removes a key. - integer removes an array element. #- removes a path.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON Path in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent. Key rules: Paths start with $. It can return multiple rows. It supports filter expressions.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Indexing JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: A GIN index on a jsonb column accelerates @>, ?, ?| and ?& queries. Key rules: Use gin (column). jsonb_ops is the default. jsonb_path_ops is smaller for containment.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON vs Relational in a production query.
interview.answer: Relational columns give typed constraints and joins, while JSONB gives flexibility for sparse or evolving attributes. Key rules: Do not hide core keys in JSON. Use JSONB for optional metadata. Index the paths you query.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Validation in a production query.
interview.answer: A CHECK constraint can require an object or a specific key, but deep schema validation often belongs in the application or a JSON schema validator. Key rules: Use jsonb_typeof. Check required keys. Do not overconstrain flexible payloads.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Common JSON Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are comparing jsonb to text, using -> when ->> is needed, and calling array functions on a non-array. Key rules: Cast literals to jsonb. Use ->> for text. Check jsonb_typeof before array expansion.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Practical API Data in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical JSONB design keeps identity and relationships relational and stores the flexible payload with a GIN index for the queries that matter. Key rules: Keep keys relational. Store the payload. Index searched paths. Validate the top level.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does JSON vs JSONB matter?
logic.answer: JSON stores the original text, while JSONB parses it into a binary form that supports indexing and efficient operators. JSON preserves formatting. JSONB is usually the better default. JSONB loses key order and duplicates.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does JSON Literals matter?
logic.answer: A JSON literal is cast with ::json or ::jsonb and can contain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Use single quotes around the literal. Cast to jsonb. JSON null is not SQL NULL.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Storing JSONB matter?
logic.answer: A jsonb column stores flexible attributes while the table keeps relational keys and constraints. Use jsonb for queryable documents. Keep stable fields as columns. Add a CHECK for jsonb_typeof.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Arrow Operator matter?
logic.answer: The -> operator returns a JSONB value, preserving quotes and structure for chaining. Returns jsonb. Works with object keys and array indexes. Chain it for nested values.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Text Arrow Operator matter?
logic.answer: The ->> operator returns text, which is what you usually want for comparisons and display. Returns text. Casts numbers and booleans to text. Use it in WHERE and ORDER BY.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Path Operators matter?
logic.answer: #> returns a JSONB value at a path array and #>> returns text at that path. The path is a text array. Use braces in a literal. Chain arrows for simple paths.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does JSONB Operators matter?
logic.answer: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents. @> tests containment. ? tests key existence. || merges objects.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Containment matter?
logic.answer: The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements. It is indexable with GIN. Objects match by key/value. Arrays match elements.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Key Existence matter?
logic.answer: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys. ? tests one key. ?| tests any key. ?& tests all keys.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does jsonb_each matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys. It returns key and value. jsonb_each_text returns text. Use it in a lateral join.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does jsonb_array_elements matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items. It requires an array. Use WITH ORDINALITY for positions. It can multiply rows.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Building JSON matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array. Build objects from key/value pairs. Build arrays from values. Aggregate rows with jsonb_agg.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Updating JSONB matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag. The path is a text array. The new value is JSONB. Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Deleting Keys matter?
logic.answer: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path. - removes a key. - integer removes an array element. #- removes a path.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does JSON Path matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent. Paths start with $. It can return multiple rows. It supports filter expressions.

modules.title: Full-Text Search
modules.goal: Build ranked, language-aware search instead of fragile LIKE patterns.

topics.title: Full-Text Search Basics
topics.simple: FTS text ko tokens aur queries me match karta hai.
topics.pro: Full-text search parses documents into normalized lexemes and matches them against a query, with ranking and highlighting.
points: It handles words, not just substrings.
It supports stemming and stop words.
It can be indexed with GIN.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('simple', 'SQL joins and indexes') @@ to_tsquery('simple', 'join & index');

topics.title: tsvector
topics.simple: tsvector normalized lexemes ka sorted document hai.
topics.pro: A tsvector stores lexemes with positions, which is the document representation used by full-text search.
points: It can be generated or stored.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The cats are running');

topics.title: tsquery
topics.simple: tsquery search terms aur boolean operators rakhta hai.
topics.pro: A tsquery combines lexemes with &, |, ! and phrase operators.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'sql & index');

topics.title: to_tsvector
topics.simple: to_tsvector document ko searchable form me badalta hai.
topics.pro: to_tsvector(config, text) normalizes a document using a text search configuration.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The SQL course covers indexes');

topics.title: to_tsquery
topics.simple: to_tsquery query string ko tsquery banata hai.
topics.pro: to_tsquery parses explicit operators and requires the caller to format the query safely.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'sql & join');

topics.title: plainto_tsquery
topics.simple: plainto_tsquery user text ko safe AND query banata hai.
topics.pro: plainto_tsquery turns plain text into a tsquery by ANDing the lexemes, ignoring operators in the input.
points: It is safer for raw input.

example.sql: SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'sql join');

topics.title: websearch_to_tsquery
topics.simple: websearch_to_tsquery search-engine style input samajhta hai.
topics.pro: websearch_to_tsquery supports quoted phrases, OR and minus terms without raising syntax errors on ordinary input.
points: It is designed for user input.

example.sql: SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'sql -mysql');

topics.title: Match Operator
topics.simple: @@ operator document aur query ko match karta hai.
topics.pro: The @@ operator returns true when a tsvector matches a tsquery.
points: It is the core FTS predicate.
It can use a GIN index.

example.sql: SELECT title FROM courses WHERE to_tsvector('english', title) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'sql');

topics.title: Ranking
topics.simple: ts_rank relevance score deta hai.
topics.pro: ts_rank scores matches by term frequency and proximity, allowing the most relevant results first.
points: Weights can favor title over body.

example.sql: SELECT title, ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', title), plainto_tsquery('english', 'sql')) AS rank FROM courses ORDER BY rank DESC;

topics.title: Highlighting
topics.simple: ts_headline matching text ko highlight karta hai.
topics.pro: ts_headline returns a snippet with query terms wrapped in markers, useful for search result previews.
points: It works on the original text.

example.sql: SELECT ts_headline('english', 'SQL joins and indexes are useful', plainto_tsquery('english', 'index'));

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.simple: Dictionaries token normalization control karte hain.
topics.pro: Text search dictionaries define stop words, stemming and synonym rules for a configuration.
points: They affect both indexing and queries.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_ts_dict;

topics.title: Stop Words
topics.simple: Stop words common words hote hain jo search me ignore hote hain.
topics.pro: Stop words such as the and and are removed because they add little discriminating value.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'the quick brown fox');

topics.title: Stemming
topics.simple: Stemming words ko root form me le aata hai.
topics.pro: Stemming maps variants such as run, runs and running to a shared lexeme, improving recall.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'running runs');

topics.title: GIN Index for FTS
topics.simple: GIN index full-text search ko fast karta hai.
topics.pro: A GIN index on the tsvector expression accelerates @@ queries.
points: Use the same configuration in queries.
It speeds reads but costs writes.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_courses_title_fts ON courses USING gin (to_tsvector('english', title));

topics.title: Search Configuration
topics.simple: Text search configuration language aur rules choose karti hai.
topics.pro: The configuration determines stop words, stemming and dictionary behavior; indexing and querying must use the same one.
points: Store a generated tsvector for control.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsvector('simple', 'running cats');

topics.title: Phrase Search
topics.simple: Phrase search words ke order aur adjacency ko match karta hai.
topics.pro: The <-> operator requires adjacent lexemes, while <n> allows a distance.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'full <-> text');

topics.title: Prefix Search
topics.simple: Prefix search partial words match karta hai.
topics.pro: The :* operator matches lexemes with a prefix, useful for search-as-you-type.

example.sql: SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'index:*');

topics.title: Common FTS Errors
topics.simple: Config mismatch, wrong operators aur unindexed expressions common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are querying a different configuration than the index, using LIKE for ranking, and forgetting to index the exact expression.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM courses WHERE to_tsvector('english', title) @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'sql');

topics.title: FTS vs LIKE
topics.simple: FTS words aur relevance deta hai; LIKE substrings deta hai.
topics.pro: LIKE is simple substring matching, while full-text search handles stemming, stop words, ranking and large documents.

example.sql: SELECT title FROM courses WHERE title ILIKE '%sql%';

topics.title: Practical Search
topics.simple: Search query, rank aur headline ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical search query filters with @@, orders by ts_rank and returns a headline snippet.

example.sql: SELECT title, ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', title), websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'sql')) AS rank FROM courses WHERE to_tsvector('english', title) @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'sql') ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 10;

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain tsvector in a production query.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain tsquery in a production query.
interview.answer: A tsquery combines lexemes with &, |, ! and phrase operators. Key rules: & means AND. | means OR. ! means NOT.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain to_tsvector in a production query.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain to_tsquery in a production query.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain plainto_tsquery in a production query.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain websearch_to_tsquery in a production query.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Match Operator in a production query.
interview.answer: The @@ operator returns true when a tsvector matches a tsquery. Key rules: It is the core FTS predicate. It can use a GIN index. Both sides need matching types.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Ranking in a production query.
interview.answer: ts_rank scores matches by term frequency and proximity, allowing the most relevant results first. Key rules: Higher is more relevant. Weights can favor title over body. It is not a probability.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Highlighting in a production query.
interview.answer: ts_headline returns a snippet with query terms wrapped in markers, useful for search result previews. Key rules: It works on the original text. Markers are configurable. It can be expensive.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Dictionaries in a production query.
interview.answer: Text search dictionaries define stop words, stemming and synonym rules for a configuration. Key rules: They are language-specific. They can be customized. They affect both indexing and queries.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Stop Words in a production query.
interview.answer: Stop words such as the and and are removed because they add little discriminating value. Key rules: They reduce index size. They can surprise phrase searches. Configurations differ by language.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Stemming in a production query.
interview.answer: Stemming maps variants such as run, runs and running to a shared lexeme, improving recall. Key rules: It improves matching. It can over-stem. The language config controls it.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain GIN Index for FTS in a production query.
interview.answer: A GIN index on the tsvector expression accelerates @@ queries. Key rules: Index the exact expression. Use the same configuration in queries. It speeds reads but costs writes.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Search Configuration in a production query.
interview.answer: The configuration determines stop words, stemming and dictionary behavior; indexing and querying must use the same one. Key rules: Use a consistent config. simple does not stem. Store a generated tsvector for control.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Phrase Search in a production query.
interview.answer: The <-> operator requires adjacent lexemes, while <n> allows a distance. Key rules: Use <-> for adjacency. Positions come from tsvector. Stop words can affect phrases.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Prefix Search in a production query.
interview.answer: The :* operator matches lexemes with a prefix, useful for search-as-you-type. Key rules: Use :* on the last term. It can be expensive. Combine with ranking.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Common FTS Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are querying a different configuration than the index, using LIKE for ranking, and forgetting to index the exact expression. Key rules: Match configurations. Use @@ not LIKE. Index the expression.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain FTS vs LIKE in a production query.
interview.answer: LIKE is simple substring matching, while full-text search handles stemming, stop words, ranking and large documents. Key rules: LIKE is literal. FTS is linguistic. FTS scales with GIN.

interview.q: Module 23 · Explain Practical Search in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical search query filters with @@, orders by ts_rank and returns a headline snippet. Key rules: Filter first. Rank second. Limit the results.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Full-Text Search Basics matter?
logic.answer: Full-text search parses documents into normalized lexemes and matches them against a query, with ranking and highlighting. It handles words, not just substrings. It supports stemming and stop words. It can be indexed with GIN.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does tsvector matter?
logic.answer: A tsvector stores lexemes with positions, which is the document representation used by full-text search. It is not plain text. Positions support phrase search. It can be generated or stored.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does tsquery matter?
logic.answer: A tsquery combines lexemes with &, |, ! and phrase operators. & means AND. | means OR. ! means NOT.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does to_tsvector matter?
logic.answer: to_tsvector(config, text) normalizes a document using a text search configuration. Choose a language config. It lowercases and stems. It removes stop words.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does to_tsquery matter?
logic.answer: to_tsquery parses explicit operators and requires the caller to format the query safely. It accepts operators. It can raise syntax errors. Use parameters for user input.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does plainto_tsquery matter?
logic.answer: plainto_tsquery turns plain text into a tsquery by ANDing the lexemes, ignoring operators in the input. It is safer for raw input. It uses AND semantics. It removes stop words.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does websearch_to_tsquery matter?
logic.answer: websearch_to_tsquery supports quoted phrases, OR and minus terms without raising syntax errors on ordinary input. It is designed for user input. Quotes create phrases. Minus excludes terms.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Match Operator matter?
logic.answer: The @@ operator returns true when a tsvector matches a tsquery. It is the core FTS predicate. It can use a GIN index. Both sides need matching types.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Ranking matter?
logic.answer: ts_rank scores matches by term frequency and proximity, allowing the most relevant results first. Higher is more relevant. Weights can favor title over body. It is not a probability.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Highlighting matter?
logic.answer: ts_headline returns a snippet with query terms wrapped in markers, useful for search result previews. It works on the original text. Markers are configurable. It can be expensive.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Dictionaries matter?
logic.answer: Text search dictionaries define stop words, stemming and synonym rules for a configuration. They are language-specific. They can be customized. They affect both indexing and queries.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Stop Words matter?
logic.answer: Stop words such as the and and are removed because they add little discriminating value. They reduce index size. They can surprise phrase searches. Configurations differ by language.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Stemming matter?
logic.answer: Stemming maps variants such as run, runs and running to a shared lexeme, improving recall. It improves matching. It can over-stem. The language config controls it.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does GIN Index for FTS matter?
logic.answer: A GIN index on the tsvector expression accelerates @@ queries. Index the exact expression. Use the same configuration in queries. It speeds reads but costs writes.

logic.q: Module 23 · Why does Search Configuration matter?
logic.answer: The configuration determines stop words, stemming and dictionary behavior; indexing and querying must use the same one. Use a consistent config. simple does not stem. Store a generated tsvector for control.

modules.title: Stored Functions and Procedures
modules.goal: Put reusable logic in the database with the right volatility, security and transaction rules.

topics.title: Function vs Procedure
topics.simple: Function value return karta hai; procedure transaction control kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: Functions return a value and run inside the caller’s statement, while procedures are invoked with CALL and can manage transactions.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION student_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;

topics.title: CREATE FUNCTION
topics.simple: CREATE FUNCTION named routine banata hai.
topics.pro: CREATE FUNCTION defines a routine with parameters, a return type, a language and a body.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p_marks integer) RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT p_marks * 2; $$;

topics.title: RETURNS
topics.simple: RETURNS function ka output type batata hai.
topics.pro: The RETURNS clause declares a scalar, table, set or void result and must match what the body produces.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION student_name(p_id bigint) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT name FROM students WHERE id = p_id; $$;

topics.title: SQL Functions
topics.simple: SQL function body plain SQL ho sakta hai.
topics.pro: A LANGUAGE sql function can contain SQL statements and is often inlined by the planner.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION high_scorers() RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, name text) LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80; $$;

topics.title: PL/pgSQL Basics
topics.simple: PL/pgSQL procedural language hai.
topics.pro: PL/pgSQL adds variables, control flow, exceptions and multiple statements to database routines.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION grade_band(p_marks integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF p_marks >= 90 THEN RETURN 'A'; ELSE RETURN 'B'; END IF; END; $$;

topics.title: Parameters
topics.simple: Function parameters input aur output ho sakte hain.
topics.pro: Parameters can be IN, OUT or INOUT; OUT parameters can define a result row without RETURNS TABLE.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION add_marks(p_id bigint, p_delta integer) RETURNS void LANGUAGE sql AS $$ UPDATE students SET marks = marks + p_delta WHERE id = p_id; $$;

topics.title: Returning Tables
topics.simple: RETURNS TABLE se multi-row result do.
topics.pro: RETURNS TABLE declares named output columns and lets the function return a set of rows.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION course_roster(p_course integer) RETURNS TABLE (student_id bigint, name text) LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT s.id, s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id = p_course; $$;

topics.title: CREATE PROCEDURE
topics.simple: Procedure CALL se chalti hai aur transaction control kar sakti hai.
topics.pro: CREATE PROCEDURE defines a routine invoked with CALL; procedures can commit or roll back inside their body.

example.sql: CREATE PROCEDURE archive_low_marks() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60; COMMIT; END; $$;

topics.title: CALL
topics.simple: CALL procedure ko invoke karta hai.
topics.pro: CALL executes a procedure with arguments and does not return a result set.

example.sql: CALL archive_low_marks();

topics.title: Transaction Control
topics.simple: Procedure ke andar COMMIT/ROLLBACK allowed hai.
topics.pro: Procedures can commit or roll back, but functions cannot; this is the key operational difference.

example.sql: CREATE PROCEDURE safe_archive() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60; COMMIT; END; $$;

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.simple: PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION block errors pakadta hai.
topics.pro: An EXCEPTION block catches errors, lets you log or recover, and can re-raise with RAISE.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION safe_divide(a numeric, b numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN a / b; EXCEPTION WHEN division_by_zero THEN RETURN NULL; END; $$;

topics.title: SECURITY DEFINER
topics.simple: SECURITY DEFINER function owner ke privileges se chalta hai.
topics.pro: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the privileges of its owner, so it must lock down search_path and validate inputs.
points: Avoid dynamic SQL with untrusted input.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION admin_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;

topics.title: Volatility
topics.simple: Volatility function ke side effects aur caching batati hai.
topics.pro: IMMUTABLE means same inputs always produce the same result, STABLE means constant within a statement, and VOLATILE can change or write.
points: VOLATILE is the default for writes.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p_marks integer) RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT p_marks * 2; $$;

topics.title: Function Overloading
topics.simple: Same name with different parameter types allowed hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL resolves overloaded functions by argument types, so ambiguous calls can fail.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION label(p_marks integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'number'; $$;

topics.title: Dropping Routines
topics.simple: DROP FUNCTION/PROCEDURE routine hataata hai.
topics.pro: DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE removes a routine; CASCADE also removes dependent objects.

example.sql: DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS double_marks(integer);

topics.title: Common Routine Errors
topics.simple: Return mismatch, missing language aur transaction misuse common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are a return type mismatch, a missing LANGUAGE clause, COMMIT inside a function and ambiguous overloads.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION bad() RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'text'; $$;
example.output: ERROR: invalid input syntax for type integer

topics.title: Routine Performance
topics.simple: SQL functions inline; PL/pgSQL loops can be slow.
topics.pro: Simple SQL functions can be inlined and optimized, while procedural row-by-row loops often lose to set-based SQL.
points: Read the plan for function calls.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT double_marks(marks) FROM students;
example.output: A plan showing the function call.

topics.title: Testing Routines
topics.simple: Functions ko known inputs aur edge cases se test karo.
topics.pro: Test return values, NULL inputs, empty sets and error paths before relying on a routine in production.

example.sql: SELECT double_marks(NULL) AS doubled;

topics.title: Practical Function
topics.simple: Reusable validation ya calculation function banao.
topics.pro: A practical function keeps a single rule in one place and is marked with the correct volatility and security.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION is_passing(p_marks integer) RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT COALESCE(p_marks >= 60, false); $$;

topics.title: Routine Maintenance
topics.simple: Routines ko version karo aur dependencies check karo.
topics.pro: Routine changes can break callers, so track signatures, test replacements and inspect dependencies before dropping.

example.sql: SELECT proname, pg_get_function_identity_arguments(oid) FROM pg_proc WHERE proname = 'double_marks';

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Function vs Procedure in a production query.
interview.answer: Functions return a value and run inside the caller’s statement, while procedures are invoked with CALL and can manage transactions. Key rules: Functions return values. Procedures use CALL. Procedures can COMMIT.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain CREATE FUNCTION in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE FUNCTION defines a routine with parameters, a return type, a language and a body. Key rules: Name the function. Declare parameters. Choose the language.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain RETURNS in a production query.
interview.answer: The RETURNS clause declares a scalar, table, set or void result and must match what the body produces. Key rules: Use RETURNS TABLE for rows. Use SETOF for sets. RETURNS void means no value.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain SQL Functions in a production query.
interview.answer: A LANGUAGE sql function can contain SQL statements and is often inlined by the planner. Key rules: Simple and optimizable. Can return scalar or table. No procedural loops.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain PL/pgSQL Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: PL/pgSQL adds variables, control flow, exceptions and multiple statements to database routines. Key rules: Use BEGIN and END. Declare variables. Return explicitly.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Parameters in a production query.
interview.answer: Parameters can be IN, OUT or INOUT; OUT parameters can define a result row without RETURNS TABLE. Key rules: IN is the default. OUT adds a result column. Name parameters clearly.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Returning Tables in a production query.
interview.answer: RETURNS TABLE declares named output columns and lets the function return a set of rows. Key rules: Declare column names and types. Return a SELECT. Use it like a table.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain CREATE PROCEDURE in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE PROCEDURE defines a routine invoked with CALL; procedures can commit or roll back inside their body. Key rules: Use CALL. Transaction control is allowed. No return value.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain CALL in a production query.
interview.answer: CALL executes a procedure with arguments and does not return a result set. Key rules: Use CALL, not SELECT. Arguments follow the name. It can manage transactions.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Transaction Control in a production query.
interview.answer: Procedures can commit or roll back, but functions cannot; this is the key operational difference. Key rules: Functions cannot COMMIT. Procedures can COMMIT. Be careful with partial success.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Exception Handling in a production query.
interview.answer: An EXCEPTION block catches errors, lets you log or recover, and can re-raise with RAISE. Key rules: Wrap risky statements. Use GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS. Re-raise when unsure.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain SECURITY DEFINER in a production query.
interview.answer: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the privileges of its owner, so it must lock down search_path and validate inputs. Key rules: It can grant controlled access. Set search_path explicitly. Avoid dynamic SQL with untrusted input.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Volatility in a production query.
interview.answer: IMMUTABLE means same inputs always produce the same result, STABLE means constant within a statement, and VOLATILE can change or write. Key rules: IMMUTABLE is strictest. STABLE reads the database. VOLATILE is the default for writes.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Function Overloading in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL resolves overloaded functions by argument types, so ambiguous calls can fail. Key rules: Overload by argument types. Avoid ambiguous defaults. Cast calls when needed.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Dropping Routines in a production query.
interview.answer: DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE removes a routine; CASCADE also removes dependent objects. Key rules: Specify argument types. Use IF EXISTS in scripts. CASCADE is destructive.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Common Routine Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are a return type mismatch, a missing LANGUAGE clause, COMMIT inside a function and ambiguous overloads. Key rules: Match RETURNS. Declare LANGUAGE. Use procedures for transactions.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Routine Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Simple SQL functions can be inlined and optimized, while procedural row-by-row loops often lose to set-based SQL. Key rules: Prefer set-based SQL. Mark volatility correctly. Read the plan for function calls.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Testing Routines in a production query.
interview.answer: Test return values, NULL inputs, empty sets and error paths before relying on a routine in production. Key rules: Test NULL. Test empty input. Test error handling.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Practical Function in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical function keeps a single rule in one place and is marked with the correct volatility and security. Key rules: Name it clearly. Type the parameters. Document the contract.

interview.q: Module 24 · Explain Routine Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Routine changes can break callers, so track signatures, test replacements and inspect dependencies before dropping. Key rules: Track signatures. Use CREATE OR REPLACE carefully. Check pg_depend.

labs.title: Function vs Procedure
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Function vs Procedure.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION student_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;

labs.title: CREATE FUNCTION
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates CREATE FUNCTION.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p_marks integer) RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT p_marks * 2; $$;

labs.title: RETURNS
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates RETURNS.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION student_name(p_id bigint) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT name FROM students WHERE id = p_id; $$;

labs.title: SQL Functions
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates SQL Functions.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION high_scorers() RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, name text) LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80; $$;

labs.title: PL/pgSQL Basics
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates PL/pgSQL Basics.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION grade_band(p_marks integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF p_marks >= 90 THEN RETURN 'A'; ELSE RETURN 'B'; END IF; END; $$;

labs.title: Parameters
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Parameters.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION add_marks(p_id bigint, p_delta integer) RETURNS void LANGUAGE sql AS $$ UPDATE students SET marks = marks + p_delta WHERE id = p_id; $$;

labs.title: Returning Tables
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Returning Tables.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION course_roster(p_course integer) RETURNS TABLE (student_id bigint, name text) LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT s.id, s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id = p_course; $$;

labs.title: CREATE PROCEDURE
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates CREATE PROCEDURE.
labs.solution: CREATE PROCEDURE archive_low_marks() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60; COMMIT; END; $$;

labs.title: CALL
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates CALL.
labs.solution: CALL archive_low_marks();

labs.title: Transaction Control
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Transaction Control.
labs.solution: CREATE PROCEDURE safe_archive() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60; COMMIT; END; $$;

labs.title: Exception Handling
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Exception Handling.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION safe_divide(a numeric, b numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN a / b; EXCEPTION WHEN division_by_zero THEN RETURN NULL; END; $$;

labs.title: SECURITY DEFINER
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates SECURITY DEFINER.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION admin_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;

labs.title: Volatility
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Volatility.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p_marks integer) RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT p_marks * 2; $$;

labs.title: Function Overloading
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Function Overloading.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION label(p_marks integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'number'; $$;

labs.title: Dropping Routines
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Dropping Routines.
labs.solution: DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS double_marks(integer);

labs.title: Common Routine Errors
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Common Routine Errors.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION bad() RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'text'; $$;
labs.expected: ERROR: invalid input syntax for type integer

labs.title: Routine Performance
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Routine Performance.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN SELECT double_marks(marks) FROM students;
labs.expected: A plan showing the function call.

labs.title: Testing Routines
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Testing Routines.
labs.solution: SELECT double_marks(NULL) AS doubled;

labs.title: Practical Function
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Practical Function.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION is_passing(p_marks integer) RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT COALESCE(p_marks >= 60, false); $$;

labs.title: Routine Maintenance
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Routine Maintenance.
labs.solution: SELECT proname, pg_get_function_identity_arguments(oid) FROM pg_proc WHERE proname = 'double_marks';

debug.title: Missing language
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p integer) RETURNS integer AS $$ SELECT p * 2; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION double_marks(p integer) RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT p * 2; $$;
debug.error: no language specified

debug.title: Return mismatch
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION bad() RETURNS integer LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'text'; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION bad() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$ SELECT 'text'; $$;
debug.error: invalid input syntax for type integer

debug.title: COMMIT in function
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN COMMIT; END; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE PROCEDURE p() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN COMMIT; END; $$;
debug.error: COMMIT is not allowed in a function

debug.title: SELECT a procedure
debug.broken: SELECT archive_low_marks();
debug.fix: CALL archive_low_marks();
debug.error: archive_low_marks is a procedure

debug.title: Ambiguous overload
debug.fix: SELECT f(1::integer);
debug.error: function f(integer) is not unique

debug.title: Search path risk
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION admin_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION admin_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;
debug.error: A caller-controlled search_path can hijack names

debug.title: Volatility lie
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION now_text() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT NOW()::text; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION now_text() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT NOW()::text; $$;
debug.error: An IMMUTABLE function must not change over time

debug.title: Drop without signature
debug.broken: DROP FUNCTION double_marks;
debug.fix: DROP FUNCTION double_marks(integer);
debug.error: function name is not unique

debug.title: Exception swallowed
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO missing_table VALUES (1); EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL; END; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO missing_table VALUES (1); EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN RAISE; END; $$;
debug.error: The error is silently swallowed

debug.title: Set-returning misuse
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM high_scorers;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM high_scorers();
debug.error: relation "high_scorers" does not exist
