modules.title: Triggers
modules.goal: Automate database-side reactions without hiding business logic or creating recursion.

topics.title: Trigger Basics
topics.simple: Trigger event par automatically chalne wala function hai.
topics.pro: A trigger binds a function to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE events on a table.
points: It can run before or after the event.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

topics.title: BEFORE Trigger
topics.simple: BEFORE trigger row change se pehle chalta hai.
topics.pro: A BEFORE trigger can validate or modify NEW before the row is written.
points: It runs once per affected row.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER validate_marks BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

topics.title: AFTER Trigger
topics.simple: AFTER trigger change ke baad chalta hai.
topics.pro: An AFTER trigger observes the committed row change and is used for auditing and side effects.
points: It cannot change NEW for the write.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

topics.title: Row vs Statement Triggers
topics.simple: Row trigger har row par chalta hai; statement trigger ek baar.
topics.pro: FOR EACH ROW fires per affected row, while FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement.
points: Statement triggers are cheaper for bulk work.
Transition tables work with statement triggers.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

topics.title: Trigger Function
topics.simple: Trigger function trigger context me chalta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger function returns trigger and uses NEW, OLD, TG_OP and TG_TABLE_NAME.
points: Return NULL to skip the operation.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: NEW and OLD
topics.simple: NEW naya row hai; OLD purana row.
topics.pro: NEW holds the proposed row for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD holds the previous row for UPDATE/DELETE.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION log_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE '% -> %', OLD.marks, NEW.marks; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Validation Trigger
topics.simple: Trigger complex validation kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger can enforce rules that span tables or need procedural logic beyond a CHECK constraint.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION require_email() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF NEW.email IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'email required'; END IF; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Audit Trigger
topics.simple: Audit trigger changes ko history table me likhta hai.
topics.pro: An audit trigger records who changed what and when, usually in an append-only table.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE student_audit (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, student_id BIGINT, action TEXT, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

topics.title: Timestamp Trigger
topics.simple: Timestamp trigger updated_at maintain karta hai.
topics.pro: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger sets updated_at automatically so every writer gets the same behavior.
points: Do not rely on the app.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Trigger Order
topics.simple: Same event par multiple triggers alphabetical order me chalte hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same kind in name order, so name them deliberately when order matters.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER a_validate BEFORE INSERT ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

topics.title: Enabling and Disabling
topics.simple: Trigger ko temporarily disable kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER helps bulk loads but bypasses important rules.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students DISABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;

topics.title: Dropping Triggers
topics.simple: DROP TRIGGER trigger hataata hai.
topics.pro: Drop the trigger before dropping its function, or use CASCADE deliberately.

example.sql: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS validate_marks ON students;

topics.title: Trigger vs Constraint
topics.simple: Simple rules constraints me rakho; complex side effects triggers me.
topics.pro: Constraints are declarative and optimized; triggers are procedural and easier to misuse.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

topics.title: Trigger Recursion
topics.simple: Trigger apne hi table par write karke recursion bana sakta hai.
topics.pro: A trigger that updates its own table can fire itself again; guard with conditions or a depth check.

example.sql: CREATE TRIGGER touch_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.marks IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.marks) EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

topics.title: Trigger Performance
topics.simple: Row triggers bulk operations ko slow karte hain.
topics.pro: Every row trigger adds function-call and write overhead, especially during large updates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 1;

topics.title: Common Trigger Errors
topics.simple: Missing RETURN, wrong timing aur recursion common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are forgetting RETURN NEW, using AFTER to modify the row, and triggering an infinite update loop.
points: Return NEW in BEFORE row triggers.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION bad_trigger() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.marks = 0; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Auditing
topics.simple: Audit trail append-only aur queryable hona chahiye.
topics.pro: A good audit table records the operation, key, before and after values, actor and timestamp.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE audit_log (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, table_name TEXT, action TEXT, row_data JSONB, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

topics.title: Trigger Security
topics.simple: Trigger function privileges carefully set karo.
topics.pro: Triggers run with the function owner’s privileges when SECURITY DEFINER is used, so validate inputs and fix search_path.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION audit_students() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, action, row_data) VALUES (TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_OP, to_jsonb(NEW)); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Practical Trigger
topics.simple: updated_at aur audit trigger ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical trigger sets updated_at and writes an audit row in one controlled function.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION before_student_update() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); INSERT INTO student_audit (student_id, action) VALUES (NEW.id, TG_OP); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

topics.title: Trigger Maintenance
topics.simple: Triggers ko version aur test karo.
topics.pro: Track trigger definitions, test them with bulk changes and review them during migrations.

example.sql: SELECT tgname, tgrelid::regclass FROM pg_trigger WHERE NOT tgisinternal;

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger binds a function to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE events on a table. Key rules: It runs automatically. It calls a trigger function. It can run before or after the event.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain BEFORE Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A BEFORE trigger can validate or modify NEW before the row is written. Key rules: It can change NEW. It can reject the row. It runs once per affected row.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain AFTER Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: An AFTER trigger observes the committed row change and is used for auditing and side effects. Key rules: It sees the final row. It cannot change NEW for the write. It can queue more work.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Row vs Statement Triggers in a production query.
interview.answer: FOR EACH ROW fires per affected row, while FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement. Key rules: Row triggers see NEW/OLD. Statement triggers are cheaper for bulk work. Transition tables work with statement triggers.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Function in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger function returns trigger and uses NEW, OLD, TG_OP and TG_TABLE_NAME. Key rules: Return NEW for row triggers. Return NULL to skip the operation. Declare LANGUAGE plpgsql.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain NEW and OLD in a production query.
interview.answer: NEW holds the proposed row for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD holds the previous row for UPDATE/DELETE. Key rules: INSERT has NEW only. DELETE has OLD only. UPDATE has both.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Validation Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger can enforce rules that span tables or need procedural logic beyond a CHECK constraint. Key rules: Prefer CHECK for simple rules. Use triggers for cross-row rules. Raise a clear exception.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Audit Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: An audit trigger records who changed what and when, usually in an append-only table. Key rules: Capture TG_OP. Store old and new values. Keep the audit insert durable.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Timestamp Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A BEFORE UPDATE trigger sets updated_at automatically so every writer gets the same behavior. Key rules: Set NEW.updated_at. Return NEW. Do not rely on the app.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Order in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same kind in name order, so name them deliberately when order matters. Key rules: Order is by name. Use BEFORE for validation. Use AFTER for side effects.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Enabling and Disabling in a production query.
interview.answer: ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER helps bulk loads but bypasses important rules. Key rules: Disable only during controlled maintenance. Re-enable immediately. Foreign-key triggers are special.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Dropping Triggers in a production query.
interview.answer: Drop the trigger before dropping its function, or use CASCADE deliberately. Key rules: Name the table and trigger. IF EXISTS is script-safe. The function remains until dropped.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger vs Constraint in a production query.
interview.answer: Constraints are declarative and optimized; triggers are procedural and easier to misuse. Key rules: Prefer constraints. Use triggers for auditing. Document every trigger.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Recursion in a production query.
interview.answer: A trigger that updates its own table can fire itself again; guard with conditions or a depth check. Key rules: Avoid self-updates. Use WHEN clauses. Test the recursion path.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Every row trigger adds function-call and write overhead, especially during large updates. Key rules: Prefer set-based SQL. Use statement triggers when possible. Measure bulk loads.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Common Trigger Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are forgetting RETURN NEW, using AFTER to modify the row, and triggering an infinite update loop. Key rules: Return NEW in BEFORE row triggers. Use BEFORE to modify. Guard recursion.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Auditing in a production query.
interview.answer: A good audit table records the operation, key, before and after values, actor and timestamp. Key rules: Record the actor. Store before/after. Never update audit rows.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Security in a production query.
interview.answer: Triggers run with the function owner’s privileges when SECURITY DEFINER is used, so validate inputs and fix search_path. Key rules: Avoid SECURITY DEFINER by default. Set search_path. Do not trust NEW blindly.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Practical Trigger in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical trigger sets updated_at and writes an audit row in one controlled function. Key rules: Set the timestamp first. Write the audit row. Return the final NEW.

interview.q: Module 25 · Explain Trigger Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Track trigger definitions, test them with bulk changes and review them during migrations. Key rules: List triggers per table. Test with multi-row statements. Drop obsolete triggers.

labs.title: Trigger Basics
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Basics.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

labs.title: BEFORE Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates BEFORE Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER validate_marks BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

labs.title: AFTER Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates AFTER Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

labs.title: Row vs Statement Triggers
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Row vs Statement Triggers.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER audit_students AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_students();

labs.title: Trigger Function
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Function.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: NEW and OLD
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates NEW and OLD.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION log_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE '% -> %', OLD.marks, NEW.marks; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Validation Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Validation Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION require_email() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF NEW.email IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'email required'; END IF; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Audit Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Audit Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE TABLE student_audit (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, student_id BIGINT, action TEXT, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

labs.title: Timestamp Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Timestamp Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Trigger Order
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Order.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER a_validate BEFORE INSERT ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION validate_marks();

labs.title: Enabling and Disabling
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Enabling and Disabling.
labs.solution: ALTER TABLE students DISABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;

labs.title: Dropping Triggers
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Dropping Triggers.
labs.solution: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS validate_marks ON students;

labs.title: Trigger vs Constraint
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger vs Constraint.
labs.solution: ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT marks_range CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100);

labs.title: Trigger Recursion
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Recursion.
labs.solution: CREATE TRIGGER touch_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.marks IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.marks) EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

labs.title: Trigger Performance
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Performance.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 1;

labs.title: Common Trigger Errors
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Common Trigger Errors.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION bad_trigger() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.marks = 0; RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Auditing
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Auditing.
labs.solution: CREATE TABLE audit_log (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, table_name TEXT, action TEXT, row_data JSONB, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

labs.title: Trigger Security
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Security.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION audit_students() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, action, row_data) VALUES (TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_OP, to_jsonb(NEW)); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Practical Trigger
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Practical Trigger.
labs.solution: CREATE FUNCTION before_student_update() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); INSERT INTO student_audit (student_id, action) VALUES (NEW.id, TG_OP); RETURN NEW; END; $$;

labs.title: Trigger Maintenance
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Trigger Maintenance.
labs.solution: SELECT tgname, tgrelid::regclass FROM pg_trigger WHERE NOT tgisinternal;

debug.title: Missing RETURN
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION touch() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); END; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION touch() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END; $$;
debug.error: control reached end of trigger procedure without RETURN

debug.title: AFTER cannot modify
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.fix: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.error: NEW changes in an AFTER trigger do not affect the stored row
debug.expected: The timestamp is set before writing.

debug.title: Row trigger on truncate
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE TRUNCATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.fix: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE TRUNCATE ON students FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.error: TRUNCATE does not support FOR EACH ROW

debug.title: Recursive update
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t AFTER UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_student();
debug.fix: Add a WHEN condition or a guard column so the trigger does not update the same row again.
debug.error: stack depth limit exceeded

debug.title: Wrong trigger return
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN NULL; END; $$;
debug.fix: Return NEW when the row should proceed.
debug.error: The operation is skipped

debug.title: Missing function
debug.broken: CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION missing_fn();
debug.fix:
CREATE FUNCTION missing_fn() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RETURN NEW; END; $$;
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION missing_fn();
debug.error: function missing_fn() does not exist

debug.title: Trigger name collision
debug.broken:
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE UPDATE ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
CREATE TRIGGER t BEFORE INSERT ON students FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();
debug.fix: Use distinct trigger names for each event.
debug.error: trigger "t" for relation "students" already exists

debug.title: Audit without actor
debug.broken: INSERT INTO audit_log (action) VALUES (TG_OP);
debug.fix: INSERT INTO audit_log (action, actor) VALUES (TG_OP, current_user);
debug.error: The audit row cannot identify who changed the data

debug.title: Disable forgotten
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students DISABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ENABLE TRIGGER validate_marks;
debug.error: Validation is bypassed indefinitely

debug.title: Drop function first
debug.broken: DROP FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
debug.fix:
DROP TRIGGER touch_updated_at ON students;
DROP FUNCTION touch_updated_at();

modules.title: Advanced Indexing
modules.goal: Use specialized indexes and index-only access without over-indexing the database.

topics.title: Index Types Review
topics.simple: B-tree, hash, GIN, GiST aur BRIN alag workloads ke liye hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL index types target different data shapes: B-tree for ordered scalars, hash for equality, GIN for composites, GiST for ranges and BRIN for correlated large tables.
points: Match the type to the data.

example.sql: SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'students';

topics.title: B-tree Deep Dive
topics.simple: B-tree ordered comparisons aur ranges support karta hai.
topics.pro: A B-tree keeps keys ordered, supporting equality, ranges, prefix LIKE and ORDER BY.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks DESC);

topics.title: Composite Index Order
topics.simple: Composite index ka order left-to-right use hota hai.
topics.pro: A composite B-tree can serve queries on its leading columns; later columns are useful only when earlier ones are constrained.
points: A skipped leading column weakens use.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student_course ON enrollments (student_id, course_id);

topics.title: Covering Indexes
topics.simple: INCLUDE payload columns index-only scan dete hain.
topics.pro: INCLUDE adds non-key columns so the index can satisfy a query without heap access.
points: INCLUDE is not part of the key.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_include ON students (marks) INCLUDE (name);

topics.title: Partial Indexes
topics.simple: Partial index predicate se index chhota hota hai.
topics.pro: A partial index stores only rows matching its WHERE clause and is useful for rare or active subsets.
points: The query must imply the predicate.
It speeds writes versus a full index.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_high_marks ON students (marks) WHERE marks >= 90;

topics.title: Expression Indexes
topics.simple: Expression index computed values ko index karta hai.
topics.pro: An expression index stores a function result, such as LOWER(email), and serves queries using the same expression.
points: It is useful for case-insensitive lookups.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_lower_email ON students (LOWER(email));

topics.title: GIN Indexes
topics.simple: GIN composite values ke containment ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GIN builds an inverted index for arrays, JSONB and text search, accelerating containment and existence operators.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_name_gin ON students USING gin (to_tsvector('simple', name));

topics.title: GiST Indexes
topics.simple: GiST ranges, geometry aur nearest-neighbor ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GiST supports balanced search trees over complex types and powers exclusion constraints.

example.sql:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date_gist ON enrollments USING gist (enrolled_on);

topics.title: BRIN Indexes
topics.simple: BRIN large ordered tables ke liye compact hai.
topics.pro: BRIN stores block-range summaries, making it tiny and effective when a column correlates with physical order, such as timestamps.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date_brin ON enrollments USING brin (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Hash Indexes
topics.simple: Hash index equality-only lookup deta hai.
topics.pro: A hash index stores hash codes and supports equality, but not ordering or ranges.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_email_hash ON students USING hash (email);

topics.title: Index-Only Scans
topics.simple: Index-only scan heap visit bachata hai.
topics.pro: When all requested columns are in the index and the visibility map is favorable, PostgreSQL can answer from the index alone.

topics.title: Index Bloat
topics.simple: Updates index bloat create karte hain.

topics.title: REINDEX

topics.title: Concurrent Index Creation

topics.title: Index Selectivity
topics.simple: Selectivity index ki usefulness batati hai.

topics.title: Multi-Column Selectivity

topics.title: Common Advanced Mistakes
topics.simple: Over-indexing, wrong opclass aur unused indexes common mistakes hain.

topics.title: Monitoring Indexes
topics.simple: pg_stat_user_indexes usage dikhata hai.

topics.title: Practical Tuning
topics.simple: Slow query se index plan tak.
topics.pro: A disciplined tuning loop captures the query, reads its plan, adds the smallest useful index and measures again.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90 ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Index Maintenance Plan
topics.simple: Indexes ko create, monitor aur retire karo.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Types Review in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL index types target different data shapes: B-tree for ordered scalars, hash for equality, GIN for composites, GiST for ranges and BRIN for correlated large tables. Key rules: Match the type to the data. B-tree is the default. Specialized indexes need operator classes.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain B-tree Deep Dive in a production query.
interview.answer: A B-tree keeps keys ordered, supporting equality, ranges, prefix LIKE and ORDER BY. Key rules: It is balanced. It supports ordering. It handles duplicates.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Composite Index Order in a production query.
interview.answer: A composite B-tree can serve queries on its leading columns; later columns are useful only when earlier ones are constrained. Key rules: Put equality first. Ranges come later. A skipped leading column weakens use.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Covering Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: INCLUDE adds non-key columns so the index can satisfy a query without heap access. Key rules: INCLUDE is not part of the key. It increases size. Visibility map affects index-only scans.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Partial Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: A partial index stores only rows matching its WHERE clause and is useful for rare or active subsets. Key rules: The query must imply the predicate. It saves space. It speeds writes versus a full index.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Expression Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: An expression index stores a function result, such as LOWER(email), and serves queries using the same expression. Key rules: Match the expression. It is useful for case-insensitive lookups. It costs write CPU.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain GIN Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: GIN builds an inverted index for arrays, JSONB and text search, accelerating containment and existence operators. Key rules: Good for @>, ?, @@. Updates can be expensive. Choose the right opclass.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain GiST Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: GiST supports balanced search trees over complex types and powers exclusion constraints. Key rules: Good for ranges. Supports KNN. Needs the right extension.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain BRIN Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: BRIN stores block-range summaries, making it tiny and effective when a column correlates with physical order, such as timestamps. Key rules: Very small. Good for append-only data. Less precise than B-tree.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Hash Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: A hash index stores hash codes and supports equality, but not ordering or ranges. Key rules: Equality only. Rarely better than B-tree. It cannot support ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index-Only Scans in a production query.
interview.answer: When all requested columns are in the index and the visibility map is favorable, PostgreSQL can answer from the index alone. Key rules: Use INCLUDE. VACUUM maintains visibility. Check EXPLAIN for Heap Fetches.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Bloat in a production query.
interview.answer: Dead index entries accumulate after updates and deletes, increasing size and slowing scans until cleanup. Key rules: Monitor size. VACUUM regularly. REINDEX when needed.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain REINDEX in a production query.
interview.answer: REINDEX rebuilds an index to remove bloat or repair corruption; it can lock the index or table. Key rules: Use CONCURRENTLY when available. It needs free space. It can be slow.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Concurrent Index Creation in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes but takes longer and cannot run in a transaction block. Key rules: Avoids write locks. Can fail and leave an invalid index. Run outside a transaction.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: An index is most useful when the predicate returns a small fraction of rows; low selectivity may favor a sequential scan. Key rules: High selectivity is better. Statistics matter. Test with real data.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Multi-Column Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: The planner estimates combined selectivity, so index columns should match the most common equality and range combinations. Key rules: Equality columns first. Range columns later. Read the plan.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Common Advanced Mistakes in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are adding indexes for every column, using GIN where B-tree fits, and never checking index usage. Key rules: Measure usage. Match operator classes. Drop unused indexes.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Monitoring Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: Index statistics show scans and tuple reads, helping identify unused or ineffective indexes. Key rules: Check idx_scan. Reset stats after changes. Correlate with query load.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Practical Tuning in a production query.
interview.answer: A disciplined tuning loop captures the query, reads its plan, adds the smallest useful index and measures again. Key rules: Capture the query. Read the plan. Add one index. Measure before and after.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Maintenance Plan in a production query.
interview.answer: A production index plan includes creation standards, usage review, bloat monitoring and safe removal of unused indexes. Key rules: Name consistently. Build concurrently. Review usage monthly. Drop with evidence.

debug.title: Wrong operator class
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX idx_title ON courses USING gin (title);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_title_fts ON courses USING gin (to_tsvector('english', title));
debug.error: data type text has no default operator class for access method "gin"

debug.title: BRIN on random data
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_brin ON students USING brin (marks);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks);
debug.error: BRIN is ineffective when values are not physically correlated

debug.title: Covering index wrong column
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_students_name ON students (marks) INCLUDE (email);
SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_name ON students (marks) INCLUDE (name);
debug.error: The requested column is not covered

debug.title: Partial predicate mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_high ON students (marks) WHERE marks > 90;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_high ON students (marks) WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.error: The query predicate does not imply the partial predicate

debug.title: Expression mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_lower ON students (LOWER(name));
SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE LOWER(name) = LOWER('Aarav');
debug.error: The expression index is not used by the plain predicate

debug.title: Invalid concurrent index
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_bad ON students (missing_column);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_bad ON students (marks);
debug.error: column "missing_column" does not exist

debug.title: Reindex in transaction
debug.fix: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_marks;
debug.error: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block

debug.title: Unused index
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;
debug.fix: Review the index and drop it only after confirming no query depends on it.
debug.error: The index still consumes writes and space

debug.title: Hash range query
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_marks_hash ON students USING hash (marks);
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_marks ON students (marks);
debug.error: The hash index cannot serve a range predicate

debug.title: Too many indexes
debug.fix: Keep only indexes used by real queries and verify with pg_stat_user_indexes.
debug.error: Every write maintains all indexes

modules.title: Query Optimization
modules.goal: Read plans, find the real bottleneck and improve queries with measurements.

topics.title: Optimization Process
topics.simple: Measure, read plan, change one thing, measure again.
topics.pro: Optimization starts with a slow query and its plan, not with guesses about indexes or configuration.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10;

topics.title: EXPLAIN
topics.simple: EXPLAIN plan estimates dikhata hai.
topics.pro: EXPLAIN shows access paths, joins and costs without executing the query.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;

topics.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
topics.simple: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actual runtime dikhata hai.
topics.pro: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports actual rows, loops and timing.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;

topics.title: Seq Scan
topics.simple: Seq scan poora table padhta hai.
topics.pro: A sequential scan reads every heap page and is often correct for small tables or large result fractions.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students;

topics.title: Index Scan
topics.simple: Index scan index se rows dhoondhta hai.
topics.pro: An index scan follows the index and fetches matching heap rows, ideal for selective predicates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Bitmap Heap Scan
topics.simple: Bitmap scan medium selectivity ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: A bitmap heap scan combines index matches and visits heap pages in physical order.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 70;

topics.title: Nested Loop
topics.simple: Nested loop small outer input ke liye achha hai.
topics.pro: A nested loop scans the inner side for each outer row, which is efficient when the outer set is small and the inner side is indexed.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE s.id = 1;

topics.title: Hash Join
topics.simple: Hash join large unsorted inputs ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: A hash join builds a hash table from one input and probes it with the other, avoiding repeated inner scans.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;

topics.title: Merge Join
topics.simple: Merge join sorted inputs ko merge karta hai.
topics.pro: A merge join reads both inputs in join-key order and merges them, often benefiting from indexes.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id ORDER BY s.id;

topics.title: Sort
topics.simple: Sort query ko order karta hai aur memory/disk use karta hai.
topics.pro: A Sort node appears when an index cannot provide the required order; large sorts spill to disk.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: HashAggregate
topics.simple: HashAggregate groups rows in memory.
topics.pro: A HashAggregate builds a hash table of groups, while GroupAggregate can use sorted input.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

topics.title: Statistics
topics.simple: Planner statistics estimates banane ke liye use hote hain.
topics.pro: Row estimates, distinct counts and histograms drive join order and access-path choices.

example.sql: SELECT attname, n_distinct FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'students';

topics.title: ANALYZE
topics.simple: ANALYZE statistics refresh karta hai.
topics.pro: ANALYZE samples table data and updates planner statistics without locking the table for long.

example.sql: ANALYZE students;

topics.title: Selectivity
topics.simple: Selectivity predicate ki filtering power hai.
topics.pro: High selectivity means few rows survive and usually favors an index; low selectivity favors a scan.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE email = 'a@example.com';

topics.title: CTE Materialization
topics.simple: CTE materialization plan ko badal sakta hai.
topics.pro: A materialized CTE is computed once and stored, which can help or hurt depending on reuse and row counts.

example.sql: EXPLAIN WITH avg_marks AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT AVG(marks) AS average FROM students) SELECT * FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > average;
example.output: A plan with a CTE Scan.

topics.title: Subquery Rewrites
topics.simple: Subquery ko join ya EXISTS me rewrite karo.
topics.pro: Correlated subqueries can become joins or semi-joins, often improving plans and avoiding repeated work.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

topics.title: Join Order
topics.simple: Join order planner choose karta hai.
topics.pro: The planner reorders joins based on statistics and cost; written order is not execution order.
points: Do not force order by nesting.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;

topics.title: Common Bottlenecks
topics.simple: Missing indexes, stale stats aur huge sorts common bottlenecks hain.
topics.pro: Most slow queries come from sequential scans on selective filters, bad estimates, missing join indexes or large sorts.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM enrollments ORDER BY enrolled_on DESC LIMIT 10;

topics.title: Benchmarking
topics.simple: Benchmark realistic data aur concurrency ke saath karo.
topics.pro: A benchmark needs realistic data volume, warm and cold cache runs, and concurrent load before it proves an improvement.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments;

topics.title: Practical Tuning
topics.simple: Slow query ko plan, index aur rewrite se tune karo.
topics.pro: A practical tuning loop documents the baseline, changes one thing, verifies the plan and measures the new runtime.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT s.name, COUNT(e.course_id) FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Optimization Process in a production query.
interview.answer: Optimization starts with a slow query and its plan, not with guesses about indexes or configuration. Key rules: Reproduce the query. Read the plan. Change one variable. Measure again.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain EXPLAIN in a production query.
interview.answer: EXPLAIN shows access paths, joins and costs without executing the query. Key rules: No execution. Estimates use statistics. Look for scans and sorts.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a production query.
interview.answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports actual rows, loops and timing. Key rules: It runs the query. Compare estimated and actual rows. Use BUFFERS for I/O detail.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Seq Scan in a production query.
interview.answer: A sequential scan reads every heap page and is often correct for small tables or large result fractions. Key rules: Good for large fractions. Bad for selective filters. Check table size.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Index Scan in a production query.
interview.answer: An index scan follows the index and fetches matching heap rows, ideal for selective predicates. Key rules: Good for few rows. Random I/O costs. Ordering may be free.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Bitmap Heap Scan in a production query.
interview.answer: A bitmap heap scan combines index matches and visits heap pages in physical order. Key rules: Good for medium selectivity. Combines indexes. Loses ordering.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Nested Loop in a production query.
interview.answer: A nested loop scans the inner side for each outer row, which is efficient when the outer set is small and the inner side is indexed. Key rules: Good for small outer sets. Index the inner join key. Watch loop counts.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Hash Join in a production query.
interview.answer: A hash join builds a hash table from one input and probes it with the other, avoiding repeated inner scans. Key rules: Good for large sets. Needs memory. No useful order.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Merge Join in a production query.
interview.answer: A merge join reads both inputs in join-key order and merges them, often benefiting from indexes. Key rules: Inputs must be sorted. Good for large ordered data. Can avoid a hash table.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Sort in a production query.
interview.answer: A Sort node appears when an index cannot provide the required order; large sorts spill to disk. Key rules: Watch sort method. Indexes can avoid sorts. LIMIT can reduce work.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain HashAggregate in a production query.
interview.answer: A HashAggregate builds a hash table of groups, while GroupAggregate can use sorted input. Key rules: Hash is common. Memory can spill. Sorted input favors GroupAggregate.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Statistics in a production query.
interview.answer: Row estimates, distinct counts and histograms drive join order and access-path choices. Key rules: Stale stats cause bad plans. ANALYZE refreshes them. Extended stats help correlations.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain ANALYZE in a production query.
interview.answer: ANALYZE samples table data and updates planner statistics without locking the table for long. Key rules: Run after large changes. It is cheap. Autovacuum does it automatically.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: High selectivity means few rows survive and usually favors an index; low selectivity favors a scan. Key rules: Unique predicates are selective. Planner estimates matter. Use real data.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain CTE Materialization in a production query.
interview.answer: A materialized CTE is computed once and stored, which can help or hurt depending on reuse and row counts. Key rules: MATERIALIZED forces it. NOT MATERIALIZED inlines it. Measure both.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Subquery Rewrites in a production query.
interview.answer: Correlated subqueries can become joins or semi-joins, often improving plans and avoiding repeated work. Key rules: EXISTS is a semi-join. JOIN can duplicate rows. Measure the rewrite.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Join Order in a production query.
interview.answer: The planner reorders joins based on statistics and cost; written order is not execution order. Key rules: Do not force order by nesting. Keep statistics fresh. Read the actual plan.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Common Bottlenecks in a production query.
interview.answer: Most slow queries come from sequential scans on selective filters, bad estimates, missing join indexes or large sorts. Key rules: Check scans. Check estimates. Check sorts.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Benchmarking in a production query.
interview.answer: A benchmark needs realistic data volume, warm and cold cache runs, and concurrent load before it proves an improvement. Key rules: Use real data size. Measure multiple runs. Watch concurrency.

interview.q: Module 27 · Explain Practical Tuning in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical tuning loop documents the baseline, changes one thing, verifies the plan and measures the new runtime. Key rules: Baseline first. Change one thing. Verify the plan. Record the result.

logic.answer: A materialized CTE is computed once and stored, which can help or hurt depending on reuse and row counts. MATERIALIZED forces it. NOT MATERIALIZED inlines it. Measure both.

debug.title: Stale statistics
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix:
ANALYZE students;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: The estimate may be far from reality

debug.title: Missing join index
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE s.id = 1;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student ON enrollments (student_id);
debug.error: The join repeatedly scans enrollments

debug.title: Sort without index
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 10;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks DESC);
debug.error: The query sorts the whole table

debug.title: Function on column
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@example.com';
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_lower_email ON students (LOWER(email));
debug.error: The plain email index is not used

debug.title: OR prevents index
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks = 90 OR name = 'Aarav';
debug.error: The OR may force a sequential scan

debug.title: Wide SELECT
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: Fetching every column increases I/O

debug.title: LIMIT without ORDER BY
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students LIMIT 10;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;
debug.error: The rows are arbitrary

debug.title: Nested loop explosion
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
debug.fix: Ensure both join keys are indexed and compare the plan at realistic volume.
debug.error: The inner side is scanned for every outer row

debug.title: CTE materialized unnecessarily
debug.broken: WITH big AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM enrollments) SELECT * FROM big WHERE course_id = 10;
debug.fix: WITH big AS NOT MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM enrollments) SELECT * FROM big WHERE course_id = 10;
debug.error: The CTE is fully materialized before filtering

debug.title: EXPLAIN without execution
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;

modules.title: Partitioning
modules.goal: Split large tables for pruning, maintenance and retention without breaking queries.

topics.title: Partitioning Basics
topics.simple: Partitioning table ko smaller pieces me todta hai.
topics.pro: A partitioned table routes rows into child partitions by a partition key, while queries use the parent name.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_partitioned (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Range Partitioning
topics.simple: Range partition values ke intervals banata hai.
topics.pro: Range partitioning assigns rows to partitions based on value ranges such as months or years.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_2026 PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2027-01-01');

topics.title: List Partitioning
topics.simple: List partition discrete values ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: List partitioning assigns rows to partitions by an explicit value list, such as region or status.
points: Each value belongs to one partition.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students_in PARTITION OF students PARTITION BY LIST (region);

topics.title: Hash Partitioning
topics.simple: Hash partition rows ko evenly distribute karta hai.
topics.pro: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and routes rows to a fixed number of partitions.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_hash PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);

topics.title: Partition Key
topics.simple: Partition key routing aur pruning decide karta hai.
topics.pro: The partition key determines which partition stores a row and which partitions a query can skip.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, created_at DATE NOT NULL, payload JSONB) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

topics.title: Partition Pruning
topics.simple: Pruning irrelevant partitions skip karta hai.
topics.pro: The planner prunes partitions whose bounds cannot match the query predicate, reducing scan work.
points: Use the partition key in predicates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on >= '2026-01-01';
example.output: A plan touching only matching partitions.

topics.title: Creating Partitions
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE PARTITION OF child banata hai.
topics.pro: A partition is created with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES ... and inherits the parent columns.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_2025 PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2026-01-01');

topics.title: Attaching Partitions
topics.simple: Existing table ko partition attach kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table after validating its rows against the bounds.
points: Use CHECK constraints to speed validation.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned ATTACH PARTITION enrollments_2025 FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2026-01-01');

topics.title: Detaching Partitions
topics.simple: DETACH PARTITION partition ko parent se alag karta hai.
topics.pro: DETACH PARTITION removes a child from the partitioned table while keeping its data as a standalone table.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned DETACH PARTITION enrollments_2025;

topics.title: Indexes on Partitions
topics.simple: Partitioned indexes parent par bhi bante hain.
topics.pro: Indexes created on the parent are propagated to partitions, and each child can also have its own indexes.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX enrollments_partitioned_student ON enrollments_partitioned (student_id);

topics.title: Constraints on Partitions
topics.simple: Partitioned tables constraints inherit karte hain.
topics.pro: CHECK, NOT NULL and foreign keys apply to partitions; unique constraints must include the partition key.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id, enrolled_on);

topics.title: Default Partition
topics.simple: Default partition unmatched rows ko catch karta hai.
topics.pro: A DEFAULT partition stores rows that match no other partition, preventing insert failures but hiding gaps.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_default PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned DEFAULT;

topics.title: Partition Maintenance
topics.simple: Old partitions detach aur archive karo.
topics.pro: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned DETACH PARTITION enrollments_2024;

topics.title: Partition vs Sharding
topics.simple: Partitioning ek database ke andar hota hai; sharding servers me.
topics.pro: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers.

example.sql: -- Partitioning keeps one connection and one catalog

topics.title: Common Partition Errors
topics.simple: Overlapping bounds, missing key aur no pruning common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key.
points: Include the key in unique constraints.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on >= '2026-01-01' AND enrolled_on < '2027-01-01';

topics.title: Partition Performance
topics.simple: Partitioning scan kam karta hai, planning badha sakta hai.
topics.pro: Partitioning helps when queries prune and maintenance targets individual partitions, but too many partitions increase planning and catalog overhead.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on = '2026-05-01';

topics.title: Monitoring Partitions
topics.simple: Partition sizes aur row counts monitor karo.
topics.pro: Monitor child sizes and growth so retention and vacuum keep up with the workload.

example.sql: SELECT relname, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname LIKE 'enrollments_%';

topics.title: Time Partitioning
topics.simple: Time-based range partitioning common pattern hai.
topics.pro: Monthly or yearly partitions make retention and time-range queries cheap.
points: Keep a default only as a safety net.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_2026_01 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-02-01');

topics.title: Subpartitioning
topics.simple: Partition ko further partition kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A partition can itself be partitioned, enabling multi-level strategies such as year then region.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_2026 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2027-01-01') PARTITION BY LIST (region);

topics.title: Practical Partitioning
topics.simple: Partition key ko query pattern se choose karo.
topics.pro: Choose a key that appears in common filters and supports retention, then verify pruning with EXPLAIN.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01';

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partitioning Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A partitioned table routes rows into child partitions by a partition key, while queries use the parent name. Key rules: The parent is logical. Partitions are physical. The key controls routing.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Range Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Range partitioning assigns rows to partitions based on value ranges such as months or years. Key rules: Good for dates. Boundaries are explicit. A default partition catches gaps.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain List Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: List partitioning assigns rows to partitions by an explicit value list, such as region or status. Key rules: Good for categories. Each value belongs to one partition. Unknown values need a default.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Hash Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and routes rows to a fixed number of partitions. Key rules: Good for even distribution. No natural range pruning. Choose a stable key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Key in a production query.
interview.answer: The partition key determines which partition stores a row and which partitions a query can skip. Key rules: Choose a common filter. Keep it immutable. Include it in primary keys.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Pruning in a production query.
interview.answer: The planner prunes partitions whose bounds cannot match the query predicate, reducing scan work. Key rules: Use the partition key in predicates. Avoid functions on the key. Check EXPLAIN.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Creating Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: A partition is created with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES ... and inherits the parent columns. Key rules: Create before inserting. Bounds must not overlap. Use a default partition carefully.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Attaching Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table after validating its rows against the bounds. Key rules: Validate the data first. It can lock. Use CHECK constraints to speed validation.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Detaching Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: DETACH PARTITION removes a child from the partitioned table while keeping its data as a standalone table. Key rules: It is useful for retention. CONCURRENTLY reduces locking. The table remains.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Indexes on Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: Indexes created on the parent are propagated to partitions, and each child can also have its own indexes. Key rules: Create on the parent. Check child indexes. Unique indexes need the key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Constraints on Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: CHECK, NOT NULL and foreign keys apply to partitions; unique constraints must include the partition key. Key rules: Primary keys include the key. Foreign keys work per partition. Validation can be costly.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Default Partition in a production query.
interview.answer: A DEFAULT partition stores rows that match no other partition, preventing insert failures but hiding gaps. Key rules: It catches mistakes. It can grow large. Move rows before adding bounds.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE. Key rules: Detach old data. Archive externally. Drop when safe.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition vs Sharding in a production query.
interview.answer: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers. Key rules: Partitioning is local. Sharding is distributed. Both need a key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Common Partition Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key. Key rules: Keep bounds disjoint. Filter the key. Include the key in unique constraints.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Partitioning helps when queries prune and maintenance targets individual partitions, but too many partitions increase planning and catalog overhead. Key rules: Prune aggressively. Avoid hundreds of tiny partitions. Measure planning time.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Monitoring Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: Monitor child sizes and growth so retention and vacuum keep up with the workload. Key rules: Check reltuples. Watch default partition growth. Automate new partitions.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Time Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Monthly or yearly partitions make retention and time-range queries cheap. Key rules: Create future partitions. Detach old ones. Keep a default only as a safety net.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Subpartitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: A partition can itself be partitioned, enabling multi-level strategies such as year then region. Key rules: Use sparingly. More levels increase planning. Keep pruning keys aligned.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Practical Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Choose a key that appears in common filters and supports retention, then verify pruning with EXPLAIN. Key rules: Match query filters. Plan retention. Test pruning. Monitor growth.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partitioning Basics matter?
logic.answer: A partitioned table routes rows into child partitions by a partition key, while queries use the parent name. The parent is logical. Partitions are physical. The key controls routing.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Range Partitioning matter?
logic.answer: Range partitioning assigns rows to partitions based on value ranges such as months or years. Good for dates. Boundaries are explicit. A default partition catches gaps.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does List Partitioning matter?
logic.answer: List partitioning assigns rows to partitions by an explicit value list, such as region or status. Good for categories. Each value belongs to one partition. Unknown values need a default.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Hash Partitioning matter?
logic.answer: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and routes rows to a fixed number of partitions. Good for even distribution. No natural range pruning. Choose a stable key.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partition Key matter?
logic.answer: The partition key determines which partition stores a row and which partitions a query can skip. Choose a common filter. Keep it immutable. Include it in primary keys.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partition Pruning matter?
logic.answer: The planner prunes partitions whose bounds cannot match the query predicate, reducing scan work. Use the partition key in predicates. Avoid functions on the key. Check EXPLAIN.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Creating Partitions matter?
logic.answer: A partition is created with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES ... and inherits the parent columns. Create before inserting. Bounds must not overlap. Use a default partition carefully.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Attaching Partitions matter?
logic.answer: ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table after validating its rows against the bounds. Validate the data first. It can lock. Use CHECK constraints to speed validation.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Detaching Partitions matter?
logic.answer: DETACH PARTITION removes a child from the partitioned table while keeping its data as a standalone table. It is useful for retention. CONCURRENTLY reduces locking. The table remains.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Indexes on Partitions matter?
logic.answer: Indexes created on the parent are propagated to partitions, and each child can also have its own indexes. Create on the parent. Check child indexes. Unique indexes need the key.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Constraints on Partitions matter?
logic.answer: CHECK, NOT NULL and foreign keys apply to partitions; unique constraints must include the partition key. Primary keys include the key. Foreign keys work per partition. Validation can be costly.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Default Partition matter?
logic.answer: A DEFAULT partition stores rows that match no other partition, preventing insert failures but hiding gaps. It catches mistakes. It can grow large. Move rows before adding bounds.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partition Maintenance matter?
logic.answer: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE. Detach old data. Archive externally. Drop when safe.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partition vs Sharding matter?
logic.answer: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers. Partitioning is local. Sharding is distributed. Both need a key.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Common Partition Errors matter?
logic.answer: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key. Keep bounds disjoint. Filter the key. Include the key in unique constraints.

debug.title: Overlapping bounds
debug.broken:
CREATE TABLE p1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-07-01');
CREATE TABLE p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-06-01') TO ('2027-01-01');
debug.fix: CREATE TABLE p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-07-01') TO ('2027-01-01');
debug.error: partition "p2" would overlap partition "p1"

debug.title: No partition for row
debug.broken: INSERT INTO events (id, created_at) VALUES (1, '2028-01-01');
debug.fix: CREATE TABLE events_2028 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2028-01-01') TO ('2029-01-01');
debug.error: no partition of relation "events" found for row

debug.title: Unique key missing partition column
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE events ADD PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at);
debug.error: unique constraint on partitioned table must include all partition key columns

debug.title: Function blocks pruning
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) = '2026-01-01';
debug.fix: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01';
debug.error: The function on the key prevents partition pruning

debug.title: Default partition growth
debug.broken: CREATE TABLE events_default PARTITION OF events DEFAULT;
debug.fix: Create explicit partitions for expected ranges and keep the default as a temporary safety net.
debug.error: The default partition accumulates unexpected rows

debug.title: Attach without validation
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION old_events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');
debug.fix:
ALTER TABLE old_events ADD CONSTRAINT old_events_check CHECK (created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01');
ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION old_events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');
debug.error: The attach scans and locks to validate rows

debug.title: Detach missing partition
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024 CONCURRENTLY;
debug.error: A normal detach can block concurrent work

debug.title: Query misses key
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id = 1;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id = 1 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01';
debug.error: The query scans every partition

debug.title: Too many partitions
debug.broken: CREATE TABLE events_2026_01_01 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-01-02');
debug.fix: Use monthly partitions instead of daily partitions unless the workload truly needs daily pruning.
debug.error: Planning and catalog overhead grows

debug.title: Drop parent
debug.broken: DROP TABLE events;
debug.fix: DROP TABLE events CASCADE;
debug.error: cannot drop table events because other objects depend on it
debug.expected: The partitioned table and children are removed.

modules.title: Security and Permissions
modules.goal: Give each role only the access it needs and keep privileged code defensible.

topics.title: Roles
topics.simple: Role user ya group ka identity hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL roles represent both login users and privilege groups, and roles can be members of other roles.
points: Roles can log in or own objects.

example.sql: CREATE ROLE app_read NOLOGIN;

topics.title: CREATE ROLE
topics.simple: CREATE ROLE naya role banata hai.
topics.pro: CREATE ROLE defines a role with optional LOGIN, PASSWORD, VALID UNTIL and connection limits.

example.sql: CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';

topics.title: GRANT
topics.simple: GRANT privileges deta hai.
topics.pro: GRANT assigns object or role privileges such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, USAGE and EXECUTE.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON students TO app_read;

topics.title: REVOKE
topics.simple: REVOKE privileges wapas leta hai.
topics.pro: REVOKE removes previously granted privileges and can cascade through role membership.

example.sql: REVOKE DELETE ON students FROM app_read;

topics.title: Object Privileges
topics.simple: Tables, sequences aur functions ke apne privileges hote hain.
topics.pro: Object privileges control specific actions on tables, sequences, functions and views.

example.sql: GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCE students_id_seq TO app_user;

topics.title: Schema Privileges
topics.simple: Schema USAGE objects tak access deta hai.
topics.pro: A role needs USAGE on a schema before it can reference objects inside it.

example.sql: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_read;

topics.title: Default Privileges
topics.simple: Default privileges future objects ke liye apply hote hain.
topics.pro: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES sets grants for objects created later by a specific role.

example.sql: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO app_read;

topics.title: Row-Level Security
topics.simple: RLS row-level access control deta hai.
topics.pro: Row-level security adds policies that filter rows per role, even when the table privilege is granted.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

topics.title: RLS Policies
topics.simple: Policy batati hai kaunsi rows dikhengi.
topics.pro: A policy uses USING for visibility and WITH CHECK for writes, scoped by command and role.

example.sql: CREATE POLICY student_self ON students FOR SELECT USING (id = current_setting('app.user_id')::bigint);

topics.title: Security Definer
topics.simple: SECURITY DEFINER owner ke rights se chalta hai.
topics.pro: A security definer function runs with the owner’s privileges, so it must validate inputs and fix search_path.

example.sql: CREATE FUNCTION admin_count() RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; $$;

topics.title: Search Path
topics.simple: Search path unqualified names resolve karta hai.
topics.pro: A mutable search_path lets a caller shadow functions or tables, so privileged routines should pin it.
points: Avoid SECURITY DEFINER with user schemas.

example.sql: SET search_path = public, pg_temp;

topics.title: Least Privilege
topics.simple: Har role ko sirf zaroori access do.
topics.pro: Least privilege limits blast radius: read-only roles read, writers write only their tables, and admin access is rare.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON students, courses TO app_read;

topics.title: Auditing
topics.simple: Sensitive actions log karo.
topics.pro: Audit logs record who accessed or changed sensitive data, using triggers, pgAudit or application logs.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE access_log (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, actor TEXT, action TEXT, at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

topics.title: Encryption
topics.simple: Data at rest aur in transit encrypt karo.
topics.pro: TLS protects connections, while disk encryption and column-level encryption protect stored data.
points: Hash passwords, never encrypt them reversibly.

example.sql: SHOW ssl;

topics.title: Secrets
topics.simple: Passwords aur keys code me na rakho.
topics.pro: Secrets belong in a secret manager or environment, rotated regularly and never committed to source control.

example.sql: -- Store the password in a secret manager, not in SQL or Git

topics.title: Common Security Errors
topics.simple: Public grants, shared accounts aur unsafe definer functions common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are leaving PUBLIC privileges, sharing one login for all users, and creating SECURITY DEFINER functions with a mutable search_path.

example.sql: REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;

topics.title: Application Role
topics.simple: App ka dedicated limited role hona chahiye.
topics.pro: The application connects with a role that has only the DML and sequence rights it needs, not superuser.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON students, courses, enrollments TO app_user;

topics.title: Read-Only Role
topics.simple: Reporting role ko SELECT-only access do.
topics.pro: A read-only role can query approved views without changing data.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON enrollment_report TO reporting_role;

topics.title: Monitoring Access
topics.simple: Privilege changes monitor karo.
topics.pro: Review role memberships, grants and failed logins so unexpected access is caught early.

example.sql: SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcanlogin FROM pg_roles;

topics.title: Practical Hardening
topics.simple: Roles, RLS, TLS aur least privilege ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A hardened database uses separate roles, minimal grants, RLS for tenant data, TLS and audited privileged functions.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Roles in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL roles represent both login users and privilege groups, and roles can be members of other roles. Key rules: Roles can log in or own objects. Membership inherits privileges. Use groups for shared access.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain CREATE ROLE in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE ROLE defines a role with optional LOGIN, PASSWORD, VALID UNTIL and connection limits. Key rules: Use LOGIN for users. Use NOLOGIN for groups. Never share human accounts.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain GRANT in a production query.
interview.answer: GRANT assigns object or role privileges such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, USAGE and EXECUTE. Key rules: Grant the minimum. Revoke PUBLIC defaults. Grant on schemas too.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain REVOKE in a production query.
interview.answer: REVOKE removes previously granted privileges and can cascade through role membership. Key rules: Revoke unused access. Check dependencies. CASCADE removes dependent grants.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Object Privileges in a production query.
interview.answer: Object privileges control specific actions on tables, sequences, functions and views. Key rules: Sequences need USAGE. Functions need EXECUTE. Views can hide base tables.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Schema Privileges in a production query.
interview.answer: A role needs USAGE on a schema before it can reference objects inside it. Key rules: USAGE allows name resolution. CREATE allows new objects. Grant schema access deliberately.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Default Privileges in a production query.
interview.answer: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES sets grants for objects created later by a specific role. Key rules: It affects future objects. It is role-specific. Existing objects need explicit grants.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Row-Level Security in a production query.
interview.answer: Row-level security adds policies that filter rows per role, even when the table privilege is granted. Key rules: Enable RLS on the table. Write policies per command. Owners bypass RLS unless forced.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain RLS Policies in a production query.
interview.answer: A policy uses USING for visibility and WITH CHECK for writes, scoped by command and role. Key rules: USING filters reads. WITH CHECK validates writes. Policies combine permissively by default.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Security Definer in a production query.
interview.answer: A security definer function runs with the owner’s privileges, so it must validate inputs and fix search_path. Key rules: Use sparingly. Set search_path. Do not expose arbitrary SQL.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Search Path in a production query.
interview.answer: A mutable search_path lets a caller shadow functions or tables, so privileged routines should pin it. Key rules: Set search_path explicitly. Qualify objects. Avoid SECURITY DEFINER with user schemas.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Least Privilege in a production query.
interview.answer: Least privilege limits blast radius: read-only roles read, writers write only their tables, and admin access is rare. Key rules: Start with no access. Grant explicitly. Review regularly.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Auditing in a production query.
interview.answer: Audit logs record who accessed or changed sensitive data, using triggers, pgAudit or application logs. Key rules: Log access and changes. Protect the audit log. Retain per policy.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Encryption in a production query.
interview.answer: TLS protects connections, while disk encryption and column-level encryption protect stored data. Key rules: Use TLS. Encrypt disks. Hash passwords, never encrypt them reversibly.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Secrets in a production query.
interview.answer: Secrets belong in a secret manager or environment, rotated regularly and never committed to source control. Key rules: Do not hardcode secrets. Rotate credentials. Limit who can read them.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Common Security Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are leaving PUBLIC privileges, sharing one login for all users, and creating SECURITY DEFINER functions with a mutable search_path. Key rules: Revoke PUBLIC. Use individual accounts. Pin search_path.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Application Role in a production query.
interview.answer: The application connects with a role that has only the DML and sequence rights it needs, not superuser. Key rules: No superuser. Only needed tables. Separate read and write roles.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Read-Only Role in a production query.
interview.answer: A read-only role can query approved views without changing data. Key rules: Grant SELECT only. Use views for column limits. Set statement timeout.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Monitoring Access in a production query.
interview.answer: Review role memberships, grants and failed logins so unexpected access is caught early. Key rules: Review grants. Alert on failures. Track role changes.

interview.q: Module 29 · Explain Practical Hardening in a production query.
interview.answer: A hardened database uses separate roles, minimal grants, RLS for tenant data, TLS and audited privileged functions. Key rules: Separate roles. Minimal grants. RLS for tenants. Audit privileged actions.
