logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Roles matter?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL roles represent both login users and privilege groups, and roles can be members of other roles. Roles can log in or own objects. Membership inherits privileges. Use groups for shared access.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does CREATE ROLE matter?
logic.answer: CREATE ROLE defines a role with optional LOGIN, PASSWORD, VALID UNTIL and connection limits. Use LOGIN for users. Use NOLOGIN for groups. Never share human accounts.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does GRANT matter?
logic.answer: GRANT assigns object or role privileges such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, USAGE and EXECUTE. Grant the minimum. Revoke PUBLIC defaults. Grant on schemas too.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does REVOKE matter?
logic.answer: REVOKE removes previously granted privileges and can cascade through role membership. Revoke unused access. Check dependencies. CASCADE removes dependent grants.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Object Privileges matter?
logic.answer: Object privileges control specific actions on tables, sequences, functions and views. Sequences need USAGE. Functions need EXECUTE. Views can hide base tables.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Schema Privileges matter?
logic.answer: A role needs USAGE on a schema before it can reference objects inside it. USAGE allows name resolution. CREATE allows new objects. Grant schema access deliberately.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Default Privileges matter?
logic.answer: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES sets grants for objects created later by a specific role. It affects future objects. It is role-specific. Existing objects need explicit grants.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Row-Level Security matter?
logic.answer: Row-level security adds policies that filter rows per role, even when the table privilege is granted. Enable RLS on the table. Write policies per command. Owners bypass RLS unless forced.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does RLS Policies matter?
logic.answer: A policy uses USING for visibility and WITH CHECK for writes, scoped by command and role. USING filters reads. WITH CHECK validates writes. Policies combine permissively by default.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Security Definer matter?
logic.answer: A security definer function runs with the owner’s privileges, so it must validate inputs and fix search_path. Use sparingly. Set search_path. Do not expose arbitrary SQL.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Search Path matter?
logic.answer: A mutable search_path lets a caller shadow functions or tables, so privileged routines should pin it. Set search_path explicitly. Qualify objects. Avoid SECURITY DEFINER with user schemas.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Least Privilege matter?
logic.answer: Least privilege limits blast radius: read-only roles read, writers write only their tables, and admin access is rare. Start with no access. Grant explicitly. Review regularly.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Auditing matter?
logic.answer: Audit logs record who accessed or changed sensitive data, using triggers, pgAudit or application logs. Log access and changes. Protect the audit log. Retain per policy.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Encryption matter?
logic.answer: TLS protects connections, while disk encryption and column-level encryption protect stored data. Use TLS. Encrypt disks. Hash passwords, never encrypt them reversibly.

logic.q: Module 29 · Why does Secrets matter?
logic.answer: Secrets belong in a secret manager or environment, rotated regularly and never committed to source control. Do not hardcode secrets. Rotate credentials. Limit who can read them.

debug.title: PUBLIC schema access
debug.broken: GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA public TO PUBLIC;
debug.fix:
REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_user;
debug.error: Every role can create objects in public

debug.title: Shared login
debug.broken: CREATE ROLE app LOGIN PASSWORD 'shared';
debug.fix: Create one role per application or user and rotate credentials.
debug.error: Actions cannot be attributed to a person

debug.title: Superuser app
debug.broken: GRANT app_user TO app;
debug.fix: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON students TO app;
debug.error: The application can do anything

debug.title: RLS not enabled
debug.broken: CREATE POLICY p ON students USING (id = 1);
debug.fix:
ALTER TABLE students ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY p ON students USING (id = 1);
debug.error: The policy has no effect until RLS is enabled

debug.title: Owner bypasses RLS
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
debug.error: The table owner still bypasses policies
debug.expected: Policies apply to the owner too.

debug.title: Definer search path
debug.broken: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS void LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER AS $$ SELECT 1; $$;
debug.fix: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS void LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT 1; $$;
debug.error: A caller-controlled search_path can hijack names

debug.title: Missing sequence grant
debug.broken: GRANT INSERT ON students TO app_user;
debug.fix:
GRANT INSERT ON students TO app_user;
GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCE students_id_seq TO app_user;
debug.error: permission denied for sequence students_id_seq
debug.expected: Inserts can use the identity sequence.

debug.title: Revoke without schema
debug.broken: REVOKE SELECT ON students FROM app_read;
debug.fix:
REVOKE SELECT ON students FROM app_read;
REVOKE USAGE ON SCHEMA public FROM app_read;
debug.error: The role can still resolve objects it cannot read

debug.title: Password in code
debug.broken: CREATE ROLE app LOGIN PASSWORD 'secret';
debug.fix: Create the role without a literal password and set it from a secret manager.
debug.error: The password is exposed in logs and source

debug.title: Default privileges missed
debug.broken: GRANT SELECT ON students TO app_read;
debug.fix: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO app_read;
debug.error: Future tables are not readable

modules.title: SQL Injection and Safe Querying
modules.goal: Treat every input as untrusted and keep SQL structure separate from data.

topics.title: Injection Basics
topics.simple: Injection input ko SQL code banata hai.
topics.pro: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a query and changes its structure.
points: Every database API is a boundary.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav' OR '1'='1';
example.output: The OR makes the predicate always true.

topics.title: String Concatenation
topics.simple: Input ko query string me jodna dangerous hai.
topics.pro: Concatenating user input into SQL lets quotes and operators escape the intended value.

example.sql: query = "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = '" + input + "'";

topics.title: Prepared Statements
topics.simple: Prepared statements query structure fix karte hain.
topics.pro: A prepared statement parses the SQL once and supplies values separately, so input cannot change the structure.

example.sql:
PREPARE find_student (text) AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;
EXECUTE find_student('Aarav');

topics.title: Parameterized Queries
topics.simple: Placeholders values ko safely bind karte hain.
topics.pro: Parameterized queries use $1, ? or named placeholders supplied by the driver, never string interpolation.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;

topics.title: ORM Safety
topics.simple: ORM raw fragments aur unsafe order clauses se bachna.
topics.pro: ORMs are safe for normal bound values but can expose injection through raw SQL, order-by strings and identifier interpolation.

example.sql: Student.where("name = ?", input)

topics.title: Identifier Quoting
topics.simple: Identifiers ko quote karo, values ko bind.
topics.pro: Identifiers cannot be parameterized like values; validate them against an allowlist and quote them correctly.
points: Do not quote values as identifiers.

example.sql: SELECT quote_ident('students');

topics.title: Dynamic SQL
topics.simple: Dynamic SQL identifiers ke liye allowlist use karo.
topics.pro: When a table or column must be dynamic, build it from a fixed allowlist and use format with %I for identifiers.

example.sql: EXECUTE format('SELECT * FROM %I WHERE id = $1', table_name) USING student_id;

topics.title: Input Validation
topics.simple: Validation format check karta hai, injection stop nahi karta.
topics.pro: Validation improves data quality but is not a substitute for parameterization because valid input can still contain SQL syntax.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE email = $1;

topics.title: Least Privilege
topics.simple: Database role ko minimum rights do.
topics.pro: A compromised query can do less damage when the application role cannot drop tables or read unrelated schemas.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON students TO app_user;

topics.title: Error Leakage
topics.simple: Errors me schema details leak na karo.
topics.pro: Detailed database errors help attackers map tables and columns; return a generic message and log the detail server-side.

example.sql: ERROR: relation "students" does not exist
example.output: A message that should not reach the client.

topics.title: Stored Procedure Safety
topics.simple: Procedures bhi dynamic SQL se vulnerable ho sakti hain.
topics.pro: PL/pgSQL EXECUTE with concatenated input is injection-prone; use USING and format %I.

example.sql: EXECUTE format('SELECT * FROM %I WHERE id = $1', table_name) USING student_id;

topics.title: Escaping Is Not Enough
topics.simple: Manual escaping fragile hota hai.
topics.pro: Escaping depends on the database, encoding and context; parameterization removes the need to escape values at all.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;

topics.title: Second-Order Injection
topics.simple: Stored input baad me query me unsafe use ho sakta hai.
topics.pro: Second-order injection occurs when safely stored data is later concatenated into dynamic SQL without binding.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;

topics.title: Common Injection Patterns
topics.simple: OR 1=1, UNION aur comment tricks common hain.
topics.pro: Classic payloads alter predicates, append UNION queries or comment out the rest of the statement.

example.output: A payload that must remain data.

topics.title: Testing for Injection
topics.simple: Quotes, comments aur boolean payloads se test karo.
topics.pro: Security tests should confirm that quotes, UNION and time-based payloads are treated as literal data.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;
example.output: A query that treats the payload as text.

topics.title: Logging
topics.simple: Queries log karo but secrets redact karo.
topics.pro: Slow-query and audit logs help detect attacks, but they must not store passwords or tokens.

example.sql: ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = 1000;

topics.title: WAF Is Not Enough
topics.simple: WAF layer help karta hai, root fix parameterization hai.
topics.pro: A web application firewall can block known payloads but cannot repair unsafe SQL or second-order paths.
points: Use WAF as defense in depth.

example.sql: -- Parameterize the query; the WAF is only an extra layer

topics.title: Safe Query Review
topics.simple: Review me string building aur dynamic SQL dhoondo.
topics.pro: A safe-query review looks for concatenation, raw SQL, dynamic identifiers and privileged roles.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = $1;

topics.title: Safe JSON and Arrays
topics.simple: JSON input ko parse karo, SQL me string na jodo.
topics.pro: JSON and array inputs should be bound as values or parsed with typed functions, not interpolated into SQL.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> $1::jsonb;

topics.title: Practical Secure Query
topics.simple: Static SQL, bound values, allowlisted identifiers aur limited role.
topics.pro: A secure query keeps structure static, binds all data, validates identifiers against an allowlist and runs with least privilege.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE email = $1;

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Injection Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a query and changes its structure. Key rules: Input must not become code. Parameters separate data. Every database API is a boundary.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain String Concatenation in a production query.
interview.answer: Concatenating user input into SQL lets quotes and operators escape the intended value. Key rules: Avoid building SQL with + or ||. Use placeholders. Never trust client validation.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Prepared Statements in a production query.
interview.answer: A prepared statement parses the SQL once and supplies values separately, so input cannot change the structure. Key rules: Parse first. Bind values later. Use the driver API.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Parameterized Queries in a production query.
interview.answer: Parameterized queries use $1, ? or named placeholders supplied by the driver, never string interpolation. Key rules: Use $1 in PostgreSQL. Bind every value. Do not concatenate identifiers.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain ORM Safety in a production query.
interview.answer: ORMs are safe for normal bound values but can expose injection through raw SQL, order-by strings and identifier interpolation. Key rules: Prefer the query builder. Bind raw fragments. Whitelist sort columns.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Identifier Quoting in a production query.
interview.answer: Identifiers cannot be parameterized like values; validate them against an allowlist and quote them correctly. Key rules: Use quote_ident in dynamic SQL. Allowlist table and column names. Do not quote values as identifiers.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Dynamic SQL in a production query.
interview.answer: When a table or column must be dynamic, build it from a fixed allowlist and use format with %I for identifiers. Key rules: Use format with %I. Allowlist names. Bind values separately.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Input Validation in a production query.
interview.answer: Validation improves data quality but is not a substitute for parameterization because valid input can still contain SQL syntax. Key rules: Validate type and length. Still bind values. Never rely on validation alone.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Least Privilege in a production query.
interview.answer: A compromised query can do less damage when the application role cannot drop tables or read unrelated schemas. Key rules: No superuser. Grant only needed tables. Separate admin access.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Error Leakage in a production query.
interview.answer: Detailed database errors help attackers map tables and columns; return a generic message and log the detail server-side. Key rules: Log internally. Show generic errors. Do not echo SQL.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Stored Procedure Safety in a production query.
interview.answer: PL/pgSQL EXECUTE with concatenated input is injection-prone; use USING and format %I. Key rules: Bind with USING. Quote identifiers with %I. Validate allowlists.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Escaping Is Not Enough in a production query.
interview.answer: Escaping depends on the database, encoding and context; parameterization removes the need to escape values at all. Key rules: Do not hand-roll escaping. Use driver parameters. Keep SQL structure static.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Second-Order Injection in a production query.
interview.answer: Second-order injection occurs when safely stored data is later concatenated into dynamic SQL without binding. Key rules: Treat stored data as untrusted. Bind on every use. Audit dynamic reporting tools.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Common Injection Patterns in a production query.
interview.answer: Classic payloads alter predicates, append UNION queries or comment out the rest of the statement. Key rules: Never concatenate. Test with quotes and operators. Use allowlists.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Testing for Injection in a production query.
interview.answer: Security tests should confirm that quotes, UNION and time-based payloads are treated as literal data. Key rules: Test quote handling. Test UNION. Test boolean and time payloads.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Logging in a production query.
interview.answer: Slow-query and audit logs help detect attacks, but they must not store passwords or tokens. Key rules: Log parameters carefully. Redact secrets. Alert on patterns.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain WAF Is Not Enough in a production query.
interview.answer: A web application firewall can block known payloads but cannot repair unsafe SQL or second-order paths. Key rules: Use WAF as defense in depth. Fix the query. Do not rely on signatures.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Safe Query Review in a production query.
interview.answer: A safe-query review looks for concatenation, raw SQL, dynamic identifiers and privileged roles. Key rules: Search for string building. Check raw ORM calls. Verify allowlists.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Safe JSON and Arrays in a production query.
interview.answer: JSON and array inputs should be bound as values or parsed with typed functions, not interpolated into SQL. Key rules: Bind JSON as a parameter. Use jsonb operators. Validate shape.

interview.q: Module 30 · Explain Practical Secure Query in a production query.
interview.answer: A secure query keeps structure static, binds all data, validates identifiers against an allowlist and runs with least privilege. Key rules: Static structure. Bound values. Allowlisted identifiers. Least privilege.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Injection Basics matter?
logic.answer: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a query and changes its structure. Input must not become code. Parameters separate data. Every database API is a boundary.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does String Concatenation matter?
logic.answer: Concatenating user input into SQL lets quotes and operators escape the intended value. Avoid building SQL with + or ||. Use placeholders. Never trust client validation.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Prepared Statements matter?
logic.answer: A prepared statement parses the SQL once and supplies values separately, so input cannot change the structure. Parse first. Bind values later. Use the driver API.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Parameterized Queries matter?
logic.answer: Parameterized queries use $1, ? or named placeholders supplied by the driver, never string interpolation. Use $1 in PostgreSQL. Bind every value. Do not concatenate identifiers.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does ORM Safety matter?
logic.answer: ORMs are safe for normal bound values but can expose injection through raw SQL, order-by strings and identifier interpolation. Prefer the query builder. Bind raw fragments. Whitelist sort columns.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Identifier Quoting matter?
logic.answer: Identifiers cannot be parameterized like values; validate them against an allowlist and quote them correctly. Use quote_ident in dynamic SQL. Allowlist table and column names. Do not quote values as identifiers.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Dynamic SQL matter?
logic.answer: When a table or column must be dynamic, build it from a fixed allowlist and use format with %I for identifiers. Use format with %I. Allowlist names. Bind values separately.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Input Validation matter?
logic.answer: Validation improves data quality but is not a substitute for parameterization because valid input can still contain SQL syntax. Validate type and length. Still bind values. Never rely on validation alone.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Least Privilege matter?
logic.answer: A compromised query can do less damage when the application role cannot drop tables or read unrelated schemas. No superuser. Grant only needed tables. Separate admin access.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Error Leakage matter?
logic.answer: Detailed database errors help attackers map tables and columns; return a generic message and log the detail server-side. Log internally. Show generic errors. Do not echo SQL.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Stored Procedure Safety matter?
logic.answer: PL/pgSQL EXECUTE with concatenated input is injection-prone; use USING and format %I. Bind with USING. Quote identifiers with %I. Validate allowlists.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Escaping Is Not Enough matter?
logic.answer: Escaping depends on the database, encoding and context; parameterization removes the need to escape values at all. Do not hand-roll escaping. Use driver parameters. Keep SQL structure static.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Second-Order Injection matter?
logic.answer: Second-order injection occurs when safely stored data is later concatenated into dynamic SQL without binding. Treat stored data as untrusted. Bind on every use. Audit dynamic reporting tools.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Common Injection Patterns matter?
logic.answer: Classic payloads alter predicates, append UNION queries or comment out the rest of the statement. Never concatenate. Test with quotes and operators. Use allowlists.

logic.q: Module 30 · Why does Testing for Injection matter?
logic.answer: Security tests should confirm that quotes, UNION and time-based payloads are treated as literal data. Test quote handling. Test UNION. Test boolean and time payloads.

debug.title: Classic concatenation
debug.broken: query = "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = '" + name + "'";
debug.fix: query = "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1"; values = [name];
debug.error: The input can change the predicate

debug.title: UNION payload
debug.broken: input = "' UNION SELECT password FROM users --";
debug.fix: Bind input as a value; never concatenate it into SQL.
debug.error: The attacker appends a second result set

debug.title: ORDER BY injection
debug.broken: query = "SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY " + sort;
debug.fix: Allowlist sort columns and use quote_ident, e.g. ORDER BY id.
debug.error: ORDER BY cannot be a bound value

debug.title: Table name injection
debug.broken: query = "SELECT * FROM " + table;
debug.fix: Allowlist the table name and quote it with format('%I', table).
debug.error: The table name changes the statement

debug.title: Escaping alone
debug.broken: query = "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = '" + input.replace(/'/g, "''") + "'";
debug.fix: Use a parameter instead of manual escaping.
debug.error: Encoding and context can defeat the escape

debug.title: Error leak
debug.broken: Return the raw PostgreSQL error to the browser.
debug.fix: Log the error server-side and return a generic message.
debug.error: The schema and SQL are exposed

debug.title: Procedure concatenation
debug.broken: EXECUTE 'SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = ' || student_id;
debug.fix: EXECUTE 'SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = $1' USING student_id;
debug.error: The input becomes SQL

debug.title: Second-order injection
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = '" || stored_name || "'";
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = $1;
debug.error: Stored data is still untrusted

debug.title: Overprivileged app
debug.broken: GRANT ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO app_user;
debug.fix: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON students TO app_user;
debug.error: A compromised query can touch every table

debug.title: Dynamic identifier unquoted
debug.broken: EXECUTE 'SELECT * FROM ' || table_name;
debug.fix: EXECUTE format('SELECT * FROM %I', table_name);
debug.error: A crafted identifier breaks the statement

modules.title: Migrations and Schema Evolution
modules.goal: Change production schemas safely, reversibly and without long locks.

topics.title: Migration Basics
topics.simple: Migration schema change ko versioned step me badalta hai.
topics.pro: A migration is a versioned, repeatable change applied in order to every environment.

example.sql:
-- 001_add_student_email.sql
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;

topics.title: Versioned Migrations
topics.simple: Migration files ka ordered history hota hai.
topics.pro: A migration tool records applied versions so each change runs once per environment.

example.sql: SELECT version, applied_at FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY version;

topics.title: Up and Down
topics.simple: Forward aur rollback migration likho.
topics.pro: An up migration applies the change and a down migration reverses it when safe.

example.sql:
-- up: ADD COLUMN email TEXT
-- down: DROP COLUMN email

topics.title: Idempotency
topics.simple: Migration dobara chalne par safe hona chahiye.
topics.pro: Idempotent migrations use IF NOT EXISTS and guards so a retry does not fail halfway.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS email TEXT;

topics.title: Adding Columns
topics.simple: Naye column ko nullable ya default ke saath add karo.
topics.pro: Adding a nullable column is cheap; adding NOT NULL with a volatile default can rewrite or lock the table.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS email TEXT;

topics.title: Dropping Columns
topics.simple: Column drop karne se pehle usage check karo.
topics.pro: Dropping a column breaks dependent code and views, so expand-contract and deprecate first.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS legacy_email;

topics.title: Renaming
topics.simple: Rename ko expand-contract se karo.
topics.pro: Renaming a column or table breaks old code; add the new name, dual-write, migrate readers, then remove the old one.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students RENAME COLUMN email TO contact_email;

topics.title: Backfills
topics.simple: Backfill data ko batches me karo.
topics.pro: A backfill updates existing rows in small batches to avoid long locks and huge transactions.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET email = 'unknown@example.com' WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000 AND email IS NULL;

topics.title: Online Migrations
topics.simple: Live traffic ke saath migration plan karo.
topics.pro: Online migrations avoid long exclusive locks and keep the old and new shapes compatible during rollout.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_email ON students (email);

topics.title: Locks
topics.simple: Migrations locks ko samajh kar chalao.
topics.pro: ALTER TABLE often takes a lock that blocks reads or writes; check lock levels and set lock_timeout.

example.sql: SET lock_timeout = '5s';

topics.title: Transactions
topics.simple: Transactional DDL use karo jahan possible ho.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a failed migration can roll back cleanly; concurrent index builds are an exception.

topics.title: Rollbacks
topics.simple: Rollback plan deploy se pehle likho.
topics.pro: A rollback plan covers code, schema and data, and is tested before production.

example.sql:
-- down migration
ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS email;

topics.title: Data Migrations
topics.simple: Schema change ke saath data transform karo.
topics.pro: Data migrations move or reshape values, often in batches with validation before and after.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 0 WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: Zero-Downtime
topics.simple: Expand, migrate, contract sequence follow karo.
topics.pro: Zero-downtime changes add compatible structures, migrate data and readers, then remove the old structures.

example.sql: -- 1 add new column, 2 backfill, 3 switch code, 4 drop old

topics.title: Expand and Contract
topics.simple: Compatibility window rakho.
topics.pro: The expand-contract pattern keeps old and new schemas working together during deployment.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN contact_email TEXT;

topics.title: Testing Migrations
topics.simple: Migrations ko real data copy par test karo.
topics.pro: Test on a production-like snapshot, measure lock time and verify both up and down paths.

example.sql: -- run migration against a staging snapshot

topics.title: Migration Tools
topics.simple: Tool version, lock aur transaction behavior samjho.
topics.pro: Tools such as Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic and Prisma differ in transaction handling, locking and rollback support.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY version;

topics.title: Production Checklist
topics.simple: Backup, lock timeout, monitoring aur rollback ready rakho.
topics.pro: A production migration checklist covers backup, compatibility, lock timeouts, observability and a tested rollback.

example.sql:
SET statement_timeout = '30s';
SET lock_timeout = '5s';

topics.title: Common Migration Errors
topics.simple: Long locks, missing defaults aur irreversible drops common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are rewriting a large table, adding NOT NULL without a backfill, and dropping a column still used by old code.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS email TEXT;

topics.title: Practical Migration
topics.simple: Add a column, backfill, constrain and switch code.
topics.pro: A practical migration adds a nullable column, backfills in batches, adds the constraint, deploys code and removes the old path.

example.sql:
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS contact_email TEXT;
UPDATE students SET contact_email = email WHERE contact_email IS NULL;

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Online Migrations in a production query.
interview.answer: Online migrations avoid long exclusive locks and keep the old and new shapes compatible during rollout. Key rules: Use concurrent index builds. Avoid table rewrites. Deploy compatible code.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Locks in a production query.
interview.answer: ALTER TABLE often takes a lock that blocks reads or writes; check lock levels and set lock_timeout. Key rules: Know the lock level. Set lock_timeout. Run at low traffic.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Transactions in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a failed migration can roll back cleanly; concurrent index builds are an exception. Key rules: Wrap in a transaction. Check tool behavior. Avoid long transactions.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Rollbacks in a production query.
interview.answer: A rollback plan covers code, schema and data, and is tested before production. Key rules: Test the down migration. Keep backups. Know the recovery time.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Data Migrations in a production query.
interview.answer: Data migrations move or reshape values, often in batches with validation before and after. Key rules: Validate before. Transform in batches. Verify counts.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Zero-Downtime in a production query.
interview.answer: Zero-downtime changes add compatible structures, migrate data and readers, then remove the old structures. Key rules: Expand. Dual-write. Migrate. Contract.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Expand and Contract in a production query.
interview.answer: The expand-contract pattern keeps old and new schemas working together during deployment. Key rules: Add before removing. Support both readers. Remove after verification.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Testing Migrations in a production query.
interview.answer: Test on a production-like snapshot, measure lock time and verify both up and down paths. Key rules: Use realistic data. Measure duration. Test rollback.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Migration Tools in a production query.
interview.answer: Tools such as Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic and Prisma differ in transaction handling, locking and rollback support. Key rules: Know the tool. Review generated SQL. Keep migrations in version control.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Production Checklist in a production query.
interview.answer: A production migration checklist covers backup, compatibility, lock timeouts, observability and a tested rollback. Key rules: Backup first. Set lock_timeout. Watch errors. Have a rollback.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Common Migration Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are rewriting a large table, adding NOT NULL without a backfill, and dropping a column still used by old code. Key rules: Avoid rewrites. Backfill first. Deprecate before dropping.

interview.q: Module 31 · Explain Practical Migration in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical migration adds a nullable column, backfills in batches, adds the constraint, deploys code and removes the old path. Key rules: Add nullable. Backfill. Constrain. Deploy. Clean up.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Migration Basics matter?
logic.answer: A migration is a versioned, repeatable change applied in order to every environment. One change per migration. Version the file. Apply in order.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Versioned Migrations matter?
logic.answer: A migration tool records applied versions so each change runs once per environment. Use numeric prefixes. Store applied versions. Never edit applied migrations.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Up and Down matter?
logic.answer: An up migration applies the change and a down migration reverses it when safe. Write both directions. Test the down path. Some data changes are irreversible.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Idempotency matter?
logic.answer: Idempotent migrations use IF NOT EXISTS and guards so a retry does not fail halfway. Use IF NOT EXISTS. Guard data changes. Record completion.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Adding Columns matter?
logic.answer: Adding a nullable column is cheap; adding NOT NULL with a volatile default can rewrite or lock the table. Add nullable first. Backfill separately. Add NOT NULL last.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Dropping Columns matter?
logic.answer: Dropping a column breaks dependent code and views, so expand-contract and deprecate first. Search usage. Deploy code first. Drop after a grace period.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Renaming matter?
logic.answer: Renaming a column or table breaks old code; add the new name, dual-write, migrate readers, then remove the old one. Add new. Dual-write. Migrate readers. Remove old.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Backfills matter?
logic.answer: A backfill updates existing rows in small batches to avoid long locks and huge transactions. Batch by key. Commit each batch. Make it resumable.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Online Migrations matter?
logic.answer: Online migrations avoid long exclusive locks and keep the old and new shapes compatible during rollout. Use concurrent index builds. Avoid table rewrites. Deploy compatible code.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Locks matter?
logic.answer: ALTER TABLE often takes a lock that blocks reads or writes; check lock levels and set lock_timeout. Know the lock level. Set lock_timeout. Run at low traffic.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Transactions matter?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a failed migration can roll back cleanly; concurrent index builds are an exception. Wrap in a transaction. Check tool behavior. Avoid long transactions.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Rollbacks matter?
logic.answer: A rollback plan covers code, schema and data, and is tested before production. Test the down migration. Keep backups. Know the recovery time.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Data Migrations matter?
logic.answer: Data migrations move or reshape values, often in batches with validation before and after. Validate before. Transform in batches. Verify counts.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Zero-Downtime matter?
logic.answer: Zero-downtime changes add compatible structures, migrate data and readers, then remove the old structures. Expand. Dual-write. Migrate. Contract.

logic.q: Module 31 · Why does Expand and Contract matter?
logic.answer: The expand-contract pattern keeps old and new schemas working together during deployment. Add before removing. Support both readers. Remove after verification.

debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT md5(random()::text);
debug.error: A volatile default can rewrite the table under a lock

debug.title: Non-concurrent index
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.error: A normal build blocks writes

debug.title: Drop before code
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN email;
debug.fix: Deploy code that no longer reads email, wait, then drop the column.
debug.error: Old application instances still query email

debug.title: Missing IF NOT EXISTS
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS email TEXT;
debug.error: column "email" of relation "students" already exists

debug.title: Backfill in one transaction
debug.broken: UPDATE students SET email = 'unknown@example.com' WHERE email IS NULL;
debug.fix: Batch by id and commit each batch.
debug.error: A huge transaction holds locks and bloats WAL

debug.title: Rename breaks readers
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students RENAME COLUMN email TO contact_email;
debug.fix: Add contact_email, dual-write, migrate readers, then remove email.
debug.error: Old code cannot find email

debug.title: Lock timeout missing
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;
debug.fix:
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;
debug.error: The migration can wait behind a long transaction

debug.title: Irreversible down
debug.broken: -- down: DROP TABLE students;
debug.fix: -- down: DROP COLUMN email;
debug.error: The rollback destroys data

debug.title: Concurrent in transaction
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_email ON students (email);
debug.error: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block

debug.title: No verification
debug.broken: Run the migration and deploy immediately.
debug.fix: Verify row counts, constraints and application errors before removing the old path.
debug.error: The change may be silently incomplete

modules.title: Backup, Restore and Recovery
modules.goal: Recover data predictably with tested backups and measured targets.

topics.title: Backup Types
topics.simple: Logical aur physical backups alag use cases ke liye hain.
topics.pro: Logical backups export SQL or archive data, while physical backups copy database files and WAL for exact recovery.
points: Physical is faster for large databases.

example.sql: pg_dump -Fc brocode > brocode.dump

topics.title: Logical Backup
topics.simple: Logical backup objects ko export karta hai.
topics.pro: pg_dump exports schema and data in a portable format that can restore into another cluster.

example.sql: pg_dump -Fc -f brocode.dump brocode

topics.title: Physical Backup
topics.simple: Physical backup data files aur WAL copy karta hai.
topics.pro: A physical backup copies the cluster’s data files and requires WAL for consistency and point-in-time recovery.

example.sql: pg_basebackup -D /backup/base -Ft -z -P

topics.title: pg_dump
topics.simple: pg_dump logical backup tool hai.
topics.pro: pg_dump supports plain SQL, custom, directory and tar formats, with compression and selective objects.

example.sql: pg_dump -Fc -f brocode.dump brocode

topics.title: pg_restore
topics.simple: pg_restore custom dump restore karta hai.
topics.pro: pg_restore can restore selectively, run in parallel and create objects in a target database.

example.sql: pg_restore -d brocode_restore -j 4 brocode.dump

topics.title: WAL
topics.simple: WAL changes ka ordered log hai.
topics.pro: Write-ahead logging records changes before data pages, enabling crash recovery and replication.

example.sql: SHOW wal_level;

topics.title: PITR
topics.simple: Point-in-time recovery WAL replay se hota hai.
topics.pro: PITR restores a base backup and replays WAL up to a target time or LSN.

example.sql: restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'

topics.title: RPO and RTO
topics.simple: RPO data loss bound hai; RTO downtime bound.
topics.pro: Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable data loss, and recovery time objective is the maximum acceptable downtime.

example.sql: -- RPO 5 minutes, RTO 30 minutes

topics.title: Restore Testing
topics.simple: Backup tabhi useful hai jab restore test ho.
topics.pro: A backup is unproven until a restore has been timed and verified against known data.

example.sql: pg_restore -d brocode_test brocode.dump

topics.title: Retention
topics.simple: Backups ko policy ke hisaab se rakho.
topics.pro: Retention balances recovery needs, storage cost and compliance, with daily, weekly and monthly tiers.

example.sql: -- keep 7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly

topics.title: Encryption
topics.simple: Backups ko encrypt karo.
topics.pro: Backups contain sensitive data and must be encrypted at rest and in transit, with keys managed separately.

example.sql: pg_dump -Fc brocode | gpg -c > brocode.dump.gpg

topics.title: Backup Monitoring
topics.simple: Backup success aur age monitor karo.
topics.pro: Monitoring catches failed jobs, stale backups and storage exhaustion before a recovery is needed.

example.sql: SELECT now() - max(completed_at) AS backup_age FROM backups;
example.output: The age of the latest backup.

topics.title: Common Backup Errors
topics.simple: Untested restores, missing WAL aur wrong permissions common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are never testing a restore, archiving WAL to a full disk and restoring with insufficient privileges.

example.sql: pg_restore -l brocode.dump | head

topics.title: Partial Restore
topics.simple: Selective restore se ek table ya schema lao.
topics.pro: pg_restore -t or -n restores selected tables or schemas from a custom dump.

example.sql: pg_restore -d brocode_restore -t students brocode.dump

topics.title: Backup Strategy
topics.simple: Full, incremental aur WAL archive ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical strategy uses periodic full backups, continuous WAL archiving and regular restore drills.

example.sql: -- weekly base backup plus continuous WAL archiving

topics.title: Recovery Drill
topics.simple: Recovery ko timed practice banao.
topics.pro: A recovery drill restores into an isolated environment, measures RTO and validates application queries.

example.sql:
createdb brocode_drill
pg_restore -d brocode_drill brocode.dump

topics.title: Disaster Recovery
topics.simple: Region ya provider failure ke liye plan banao.
topics.pro: Disaster recovery covers off-site copies, alternate infrastructure and clear ownership for recovery decisions.

example.sql: -- replicate backups to a second region

topics.title: Backup Security
topics.simple: Backups least privilege aur audit ke saath protect karo.
topics.pro: Restrict who can read backups, audit access and separate backup credentials from application credentials.

example.sql: REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION pg_read_file(text) FROM PUBLIC;

topics.title: Restore Verification
topics.simple: Restore ke baad counts aur constraints check karo.
topics.pro: Verification compares row counts, checks constraints and runs representative queries against the restored database.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;

topics.title: Practical Recovery Plan
topics.simple: Backup, WAL, restore test aur runbook ready rakho.
topics.pro: A production recovery plan documents the schedule, retention, encryption, restore steps, owners and measured targets.

example.sql: pg_dump -Fc -f /backups/brocode.dump brocode

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain WAL in a production query.
interview.answer: Write-ahead logging records changes before data pages, enabling crash recovery and replication. Key rules: WAL is required for durability. It enables PITR. Archive it continuously.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain PITR in a production query.
interview.answer: PITR restores a base backup and replays WAL up to a target time or LSN. Key rules: Restore the base. Configure recovery target. Replay WAL.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain RPO and RTO in a production query.
interview.answer: Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable data loss, and recovery time objective is the maximum acceptable downtime. Key rules: RPO drives backup frequency. RTO drives restore speed. Measure both.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Restore Testing in a production query.
interview.answer: A backup is unproven until a restore has been timed and verified against known data. Key rules: Restore regularly. Measure duration. Verify row counts.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Retention in a production query.
interview.answer: Retention balances recovery needs, storage cost and compliance, with daily, weekly and monthly tiers. Key rules: Define retention. Automate pruning. Keep off-site copies.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Encryption in a production query.
interview.answer: Backups contain sensitive data and must be encrypted at rest and in transit, with keys managed separately. Key rules: Encrypt dumps. Protect keys. Test decryption.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Backup Monitoring in a production query.
interview.answer: Monitoring catches failed jobs, stale backups and storage exhaustion before a recovery is needed. Key rules: Alert on failure. Track age. Track size.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Common Backup Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are never testing a restore, archiving WAL to a full disk and restoring with insufficient privileges. Key rules: Test restores. Monitor WAL. Check permissions.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Partial Restore in a production query.
interview.answer: pg_restore -t or -n restores selected tables or schemas from a custom dump. Key rules: Use -t for tables. Use -n for schemas. Verify dependencies.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Backup Strategy in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical strategy uses periodic full backups, continuous WAL archiving and regular restore drills. Key rules: Full base. WAL archive. Restore drills.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Recovery Drill in a production query.
interview.answer: A recovery drill restores into an isolated environment, measures RTO and validates application queries. Key rules: Isolate the target. Time the restore. Run checks.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Disaster Recovery in a production query.
interview.answer: Disaster recovery covers off-site copies, alternate infrastructure and clear ownership for recovery decisions. Key rules: Off-site copies. Alternate region. Named owners.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Backup Security in a production query.
interview.answer: Restrict who can read backups, audit access and separate backup credentials from application credentials. Key rules: Restrict access. Audit reads. Separate credentials.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Restore Verification in a production query.
interview.answer: Verification compares row counts, checks constraints and runs representative queries against the restored database. Key rules: Compare counts. Validate constraints. Run smoke queries.

interview.q: Module 32 · Explain Practical Recovery Plan in a production query.
interview.answer: A production recovery plan documents the schedule, retention, encryption, restore steps, owners and measured targets. Key rules: Schedule backups. Archive WAL. Test restores. Document the runbook.

logic.q: Module 32 · Why does Logical Backup matter?

logic.q: Module 32 · Why does Physical Backup matter?

logic.q: Module 32 · Why does pg_dump matter?

modules.title: Replication and High Availability
modules.goal: Keep a second copy ready and understand lag, failover and split-brain risks.

topics.title: Replication Basics
topics.simple: Replication data ko doosre node par copy karta hai.
topics.pro: Replication streams changes from a primary to one or more replicas for availability and read scaling.

example.sql: SHOW wal_level;

topics.title: Streaming Replication
topics.simple: Streaming replication WAL continuously bhejta hai.
topics.pro: Physical streaming replication ships WAL records to a standby that applies them continuously.
points: Lag is measured in WAL bytes or time.

example.sql: SELECT application_name, state, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;

topics.title: Logical Replication
topics.simple: Logical replication selected changes publish karta hai.
topics.pro: Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes and applies them through publications and subscriptions.
points: It does not copy the whole cluster.

example.sql: CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE students, courses;

topics.title: Primary and Replica
topics.simple: Primary writes leta hai; replica read-only hota hai.
topics.pro: A hot standby accepts read-only queries while applying WAL, so reporting can be isolated from write load.

example.sql: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

topics.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous
topics.simple: Sync replication commit wait karta hai; async nahi.
topics.pro: Synchronous replication waits for a standby acknowledgement before commit, trading latency for lower data loss.
points: Sync can block writes if the standby is slow.

example.sql: synchronous_commit = on

topics.title: Failover
topics.simple: Failover replica ko primary banata hai.
topics.pro: Failover promotes a standby when the primary fails, ideally through an orchestrator that fences the old primary.

example.sql: SELECT pg_promote();

topics.title: Replication Lag
topics.simple: Lag replica ki primary se doori batata hai.
topics.pro: Lag is the delay between a primary commit and its visibility on a replica, measured in time or LSN.

example.sql: SELECT client_addr, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

topics.title: Read Scaling
topics.simple: Replicas read traffic distribute karte hain.
topics.pro: Read replicas offload reporting and read-heavy endpoints, but applications must tolerate stale reads.
points: Do not send writes to replicas.
Handle lag-sensitive reads on the primary.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students;
example.output: A read that can run on a replica.

topics.title: Promotion
topics.simple: Promotion replica ko writable banata hai.
topics.pro: Promotion ends recovery and makes the standby a primary; it must be coordinated with client routing and fencing.

example.sql: SELECT pg_promote(true, 60);

topics.title: Split Brain
topics.simple: Split brain do primaries ko accept karne ki state hai.
topics.pro: Split brain happens when the old primary and the promoted standby both accept writes, causing divergent data.

example.sql: -- Fence the old primary before promotion

topics.title: Conflict Handling
topics.simple: Logical replication conflicts resolve karne padte hain.
topics.pro: Logical replication can conflict on primary keys or constraints; the subscription can stop or skip depending on configuration.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_subscription;

topics.title: Replication Slots
topics.simple: Slot WAL retention ko control karta hai.
topics.pro: A replication slot prevents WAL removal until the consumer catches up, which protects replicas but can fill disk.

example.sql: SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn FROM pg_replication_slots;

topics.title: Monitoring Replication
topics.simple: Lag, state aur slots monitor karo.
topics.pro: Monitoring tracks replication state, lag, slot retention and failover readiness.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication;

topics.title: Failover Testing
topics.simple: Failover ko regularly test karo.
topics.pro: A failover drill measures promotion time, application reconnection and data loss against RTO and RPO.

example.sql: SELECT pg_promote();

topics.title: Read-Your-Writes
topics.simple: Lag-sensitive reads primary se karo.
topics.pro: After a write, a replica may not yet show it; route that user’s next read to the primary or wait for the LSN.

example.sql: SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

topics.title: Connection Routing
topics.simple: Clients ko primary aur replicas ke behes route karo.
topics.pro: A router or load balancer sends writes to the primary and reads to replicas, with health checks and failover awareness.

example.sql: -- primary: db-primary:5432, replica: db-replica:5432

topics.title: Common Replication Errors
topics.simple: Lag, full disk aur split brain common failures hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are an inactive slot filling disk, a replica promoted while the old primary still writes, and reads routed to a lagging replica.

example.sql: SELECT slot_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots;

topics.title: High Availability Design
topics.simple: HA ke liye redundancy, health checks aur failover chahiye.
topics.pro: High availability combines replicas, automated health checks, quorum and tested failover, not just a standby.

example.sql: -- primary plus synchronous standby plus witness

topics.title: Backup vs Replica
topics.simple: Replica backup nahi hai.
topics.pro: A replica protects availability but does not protect against accidental deletes, corruption or ransomware without separate backups.

example.sql: -- Keep a separate encrypted backup even with replicas

topics.title: Practical HA Runbook
topics.simple: Detect, fence, promote, redirect, verify.
topics.pro: A runbook makes failover deterministic: detect the failure, fence the old primary, promote the standby, redirect clients and verify writes.

example.sql: SELECT pg_promote();

interview.answer: Replication streams changes from a primary to one or more replicas for availability and read scaling. Key rules: Primary accepts writes. Replicas receive changes. Replication is not backup.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Streaming Replication in a production query.
interview.answer: Physical streaming replication ships WAL records to a standby that applies them continuously. Key rules: It copies the cluster. It supports hot standby reads. Lag is measured in WAL bytes or time.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Logical Replication in a production query.
interview.answer: Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes and applies them through publications and subscriptions. Key rules: It is table-level. It can cross versions. It does not copy the whole cluster.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Primary and Replica in a production query.
interview.answer: A hot standby accepts read-only queries while applying WAL, so reporting can be isolated from write load. Key rules: Writes go to the primary. Replicas can serve reads. Replica reads can be stale.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Synchronous vs Asynchronous in a production query.
interview.answer: Synchronous replication waits for a standby acknowledgement before commit, trading latency for lower data loss. Key rules: Sync reduces RPO. Async is faster. Sync can block writes if the standby is slow.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Failover in a production query.
interview.answer: Failover promotes a standby when the primary fails, ideally through an orchestrator that fences the old primary. Key rules: Promote the standby. Redirect clients. Prevent split brain.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Replication Lag in a production query.
interview.answer: Lag is the delay between a primary commit and its visibility on a replica, measured in time or LSN. Key rules: Lag grows under load. Read-your-writes can fail. Monitor continuously.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Read Scaling in a production query.
interview.answer: Read replicas offload reporting and read-heavy endpoints, but applications must tolerate stale reads. Key rules: Route reads deliberately. Do not send writes to replicas. Handle lag-sensitive reads on the primary.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Promotion in a production query.
interview.answer: Promotion ends recovery and makes the standby a primary; it must be coordinated with client routing and fencing. Key rules: Promote once. Fence the old primary. Update connection strings.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Split Brain in a production query.
interview.answer: Split brain happens when the old primary and the promoted standby both accept writes, causing divergent data. Key rules: Use fencing. Use a quorum. Reconcile carefully.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Conflict Handling in a production query.
interview.answer: Logical replication can conflict on primary keys or constraints; the subscription can stop or skip depending on configuration. Key rules: Monitor conflicts. Design keys carefully. Decide skip versus stop.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Replication Slots in a production query.
interview.answer: A replication slot prevents WAL removal until the consumer catches up, which protects replicas but can fill disk. Key rules: Monitor slot lag. Drop unused slots. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Monitoring Replication in a production query.
interview.answer: Monitoring tracks replication state, lag, slot retention and failover readiness. Key rules: Track pg_stat_replication. Track slot size. Alert on lag.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Failover Testing in a production query.
interview.answer: A failover drill measures promotion time, application reconnection and data loss against RTO and RPO. Key rules: Schedule drills. Measure RTO. Verify data.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Read-Your-Writes in a production query.
interview.answer: After a write, a replica may not yet show it; route that user’s next read to the primary or wait for the LSN. Key rules: Track write LSN. Route sensitive reads. Do not assume zero lag.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Connection Routing in a production query.
interview.answer: A router or load balancer sends writes to the primary and reads to replicas, with health checks and failover awareness. Key rules: Separate endpoints. Health-check nodes. Update routes on promotion.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Common Replication Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are an inactive slot filling disk, a replica promoted while the old primary still writes, and reads routed to a lagging replica. Key rules: Monitor slots. Fence promotions. Measure lag.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain High Availability Design in a production query.
interview.answer: High availability combines replicas, automated health checks, quorum and tested failover, not just a standby. Key rules: Redundant nodes. Health checks. Automated promotion. Client redirect.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Backup vs Replica in a production query.
interview.answer: A replica protects availability but does not protect against accidental deletes, corruption or ransomware without separate backups. Key rules: Replicas replicate mistakes. Keep independent backups. Test restores.

interview.q: Module 33 · Explain Practical HA Runbook in a production query.
interview.answer: A runbook makes failover deterministic: detect the failure, fence the old primary, promote the standby, redirect clients and verify writes. Key rules: Detect. Fence. Promote. Redirect. Verify.

debug.title: Writes on replica
debug.broken: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Zara');
debug.fix: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Zara') on the primary.
debug.error: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

debug.title: Replica lag read
debug.broken: Write on primary, immediately read the same row from a replica.
debug.fix: Read from the primary until the replica reaches the write LSN.
debug.error: The replica may not have the row yet

debug.title: Inactive slot
debug.broken: SELECT slot_name FROM pg_replication_slots;
debug.fix: Drop the unused slot or restore its consumer, then monitor retained WAL.
debug.error: WAL accumulates until the disk fills

debug.title: Split brain
debug.broken: Promote the standby while the old primary is still reachable.
debug.fix: Fence the old primary first, then promote.
debug.error: Two nodes accept writes

debug.title: Async data loss
debug.broken: synchronous_commit = off
debug.fix: Use synchronous replication for data that cannot be lost.
debug.error: A crash can lose recent commits

debug.title: Replica as backup
debug.broken: Delete the primary table and rely on the replica.
debug.fix: Restore from a separate backup.
debug.error: The delete replicates to the standby

debug.title: Slot disk growth
debug.broken: max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1
debug.fix: Set a bound and alert on retained WAL.
debug.error: A stalled consumer can fill the disk

debug.title: Wrong endpoint
debug.broken: Application writes to db-replica:5432.
debug.fix: Route writes to db-primary:5432.
debug.error: read-only transaction errors

debug.title: Promotion without redirect
debug.broken: SELECT pg_promote();
debug.fix: Promote, then update the application endpoint and verify writes.
debug.error: Clients still connect to the old primary

debug.title: Logical conflict
debug.broken: Subscription stops on a duplicate primary key.
debug.fix: Resolve the conflicting row and restart the subscription with a documented policy.
debug.error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint

modules.title: Analytics and Reporting
modules.goal: Turn transactional rows into cohorts, funnels, retention and time-series reports.

topics.title: Reporting SQL
topics.simple: Reporting queries business questions ko rows me badalte hain.
topics.pro: A reporting query defines the grain, filters the population, aggregates the measure and orders the result.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id ORDER BY enrolled DESC;

topics.title: Cohort Analysis
topics.simple: Cohort users ko shared start period me group karta hai.
topics.pro: A cohort groups entities by their first event period and tracks later behavior within each cohort.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(enrolled_on)) AS cohort, student_id FROM enrollments GROUP BY student_id;

topics.title: Funnel Analysis
topics.simple: Funnel steps ke conversions count karta hai.
topics.pro: A funnel counts how many entities reach each step, usually with conditional aggregation or self-joins.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) FILTER (WHERE course_id = 10) AS step1 FROM enrollments;

topics.title: Retention
topics.simple: Retention wapas aane wale users count karta hai.
topics.pro: Retention compares a cohort’s later activity with its original size, often by period.

example.sql: SELECT student_id, COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) AS courses FROM enrollments GROUP BY student_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) > 1;
example.output: Students with more than one course.

topics.title: Time Series
topics.simple: Time series periods ke measures dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Time-series reports bucket dates with DATE_TRUNC and fill missing periods when the chart requires continuity.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

topics.title: Pivot with CASE
topics.simple: CASE se rows ko columns me pivot karo.
topics.pro: Conditional aggregation pivots categories into columns without a dedicated pivot operator.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE enrolled_on >= DATE '2026-01-01') AS recent, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE enrolled_on < DATE '2026-01-01') AS older FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
example.output: Course rows with recent and older count columns.

topics.title: Crosstab
topics.simple: Crosstab rows aur columns ka matrix banata hai.
topics.pro: The tablefunc crosstab function turns long category rows into a wide matrix.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM crosstab('SELECT course_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM enrolled_on)::int, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2') AS ct(course_id int, y2025 bigint, y2026 bigint);

topics.title: Running Totals
topics.simple: Running totals cumulative progress dikhate hain.
topics.pro: A window SUM ordered by time produces cumulative totals for charts and targets.

example.sql: SELECT enrolled_on, COUNT(*) AS day_count, SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (ORDER BY enrolled_on) AS running FROM enrollments GROUP BY enrolled_on ORDER BY enrolled_on;

topics.title: Percent of Total
topics.simple: Percent of total share dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Divide the group measure by a window total to show each row’s share of the whole.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

topics.title: Ranking
topics.simple: Ranking report ko ordered priority deta hai.
topics.pro: Window ranking orders groups by a measure while preserving every group row.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rank FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

topics.title: Period Comparisons
topics.simple: Previous period se compare karo.
topics.pro: LAG or self-joins compare a period with the prior period, producing growth and deltas.

example.sql: SELECT month, total, total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta FROM monthly_counts;

topics.title: Cohort Retention Table
topics.simple: Cohort ke har period ki retention calculate karo.
topics.pro: A cohort retention table joins each entity’s cohort month to later activity months and counts distinct returning entities.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', e.enrolled_on) AS activity_month, COUNT(DISTINCT e.student_id) AS active FROM enrollments e GROUP BY activity_month ORDER BY activity_month;

topics.title: Common Reporting Errors
topics.simple: Wrong grain, double counting aur timezone bugs common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are joining one-to-many tables before aggregating, counting rows instead of entities, and mixing time zones.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) FROM enrollments;

topics.title: Reporting Performance
topics.simple: Pre-aggregate aur index reporting queries.
topics.pro: Reports often scan large ranges; pre-aggregation, materialized views and date indexes reduce repeated work.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date ON enrollments (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Dashboard Queries
topics.simple: Dashboard ke liye fast, stable queries chahiye.
topics.pro: Dashboard queries should be bounded, indexed and cached where freshness allows.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE enrolled_on >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

topics.title: Export Queries
topics.simple: Export ke liye deterministic ordering aur columns do.
topics.pro: Exports need stable column names, explicit ordering and no accidental row limits.

example.sql: SELECT student_id, course_id, enrolled_on FROM enrollments ORDER BY enrolled_on, student_id;

topics.title: Data Quality Checks
topics.simple: Reporting se pehle data quality check karo.
topics.pro: Checks catch NULLs, duplicates, orphan keys and impossible values before they distort a report.

example.sql: SELECT student_id, course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

topics.title: Timezone Reporting
topics.simple: Timestamps ko ek timezone me report karo.
topics.pro: TIMESTAMPTZ stores instants; convert to the reporting time zone before truncating dates.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', enrolled_on AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata') AS day, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY day;

topics.title: Narrative Metrics
topics.simple: Metrics ke saath denominator aur definition do.
topics.pro: A trustworthy report states the denominator, the time window and the exact definition of each metric.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;
example.output: Passed and total with a clear denominator.

topics.title: Practical Dashboard
topics.simple: Cohort, funnel aur time series ko combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical dashboard query produces one row per period with counts, shares and comparisons, bounded to a recent window.

example.sql: WITH monthly AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month) SELECT month, total, total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

learn.answer: Data Quality Checks: Reporting se pehle data quality check karo.
learn.why: Checks catch NULLs, duplicates, orphan keys and impossible values before they distort a report.

learn.q: Module 34 · Timezone Reporting: what is the main purpose?

Time Series: Time series periods ke measures dikhata hai.

Timezone Reporting: Timestamps ko ek timezone me report karo.
learn.answer: Timezone Reporting: Timestamps ko ek timezone me report karo.
learn.why: TIMESTAMPTZ stores instants; convert to the reporting time zone before truncating dates.

learn.q: Module 34 · Narrative Metrics: what is the main purpose?

learn.answer: Narrative Metrics: Metrics ke saath denominator aur definition do.
learn.why: A trustworthy report states the denominator, the time window and the exact definition of each metric.

learn.q: Module 34 · Practical Dashboard: what is the main purpose?
options: Common Reporting Errors: Wrong grain, double counting aur timezone bugs common errors hain.
Practical Dashboard: Cohort, funnel aur time series ko combine karo.

learn.answer: Practical Dashboard: Cohort, funnel aur time series ko combine karo.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Reporting SQL in a production query.
interview.answer: A reporting query defines the grain, filters the population, aggregates the measure and orders the result. Key rules: State the grain. Define the population. Choose the measure.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Cohort Analysis in a production query.
interview.answer: A cohort groups entities by their first event period and tracks later behavior within each cohort. Key rules: Define the cohort date. Group by cohort. Measure later activity.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Funnel Analysis in a production query.
interview.answer: A funnel counts how many entities reach each step, usually with conditional aggregation or self-joins. Key rules: Define ordered steps. Count distinct entities. Compare step counts.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Retention in a production query.
interview.answer: Retention compares a cohort’s later activity with its original size, often by period. Key rules: Define active. Fix the cohort. Calculate the ratio.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Time Series in a production query.
interview.answer: Time-series reports bucket dates with DATE_TRUNC and fill missing periods when the chart requires continuity. Key rules: Bucket the date. Aggregate the measure. Fill gaps explicitly.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Pivot with CASE in a production query.
interview.answer: Conditional aggregation pivots categories into columns without a dedicated pivot operator. Key rules: One CASE per column. Aggregate each CASE. Group by the row key.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Crosstab in a production query.
interview.answer: The tablefunc crosstab function turns long category rows into a wide matrix. Key rules: Enable tablefunc. Define row and category columns. Name the output columns.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Running Totals in a production query.
interview.answer: A window SUM ordered by time produces cumulative totals for charts and targets. Key rules: Order by the period. Use an unbounded frame. Partition when needed.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Percent of Total in a production query.
interview.answer: Divide the group measure by a window total to show each row’s share of the whole. Key rules: Use SUM(...) OVER (). Guard zero. Round for display.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Ranking in a production query.
interview.answer: Window ranking orders groups by a measure while preserving every group row. Key rules: Rank by the measure. Break ties. Filter after ranking.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Period Comparisons in a production query.
interview.answer: LAG or self-joins compare a period with the prior period, producing growth and deltas. Key rules: Order periods. Use LAG. Handle missing periods.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Cohort Retention Table in a production query.
interview.answer: A cohort retention table joins each entity’s cohort month to later activity months and counts distinct returning entities. Key rules: Cohort month. Activity month. Count distinct entities. Divide by cohort size.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Common Reporting Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are joining one-to-many tables before aggregating, counting rows instead of entities, and mixing time zones. Key rules: Check the grain. Count distinct entities. Normalize time zones.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Reporting Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Reports often scan large ranges; pre-aggregation, materialized views and date indexes reduce repeated work. Key rules: Filter on dates. Pre-aggregate. Refresh materialized views.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Dashboard Queries in a production query.
interview.answer: Dashboard queries should be bounded, indexed and cached where freshness allows. Key rules: Bound the date range. Limit rows. Cache or materialize.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Export Queries in a production query.
interview.answer: Exports need stable column names, explicit ordering and no accidental row limits. Key rules: Order explicitly. Select explicit columns. Avoid SELECT *.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Data Quality Checks in a production query.
interview.answer: Checks catch NULLs, duplicates, orphan keys and impossible values before they distort a report. Key rules: Check duplicates. Check orphans. Check ranges.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Timezone Reporting in a production query.
interview.answer: TIMESTAMPTZ stores instants; convert to the reporting time zone before truncating dates. Key rules: Store timestamptz. Convert at the boundary. Document the zone.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Narrative Metrics in a production query.
interview.answer: A trustworthy report states the denominator, the time window and the exact definition of each metric. Key rules: Define the metric. Show the denominator. State the window.

interview.q: Module 34 · Explain Practical Dashboard in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical dashboard query produces one row per period with counts, shares and comparisons, bounded to a recent window. Key rules: Bound the window. Use CTEs. Keep the grain explicit.

labs.title: Reporting SQL
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Reporting SQL.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id ORDER BY enrolled DESC;

labs.title: Cohort Analysis
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Cohort Analysis.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(enrolled_on)) AS cohort, student_id FROM enrollments GROUP BY student_id;

labs.title: Funnel Analysis
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Funnel Analysis.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) FILTER (WHERE course_id = 10) AS step1 FROM enrollments;

labs.title: Retention
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Retention.
labs.solution: SELECT student_id, COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) AS courses FROM enrollments GROUP BY student_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) > 1;
labs.expected: Students with more than one course.

labs.title: Time Series
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Time Series.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

labs.title: Pivot with CASE
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Pivot with CASE.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE enrolled_on >= DATE '2026-01-01') AS recent, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE enrolled_on < DATE '2026-01-01') AS older FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
labs.expected: Course rows with recent and older count columns.

labs.title: Crosstab
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Crosstab.
labs.solution: SELECT * FROM crosstab('SELECT course_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM enrolled_on)::int, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2') AS ct(course_id int, y2025 bigint, y2026 bigint);

labs.title: Running Totals
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Running Totals.
labs.solution: SELECT enrolled_on, COUNT(*) AS day_count, SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (ORDER BY enrolled_on) AS running FROM enrollments GROUP BY enrolled_on ORDER BY enrolled_on;

labs.title: Percent of Total
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Percent of Total.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

labs.title: Ranking
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Ranking.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rank FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

labs.title: Period Comparisons
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Period Comparisons.
labs.solution: SELECT month, total, total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta FROM monthly_counts;

labs.title: Cohort Retention Table
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Cohort Retention Table.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', e.enrolled_on) AS activity_month, COUNT(DISTINCT e.student_id) AS active FROM enrollments e GROUP BY activity_month ORDER BY activity_month;

labs.title: Common Reporting Errors
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Common Reporting Errors.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) FROM enrollments;

labs.title: Reporting Performance
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Reporting Performance.
labs.solution: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date ON enrollments (enrolled_on);

labs.title: Dashboard Queries
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Dashboard Queries.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE enrolled_on >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

labs.title: Export Queries
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Export Queries.
labs.solution: SELECT student_id, course_id, enrolled_on FROM enrollments ORDER BY enrolled_on, student_id;

labs.title: Data Quality Checks
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Data Quality Checks.
labs.solution: SELECT student_id, course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

labs.title: Timezone Reporting
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Timezone Reporting.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', enrolled_on AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata') AS day, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY day;

labs.title: Narrative Metrics
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Narrative Metrics.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;
labs.expected: Passed and total with a clear denominator.

labs.title: Practical Dashboard
labs.task: Write a SQL example that demonstrates Practical Dashboard.
labs.solution: WITH monthly AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month) SELECT month, total, total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta FROM monthly ORDER BY month;
